Rich in dung-fuel, fruit-bearing, the ancestral share and refreshment — in our home, by the radiance of the udumbara, may Dhātṛ bestow prosperity upon me.
Whatever foods and saps belong to the two-footed and the four-footed — I seize the abundance of all those, bearing the udumbara amulet.
I have grasped round about the prosperity of the livestock — of the four-footed, the two-footed, and whatever is grain. May Bṛhaspati and Savitṛ bestow upon me the milk of the cattle and the sap of the herbs.
May I be the overlord of the cattle; may the Lord of Prosperity place prosperity in me. May the udumbara amulet bestow wealth upon me.
Let the udumbara amulet come to me with offspring and with wealth. Quickened by Indra, may the amulet come to me together with vital lustre.
The divine amulet, slayer of rivals, wealth-winning for the winning of wealth — may it bestow the abundance of livestock and food and the thriving of the cattle.
As you, O tree-lord, were born in the beginning together with prosperity, so may Sarasvatī establish for me the thriving of wealth.
May Sarasvatī bring wealth to me, the flourishing of milk and grain; and may Sinīvālī likewise bring it, and this udumbara amulet too.
You are the overlord of amulets, a bull; in you the Lord of Prosperity engendered prosperity. In you are all these prizes and all these riches — O udumbara, you: overpower far from us the demon of niggardliness, the want of wisdom, and hunger.
You are the headman, consecrated to the office of headman — sprinkle me with vital lustre. You are radiance: hold radiance within me supremely. You are wealth: place wealth in me.
You are prosperity — anoint me thoroughly with prosperity; as the guardian of the household, make me the master of the house. O udumbara, you: bestow upon us wealth with all its heroes; I release you for the increase of riches.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
This udumbara amulet, heroic, is bound on for the hero. May it make our acquisition sweet and honeyed, and may it bestow upon us wealth with all its heroes.
May we attain the favour of Bhaga the king, whom human beings invoke in many ways. He who acts in accordance with dharma wins Bhaga as his own — may He make us fortunate among the people.
Awakening to the east, may we behold the divine Dawn shining forth. The bright one facing toward us, bringing Bhaga together with wealth — may Aditi come to us bearing good fortune.
May Bhaga today, at dawn, bestow upon us favour and lead us here along the path of the gods. May auspicious benevolence come toward us; and then may our kindling-fire glow bright with Bhaga.
By Bhaga's impulsion, splendid in lustre, may I speak a speech directed by Sarasvatī, honeyed. May what is given by Bhaga come to me in abundance, so that radiant with lustre I may speak in the assembly.
May Bhaga protect me in cattle; may Bhaga protect me in grain. May Bhaga protect me in dice-play, in women; may Bhaga protect me with vital lustre.
May Bhaga protect me at evening; may Bhaga protect me through the night. May Bhaga come to me in the morning among those who lie down.
May Bhaga protect me at morning; may Bhaga protect me at midday. In the afternoon we wrap Bhaga around us like a garment.
Bhaga surpassing the gods, Bhaga surpassing men — from heaven, from earth, from the atmosphere I choose Bhaga. May He, O Agni, take delight in me; may He protect me with vital lustre.
Choosing Bhaga, they bear the bride to her home; proceeding onward they invoke Bhaga alone. May what is given by Bhaga come to me in abundance — all auspicious being, all benign riches.
With Bhaga we have come together with the gods — He who encompasses all these worlds. He goes about bestowing riches in many ways; may He bestow upon us whatever is most excellent.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Vāyu the Bhaga, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Agni — may the mistress of the field be easily invocable for us. He of the golden eye, the far-seer, the man-surveyor — come to us, accompanied by all.
Arise, O divine Sūrya, together with good fortune; together with the prize-winning strength of the bull, together with the means of protection.
[Colophon:] "With the golden one" — thus the single verse.
May the bull guard thee with cattle; may the stallion guard thee with prizes of victory. May Vāyu guard thee with sacred formulas; may Indra guard thee with powers of might.
May Soma guard thee with healing herbs; may the Sun guard thee with the lunar mansions. May the Moon guard thee with exhilarating draughts; may Vāta, the slayer of Vṛtra, protect thee with vital breath.
Three heavens, three earths, three atmospheres, four oceans — the waters call the threefold hymn-of-praise threefold; may they guard thee, threefold, with their threefold [powers].
Three vault-heavens, three oceans, three radiant [solar orbs], three [vault-dwelling] supporters; three Mātariśvans, three Suns — these guardians I arrange for thee.
With ghee I anoint thee thoroughly, O Agni, increasing thee with clarified butter. May the deceivers not harm the vital breath of Agni, of the Moon, of the Sun.
May deceivers not harm your in-breath, not your out-breath, not [your] vital heat. You brilliant gods, all-knowing ones, protect me with your divine [power].
With vital breath they unite Agni; Vāta is held together by vital breath. With vital breath the gods generated the Sun, who faces all directions.
Live with the life-span of those who have made long life; live long, do not die. Live by the vital breath of those endowed with self; do not come under the sway of Death.
The treasure laid away by the gods, which Indra found by the god-traveled paths — the waters guarded the gold with their threefold [power]; may they guard thee, threefold, with their threefold [powers].

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The thirty-three deities, along with three heroic powers, took delight and guarded [them] within the waters. Whatever gold rests upon this Moon — by that may this one accomplish heroic deeds.
You gods who are eleven in heaven — you divine ones, take pleasure in this oblation.
You gods who are eleven in the atmosphere — [take pleasure in this oblation].
You gods who are eleven on the earth — you divine ones, take pleasure in this oblation.
Free of rivals before us; behind us fearlessness has been made. May Savitṛ [guard] me from the south; from the north may Śacī's lord [guard me].
May the Ādityas protect me from the sky; may the fires protect me from the earth. May Indra and Agni protect me from the front; may the Aśvins grant me shelter on both sides. May Jātavedas protect me from the oblique [directions]; may those who created beings be my armor on all sides.
Those fires that have entered into the waters — the scalding [fever], the mind-slayer, the excavating [pain], the consuming [fire], the defiler of the self, the defiler of the body — these I now drive away. I expel sin; I expel falsehood.
From [the power of] non-being and of evil being, I expel evil dreaming. May Vasiṣṭha and Arundhatī protect me; may the litter-grass of Prajāpati [and] the hair-locks of Bṛhaspati [guard me].
An undimmed eye; well-hearing ears; my in-breath and out-breath unimpaired. May my heart not forsake old age for me; may I suffer no harm in my midst.
May the waters cleanse me from wrong-doing, from the misdeeds we have committed. May we go forth purified, risen up, with our bodies [restored].
May Vaiśvānara purify us with his rays; may Vāta, the swift one, [purify us] with vital breath and with reverences. May Heaven-and-Earth, abounding in milk, upholding cosmic order, worthy of sacrifice, purify me.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
May the Gārhapatya fires purify me; may the bold, god-summoning [fires] purify me. May the Śakvarī verses, borne on Soma's back, the purifying [streams], the swift ones, purify me.
Let him who is the Potṛ [priest] purify me, O god Savitṛ, with the great and loftiest [rites], even as [he purifies] the sky above.
May [Savitṛ] purify me with brahman-pressings; may he purify me with kingly pressings. A hundred purifying [filters] are spread out obliquely — with those may the god Savitṛ purify me.
May a hundred purifiers cleanse me, and a thousand waters at the flowing streams. I am purified as the waters [are pure], bright as Agni, clear-sighted as the Sun.
Those two wide-nostriled, life-drinking, Udumbara-hued messengers of Yama roam among the people — may those two grant back to us, for sight of the Sun, our vital breath here today, [bestowing] the auspicious.
We have reached the gods, we have reached the heavenly realm — we have reached the light, we have reached the light. You are Mahendra, Parameṣṭhin, Sumitrā, Viśvatomukha; may we never be sundered from your sight.
O you of wondrous greatness, rising today, smite down my rivals. Smite them by day with your rays; let Night slay them with darkness — may they go to the lowest darkness.
I turn in accordance with the course of Sūrya, I turn in accordance with the southward course. May I become radiant with the brilliance of Agni; may I become endowed with power through the might of Indra.
With the brilliance of Agni, with the might of Indra, with the splendor of Soma, with the efficacy of all the gods — I now wind round and bind away the luster, the radiance, the vital power, the life-breath, and the lifespan of that man, son of such a woman, from such a family.
(…) may he restrain his lifespan.
With the brilliance of Agni, with the might of Indra, with the splendor of Soma, with the efficacy of all the gods — I now take away and claim for myself the luster, the radiance, the vital power, the life-breath, and the lifespan of that man, son of such a woman, from such a family.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Having bound him in the noose of ill-fortune and entangled him with evil dreams, I place him within the gaping mouth of Death.
He who seeks to slay us — whether one of our own, or a stranger, or a rival kinsman — may Indra and Agni find his vital spots in his shoulders.
He who seeks to slay me when I am lying awake, and he who seeks to slay me when I am asleep — may Indra and Agni cut into his arms at the vital joints.
He who seeks to slay me while I am walking, while I am standing, or while I am sitting — may Indra and Agni discharge evil back upon him.
He who seeks to slay me with his eye, he who seeks to slay me with his mind, and he who seeks to slay me with his speech — may Indra and Agni carry away his sins from this place.
The piśāca, the yātudhāna, the flesh-devouring demon who seeks to slay me — may Indra and Agni pierce his head through.
He who seeks to slay me by means of sacred knowledge, by means of ascetic heat, and he who seeks to slay me by means of sacrifices — may Indra and Agni pierce him through and through in his heart.
He who seeks to slay my sacred power, my ascetic heat, my foremost strength — may Indra and Agni, both wrathful, shoot their envenomed arrows at him.
He who seeks to destroy my food, my vital sap, my foremost speech — may Indra and Agni hurl the śambaṭkāra curse at him.
He who seeks to destroy my lineage, my offspring, my sight, my hearing — may Indra and Agni find for him the divine weapon among the gods.
He who envies me my cattle, my horses, my men — may Indra and Agni find for him loss and ruin among the gods.
He who seeks to destroy my prosperity free from disease, my wealth, my lifespan — may Indra and Agni hurl the stone of heaven at him.
He who seeks to destroy my house, my assembly hall, my foremost glory — may Indra and Agni spread the sorcery-curse back through his own home.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
He who wishes upon me death and ill-fortune by day and by night — may Indra and Agni burn his own self with their flames.
He who seeks to destroy my in-breath, my out-breath, my foremost diffused breath — may Indra and Agni smite his breath with the breath-slayer.
He who has oppressed me through divine beings, through serpents, through lightning, through sacred lore — with Agastya as ally, may Indra and Agni slay him.
Let Agni Vaiśvānara, the bull of true might, burn that one utterly — he who regards me with ill intent and he who, knowing, seeks to harm me.
He who would harm me though I have not harmed him, and he who seeks to harm the one who seeks to harm — I place him between the fangs of Agni Vaiśvānara.
Let Heaven-and-Earth scorch him from every side; let him be flung down upon the heated cauldron. Let him be slain by Nirṛti's noose — he who devises evil against us.
These rivals, of dreadful aspect, hurled back by the counter-blow — may Indra and Agni cut them apart; let not one of them survive.
O counter-blow, strike back, smite back my hateful rivals. Severing their out-breath from their in-breath, cast those who hate me downward.
O Agni, those who seek to slay me, O Agni, those who hate me, O Agni, those who oppress me — smite the one dearest to them.
This one who hated me I have struck down, wrapped in blind darkness. Fall upon this one, O Mṛtyu — let not the great-bellied one be released from you.
Let Dyāvāpṛthivī — Heaven-and-Earth — bind themselves together, conquering for my kingdom, hurling the missile against enemies.
Let the two Winds, the Purifying Breezes, bind themselves together, conquering for my kingdom, hurling the missile against enemies.
Let Indrāgnī — Indra-and-Agni — bind themselves together, conquering for my kingdom, hurling the missile against enemies.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Let Mitrāvaruṇā — Mitra-and-Varuṇa — bind themselves together, conquering for my kingdom, hurling the missile against enemies.
Let Bhavāśarvā — Bhava-and-Śarva — bind themselves together, conquering for my kingdom, hurling the missile against enemies.
Let the two Aśvins bind themselves together, conquering for my kingdom, hurling the missile against enemies.
Let the Maruts bind themselves together, conquering for my kingdom, hurling the missile against enemies.
Let the Pitṛs — the Ancestral Fathers — bind themselves together, conquering for my kingdom, hurling the missile against enemies.
Let Sūrya-and-Candramās — Sun and Moon — bind themselves together, conquering for my kingdom, hurling the missile against enemies.
Let Day-and-Night bind themselves together, conquering for my kingdom, hurling the missile against enemies.
Let the Gandharvas and Apsarasas bind themselves together, conquering for my kingdom, hurling the missile against enemies.
Let the Serpents and the Puṇyajanas bind themselves together, conquering for my kingdom, hurling the missile against enemies.
Let the Forest-Trees (Vanaspatayaḥ) bind themselves together, conquering for my kingdom, hurling the missile against enemies.
Let the offspring of forest-trees (Vānaspatyāḥ) bind themselves together, conquering for my kingdom, hurling the missile against enemies.
Let the healing Plants (Oṣadhayaḥ) bind themselves together, conquering for my kingdom, hurling the missile against enemies.
Let the creeping herbs (Vīrudhaḥ) bind themselves together, conquering for my kingdom, hurling the missile against enemies.
O Bṛhaspati, bind yourself together, conquering for my kingdom, hurling the missile against enemies.
O Prajāpati, bind yourself together, conquering for my kingdom, hurling the missile against enemies.
O Parameṣṭhin, bind yourself together, conquering for my kingdom, hurling the missile against enemies.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Rise up, ye exalted ones; let all beings bind themselves together, conquering for my kingdom, hurling the missile against enemies.
Agni is the guardian; may he protect this army. O executor, stand by; may all heroes be mine.
Indra is the guardian; may he protect this army. O executor, stand by; may all heroes be mine.
Soma is the guardian; may he protect this army. O executor, stand by; may all heroes be mine.
Varuṇa is the guardian; may he protect this army. O executor, stand by; may all heroes be mine.
Vāyu is the guardian; may he protect this army. O executor, stand by; may all heroes be mine.
Tvaṣṭā is the guardian; may he protect this army. O executor, stand by; may all heroes be mine.
Dhātā is the guardian; may he protect this army. O executor, stand by; may all heroes be mine.
Savitā is the guardian; may he protect this army. O executor, stand by; may all heroes be mine.
Sūrya is the guardian; may he protect this army. O executor, stand by; may all heroes be mine.
Candramā — the Moon — is the guardian; may he protect this army. O executor, stand by; may all heroes be mine.
Day is the guardian — let it protect this army. O attendant, follow and stand firm; may all heroes be mine.
Night is the guardian — let her protect this army. O female attendant, follow and stand firm; may all heroes be mine.
Indrāṇī is the guardian — let her protect this army. O female attendant, follow and stand firm; may all heroes be mine.
Varuṇānī is the guardian — let her protect this army. O female attendant, follow and stand firm; may all heroes be mine.
Sinīvālī is the guardian — let her protect this army. O female attendant, follow and stand firm; may all heroes be mine.
Samudra is the guardian — let him protect this army. O attendant, follow and stand firm; may all heroes be mine.
Parjanya is the guardian — let him protect this army. O attendant, follow and stand firm; may all heroes be mine.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Bṛhaspati is the guardian — let him protect this army. O attendant, follow and stand firm; may all heroes be mine.
Prajāpati is the guardian — let him protect this army. O attendant, follow and stand firm; may all heroes be mine.
Parameṣṭhin is the guardian — let him protect this army. O attendant, follow and stand firm; may all heroes be mine.
The All-Gods are the guardians — let them protect this army. O attendants, follow and stand firm; may all heroes be mine.
I, the potent one, place an embryo in your womb for one who craves a bull-like male offspring; if, sustained by the gods, you do not obtain progeny nor a child.
May Dhātṛ grant you that; may Sinīvālī, may Varuṇānī bestow it; may Indrāṇī place in you a male son, one who bestows a hundredfold.
The embryo enclosed within your flanks has been fashioned as a male by a male; may he be born complete in all limbs, as fire arises from the two araṇī fire-sticks.
Bear a heroic, capable son; I make of you a good breeder, I render the unmated one subject. From your own blood let a potent embryo be formed.
May Tvaṣṭṛ fashion your offspring; may Dhātṛ establish a child for you; may Rākā sew with her needle — she who is sovereign of what has come to be and of the world, the goddess.
Sinīvālī, Anumati, Rākā, Guṅgu, and Sarasvatī — the divine consorts of the gods, those goddesses — and Indrāṇī I invoke for protection.
Unbroken in the egg, with a fully grown embryo, unharmed, a bearer of heroes — may she give birth, may she bring forth abundantly; may she become one blessed with many sons.
Release the embryo, place it — do not hold back, do not expel the blood; may the child be born undeficient, complete, unexhausted, uninjured, uncontaminated by Piśācas.
You sustain the embryo and the offspring of every form for the biped and the quadruped as they quicken; O Prajāpati, bull that roars and bears a mighty member, place the embryo in the bodies.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Roaring forth with his thunder, flashing, the purifying wind places the embryo with the plants; may Parjanya water this earth with seed, with the essences of waters, of plants, of cattle.
I lead to you the potent one who is Prajāpati of creatures; may he place in your womb the embryo in its due season, the offspring of noble birth.
Those potent ones who are creators of the embryo among those who come at the right season, guilt-sharing — those I summon for you; and may that prosper and be fulfilled for you.
From Agni, from Tvaṣṭṛ, from Varuṇa, from Indra, from Soma, from Bṛhaspati — for you who desire a son, I fashion offspring from the gods.
May it flow together from limb to limb; may it find its place in the womb; the offspring that lies in your flanks — may that seed of yours sprout forth.
From overeating, from indigestion, from distress, from failure — these engendered the disease viśara; this Indra, who has a thousandfold share, destroys the viśara for you.
That which is to be done, and that which has been done, that which is self-born, and that which is stolen — may the gods with Indra as chief destroy the viśara for you.
The arrow is the mother of viśara and its spreading; the bow is the father; the Ādityas are the sons — may the Ādityas destroy the viśara for you.
From the bowstring of the bow, from the arrow, from the arms of the prop; from the iron, from the horn, from the kurmalā — I destroy the viśara for you.
The alavatī with its ruru-skull head, and that arrow whose face is iron — to the divine arrow begotten of Parjanya's seed, make obeisance.
The herb that the Atris, the Āṅgirasas, and the Gotamas have known — with that herb Bharadvāja and Kaṇva destroy the viśara for you.
That which has spread from a woman's wound, that which has mounted over a man — the sinew weakened and afflicted together, that too we set right for you.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
As the wind drives away a cloud, I drive away the disease from your body all around; what they have made heavy upon you by speech, that we make light by the sacred verse; with this truth-utterance I destroy the viśara for you.
As a man is not always able to speak the truth — so too: the viṣkandha, the viśara that has gone away from you, the disease of wasting, the jambha, the hanugrābha, the śaṅkha — all these we drive away with the she-goat driven forth.
For the good of you all do I distribute the herbs for healing; those that are bringers of wealth, bringers of lasting life, able to carry a man across to safety.
Self-protecting, impelled by the gods, the herb made for long life — with that one, given by Indra, I destroy the viśara for you.
From the lazy one, from the condiment, from the wrapping, and from the leaf-holder; from the knot, from the bowstring, from the arrow — I destroy the viśara for you.
Fly away together, O viṣkandha, along with the bluejay and the kikidīvī bird; perish together with the rushing of the wind, together with the nihākā.
You are jaṅgiḍa; you are the protector, jaṅgiḍa; may jaṅgiḍa protect all that is ours — biped and quadruped.
The gṛtyas fifty-three in number, and the hundred who have fabricated kṛtyas — all of them jaṅgiḍa has made devoid of power and shorn of potency.
The powerless artificial reed, the seven powerless visrasas — drive away the hostility of jaṅgiḍa's adversary as one dispatches an arrow.
He is the destroyer of kṛtyā-sorcery; he is the destroyer of enmity as well; and mighty jaṅgiḍa shall carry our lives across to safety.
May that greatness of jaṅgiḍa protect us on all sides — he by whose might he has overpowered the viṣkandha and the saṃskanda with force upon force.
Having sought him eagerly, the gods generated him established upon the earth; him the ancient brahmin seers of the Āṅgirasa lineage too have known as such.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Let neither the older herbs surpass you, nor those that are new; thrust-aside-all, fierce jaṅgiḍa, all-protecting, most auspicious.
O revered jaṅgiḍa of immeasurable virility, with horse's hoof-prints — formerly, when you were fierce, Upendra gave you your virility.
Indeed, Indra placed fierce power in you, O lord of the forest; scattering all diseases, strike down the rākṣasas, O herb.
Aśarīka, viśarīka, balāsa, the disease of wasting, the takman that recurs each autumn — all these jaṅgiḍa has made powerless.
Invoking the name of Indra, the seers bestowed the jaṅgiḍa amulet; that which the gods fashioned at the outset as a remedy, a destroyer of viṣkandha.
May jaṅgiḍa protect us — guardian of wealth, like wealth itself; that which gods and brāhmaṇas fashioned as a shield on all sides, a slayer of the foe.
Those who come with malice in their hearts, with dreadful gaze, having wrought evil — them do thou, O thousand-eyed one, destroy with thy awakening power; thou art the all-encompassing guardian, O jaṅgiḍa.
Guard me from the sky, guard me from the earth, from the mid-air, guard me from the plants; guard me from what has come into being and from what is yet to be — may jaṅgiḍa protect us from every quarter and every direction.
The missiles fashioned by the gods, and those borne by the malevolent ones that strike down — all of these may jaṅgiḍa, the universal healer, render powerless.
Receive, O Earth, this body brought hither, churned from clarified butter; do thou protect this cow of its giver upon the sacred grass, as it rightfully should be.
They call thee too the wife of Varuṇa; they also call thee Aditi of all forms. Over the after-birth at the libation-pouring I pour oblation into the fire that carries the offering — her greatness do I offer.
He has stretched out a thousand-fold thread; he has accomplished ten agniṣṭoma sacrifices in full. He who gives a cow with its calf along with the birth-membrane — him verily the gods cause to ascend to the heavenly world.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
By the birth-membrane they cause him to ascend to heaven — the good-milching cow bestowed with it, bearer of vitality; may she yield for him an inexhaustible hundred-streamed milk in yonder world, in the highest firmament.
A cow that has calved before, together with the former calf — her other calf is the birth-membrane; and that third flesh which is formed around it — for that reason the gods call it the adhijarāyu.
Run hither, O thou who hast grown mighty with strength — set thy renown upon him from above. Protect this man, O Indra, from great transgression; unite him with offspring, with his body, and with strength.
From the difficult-to-know side, from afar in many ways, all the gods behold the cow as she comes. She who is auspicious, who flows rightly on every side — may that oblation of mine be lavish with clarified butter.
He who performs the rite bestows upon the brahmin a cow that has calved once, along with the birth-membrane and the self-sustaining offering; may she yield for him an inexhaustible hundred-streamed milk in yonder world in the age that follows.
He who gives us the calf, the birth-membrane as the milker's counterpart, the beestings, and a good-milching cow — may the gods extend that man's life-span; may he ascend to the world of those who have done good.
The living man has given at the outset, in combat, the calf-encasing birth-membrane. Enter here pleasantly for us, peacefully, propitiously; do not harm us with divine fury.
Wrought with good fortune, well-fashioned, truly beneficent, wholly apt — I receive her as she comes: she whose beauty is clarified butter, dwelling together in the two regions of sky and air — gods, humans, asuras, and the seers.
Five gods drink of her: Indra, Tvaṣṭṛ, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Agni. All of them have given her to me; by means of her, living here, extend thy life-span.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Kaśyapa here, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha — seers have won her for us at the outset; Bharadvāja, Gautama, Atri give her to us as an auspicious blessing, and Viśvāmitra extends the life-span of the donor.
O auspicious one, bring strength-sustenance to the gods; bring strength-sustenance to humankind; bring strength-sustenance to the ancestors, O inviolable cow — enter here laden with nourishment.
The plants that were born three ages before the gods — I reckon now the tawny ones to have a hundred and seven abodes.
A hundred are your abodes, O mothers, and a thousand your growths; therefore, a hundredfold do ye render this man free of disease for me.
Bearing flowers, bearing fruit, fruit-bearing and fruitless alike — ye plants are like victorious horses; ye are the herbs capable of bringing one across to safety.
As oṣadhīs — herbs — O divine mothers, I address you; crushing wounds and driving away rākṣasas, come hither.
Niṣkṛti — Release — is the name of your mother; Niṣkṛti — Release — is the name of your father; ye are swift ones, winged, wherever Niṣkṛti cures disease.
In the aśvattha tree is your resting-place; in its leaf your dwelling has been made; verily ye are sharers of the cow, when ye win for the man his prize.
When I, seeking vigor, take up these herbs in my hand, may the very essence of wasting disease perish — as a life-snatcher destroyed before it strikes.
The vital forces of the herbs rise up like cows issuing from the cowpen; the man wins for himself the wealth of those plants that are about to grant him gain.
When the herbs come together like kings in an assembly, that inspired one is called the physician — the expeller of rākṣasas and the dispeller of disease.
Her who contains the horse-plant, her who contains soma, her who bestows strength, her who possesses surpassing vigor — I have found all the herbs, saying: "From here bring me across to safety."

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Like a thief that has broken through all enclosures into the fold, the herbs have shaken loose whatsoever blemish there is upon the body.
O herbs, as ye creep through limb by limb, joint by joint, drive out from him the yakṣma, as the fierce one who strikes from the middle.
Let one of you aid another; let each come to the assistance of the other. O herbs, being of one accord, favor this my word.
The herbs, descending footlessly from heaven all around — whichever living man we lay hold of with them, that man shall not be harmed.
The herbs that are queens of Soma, the many possessed of a hundredfold discernment, sent forth by Bṛhaspati — may they release us from distress.
Those that bear fruit, those that are fruitless, those that lack a sheath, and those that are leafy — sent forth by Bṛhaspati, may they release us from distress.
I bind upon thee the herb Jīvalā, the Naghāriṣā — that which shall bring thee life and drive the rakṣas away.
Kāla, the horse with seven reins, carries on — thousand-eyed, unaging, of abundant seed. The seers, the far-seeing, mount him; his wheels are all the worlds.
This Kāla draws seven wheels; seven are his nave-hubs; his axle is immortality. He, encompassing all these worlds, Kāla, moves on — he is verily the foremost god.
A full jar has been placed upon Kāla; him we behold as existing in many forms. He, facing all these worlds — they call that Kāla in the highest heaven.
He alone, being present, upheld the worlds; he alone, being present, encompassed the worlds. Being their father, he became their son — therefore there is no higher radiance than he.
Kāla generated yonder heaven; Kāla also generated this earth. By Kāla, the past and the future, impelled, stand spread forth.
Kāla created prosperity; in Kāla the sun blazes. In Kāla are all beings; in Kāla the eye sees far.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
In Kāla is mind; in Kāla is breath; in Kāla is name gathered up. By Kāla arrived, all these creatures rejoice.
In Kāla is austerity; in Kāla is the exalted; in Kāla brahman is gathered. Kāla is verily the lord of all — he who was the father of Prajāpati.
By him it is impelled; by him it is born; in him, moreover, it is established. Kāla, having become brahman, sustains Parameṣṭhin.
Kāla generated creatures; Kāla in the beginning generated Prajāpati. The self-existent Kaśyapa and austerity — from Kāla they were born.
From Kāla the waters came together; from Kāla brahman, austerity, and the directions. By Kāla the sun rises; in Kāla he enters again.
By Kāla the wind blows; by Kāla the great earth and the great heaven are established in Kāla. Kāla indeed begat the past and the future as his sons before all.
From Kāla the ṛc-verses came together; the yajus was born from Kāla. Kāla set in motion the sacrifice, the imperishable share belonging to the gods.
In Kāla are the Gandharvāpsarases; in Kāla the worlds are gathered. In Kāla this divine Aṅgiras and Atharvan stand supreme.
This world and the highest world, the blessed worlds and the blessed sustaining powers — having conquered all worlds with brahman, that Kāla moves on: he is verily the supreme god.
Seven it is, seven ṛṣis, the thorn-makers twelve — they fashioned the piercing thorn that is the Indra-heap, the great-bellied one.
Mitra and Varuṇa cut out the Indra-heap, that which had been pierced within; it was brought forth by fierce Indra, from one who is no fit father for brāhmaṇas.
No non-brāhmaṇa should eat of it, nor should he carry it away to his own home; bitter as the taimāta poison, the Indra-heap lies upon the threshing-floor.
This one lies here protecting its own body — whosoever eats of it heedlessly — the great-bellied Indra-heap, fashioned in the midst of the threshing-floor.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
And this one too becomes a disease — the Indra-heap, the great-bellied — terrible in the semblance of food; like a horse it devours the reeds of the marshland.
He who winnows and augments the Indra-heap, the pride of the threshing-floor — may he obtain the abundance of the floor and may his cattle flourish greatly.
That which Śunaḥśepa carried, that which Indra and Bṛhaspati carried — that the ṛṣis have made auspicious for us, a pleasant thing for our living.
He set it down as an impaled plant; the offering to the dog-demon had been given. Fifteen lay suffering, those who ate the oblation that had been offered improperly.
From the sweat and toil of the ploughman, from the draught-oxen with dappled hooves, from those that draw and those that bear burdens — the Indra-heap was born.
When the ploughman's sweat flows from his scorched body all around — as cows thirst for water, so he consumes the Indra-heap.
Whatever the lord of the plough strikes with the rod in his anger at the ploughman, and whatever of the threshing-floor pertaining to the perennial horse-offering — all that is deposited in the Indra-heap.
Rouse those, the mortar and pestle; O woman, make the winnowing-fan for the fanning. May Gotama make the sweet Indra-heap ready for his son, the bearer.
O singer of praise, bring this winnowing-fan hither; come, O pot, to the mortar and pestle. May our sons today, on this day of fair brightness, eat the sweet sap, the portion of the father.
Agni has come here, dispatched as our messenger; may he render all our food free from poison. That which is unpierced and unprocessed — from this brāhmaṇa here — eat, ye who are born, the intoxicating portion of the father.
O sweet food, O honey-food, come unto us for our nourishment, O food; auspicious, with auspicious protections.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Having become a lion, it crushes the cattle; having become fire, it consumes the grain. The Indra-heap, when unpropitiated, goes down along with the peacock.
The hundred-stemmed, the unshakeable, the thousand-leafed, the lofty — darbha, the fierce herb: I bind you with it for long life.
They do not shave his hair, nor do they strike a blow upon his chest — to him to whom shelter is granted with the uncut-leafed darbha.
In heaven is your tuft, O herb; upon the earth you are firmly established. By you, O thousand-stemmed one, we cause long life to increase.
The three heavens you pierced through, and these three earths likewise. With it I cut off the tongue and the speech of all the ill-willed.
You are the overpowering one; I am the possessor of overpowering strength. Both of us, having become mighty, let us overcome the rivals.
Overpower the malice against us; overpower the one who marches in battle-array. Overpower all the ill-willed; make my well-wishers many.
With the darbha born of the gods, the perpetual pillar of heaven — with it I shall win people forever and shall obtain boons.
Make me dear through the darbha to the brāhmaṇa and the rājanya, to the śūdra and the ārya, to whomsoever we wish, and to every far-sighted one.
He who at his birth made the earth firm, who propped up the atmosphere and heaven — the evil has never known him as he is borne: may this darbha be a sustainer, a shining one for us.
The hundred-stemmed, the rival-slayer, the mighty — first among herbs it came into being. May this darbha guard us on all sides; with it may I overcome the battle-lines of those who battle against us.
Worth a thousand, hundred-stalked, full of sap, the fire of waters among plants, the royal-consecration among herbs — may this darbha grass of ours, this divine amulet, protect us on every side and unite us with long life.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Anointed with ghee, sweet with honey, full of milk, fast-rooted in the earth, immovable and yet inclining — thrusting rivals down and making them inferior, ascend, O Darbha, with great and mighty virile power.
You traverse the earth with vigor; you sit beautifully upon the vedi at the sacrifice; the seers carried you as a purifier — do you purify from us all the things that go wrong.
Sharp king, conqueror of poison, slayer of rākṣasas, beholder of all creatures — this is the fiery splendor and the fierce strength of the gods; that I bind upon you for old age and for well-being.
With darbha, accomplish heroic deeds; bearing darbha, do not tremble within yourself; stand pre-eminent — grow bright in glory above others; shine like the sun upon the four quarters.
Let the earth, the giver of sustenance, be stirred up; let the cold wind, bearing rain within, blow upon her; let the seasonally endowed earth receive the seed — she who causes good plants to spring up, yielding a thousandfold growth.
Indra with his bay horses, or Agni with his red horses, and the Aśvins with their ass-and-horse team — they have yoked the divine field.
Draw the yoke-strap auspiciously; auspiciously raise the goad; auspiciously let the ploughshare cut; auspiciously let the plough be drawn.
Yoke the draft animals, stretch the yoke-ropes wide; in the prepared field sow the seed here. So too may Dhātṛ, so may Bhaga, so may the Aśvins accomplish it, so may the goddess Sarasvatī.
May the herbs be richly berried, neither stripped of berries nor fallen away. Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Aśvins — extend this my word of mine.
Dhātṛ, Pūṣan, Bṛhaspati — they have come together for prosperity; the gods who know the way to heaven have come to the field.
She who is auspicious, like fair fortune, desirable in form at the place of establishment — may she draw forth for us the sweet-flowing sap.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Abundance of food, abundance of men, abundance of cattle — may these take up their abode here; let the rains rain fiercely for existence, for greatness, for growth.
Let Parjanya stand swelling with the ridge-waters; the sun goes forth; barley generating joy, driving away all grudging niggardliness.
Open wide the earth, O snake; be split apart with your wing — be propitious; let the grain sprout auspiciously.
Drive out, drive away; drive the cattle and acquire great wealth here; may the clutching trap not harm you, may the plough not splinter upon you.
May no fierce, seized bodies of ours be harmed in anything whatsoever. O Śunāsīrā, increase of wealth — and also the fortune that belongs to the furrow.
The sea that appoints, Sinīvālī — may they two impel our ploughed field; these five directions here — may the wind impel them; like warriors on the battle-ground, let the rains rain fiercely.
Auspiciously let the ploughman follow the draft animals; auspiciously let the ploughshare go cleaving the earth; O Śunāsīrā, strengthened by the oblation, make our grains auspicious for us.
That which for us, O Aśvins, is luminous and pierces through the darkness — may you two bestow that nourishment upon us.
Those waters that are herbs and forest-trees — verily those are called the Upward-Standing (ūrdhvaśritāḥ); Agni is their overlord. Whoso knows these Upward-Standing waters, knowing Agni as their overlord — even as those waters stand upright before him, so do they stand upright before this knower; he becomes overlord among his own people and among others — he who knows thus.
Those waters that are the dew-drops (pṛṣvāḥ) — verily those are called the Leaping-Forth (praskadvarīḥ); Āditya is their overlord. Whoso knows these Leaping-Forth waters, knowing Āditya as their overlord — even as they leap forth when he rises and leap forth when he comes back, so does he become overlord [among his own and among others, he who knows thus].

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Those waters that flow in channels (sūdayāḥ) — verily those are called the Swift-Running (takvarīḥ); Pṛthivī is their overlord. Whoso knows these Swift-Running waters, knowing Pṛthivī as their overlord — even as those waters, when driven forth upon her, run swiftly away, so are his enemies driven forth and run away; he becomes overlord [among his own and among others, he who knows thus].
Those waters that glide in streams (syandante) — verily those are called the Obedient (vaśinīḥ); Varuṇa is their overlord. Whoso knows these Obedient waters, knowing Varuṇa as their overlord — even as he takes those streaming waters under his will, so does he take his foes under his will; he becomes overlord [among his own and among others, he who knows thus].
Those waters that are cows — verily those are called the Vigour-Waters (ūrjāḥ); Tvaṣṭṛ is their overlord. Whoso knows these Vigour-Waters, knowing Tvaṣṭṛ as their overlord — he becomes rich in vigour, radiant with splendour; he gains cattle by the thousand; he becomes overlord [among his own and among others, he who knows thus].
Those waters that are clarified butter (ghṛta) — verily those are called the Lustre-Waters (varcāḥ); Pūṣan is their overlord. Whoso knows these Lustre-Waters, knowing Pūṣan as their overlord — he becomes lustrous and radiant with splendour; and even the face of this one, though unanointed, shines bright; he becomes overlord [among his own and among others, he who knows thus].
Those waters that are honey (madhu) — verily those are called the Might-Waters (ojāḥ); Indra is their overlord. Whoso knows these Might-Waters, knowing Indra as their overlord — he becomes mighty, heroic, possessed of vital force; he obtains the honey-mixture (madhuparka) in the royal assembly; he becomes overlord [among his own and among others, he who knows thus].

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Those waters that are the hailstones (dhrādunayaḥ) — verily those are called the Fierce-Waters (ugrāḥ); the Maruts are their overlords. Whoso knows these Fierce-Waters, knowing the Maruts as their overlords — he becomes fierce and powerful; people call him 'the host of Maruts (mārutaṃ śardhaḥ)'; he becomes overlord [among his own and among others, he who knows thus].
Those waters that are rain (varṣa) — verily those are called the Great-Waters (mahāḥ); Parjanya is their overlord. Whoso knows these Great-Waters, knowing Parjanya as their overlord — he becomes great, with far-reaching friendship; his own people rejoice in him, saying 'He is ours.' Therefore everyone exults at rain; he becomes overlord [among his own and among others, he who knows thus].
Those waters that are spirituous liquor (surā) — verily those are called the Exceedingly-Proud (atimanyāḥ); the two Aśvins are their overlords. Whoso knows these Exceedingly-Proud waters, knowing the two Aśvins as their overlords — he is prouder than his rivals; his rivals are not prouder than he. That is why an intoxicated man is prouder than another intoxicated man; he becomes overlord [among his own and among others, he who knows thus].
Those waters that flow in furrows (karṣvāḥ) — verily those are called the Gathered-Round (paricitāḥ); Yama is their overlord. Whoso knows these Gathered-Round waters, knowing Yama as their overlord — both his own kinsmen and his clansmen gather around him in submission; he becomes overlord [among his own and among others, he who knows thus].
Those waters that are women (striyaḥ) — verily those are called the Delightful-Waters (rantayaḥ); Kāma is their overlord. Whoso knows these Delightful-Waters, knowing Kāma as their overlord — people take pleasure in him; he becomes delightful, as Kāma is overlord among women; he becomes overlord [among his own and among others, he who knows thus].

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Those waters that are the human person (puruṣa) — verily those are called the All-Sustaining (viśvabhṛtāḥ); Mṛtyu is their overlord. Whoso knows these All-Sustaining waters, knowing Mṛtyu as their overlord — he becomes the sustainer of all; all sustain him. In his house the three sacrificial fires are established: the Dakṣiṇāgni, the Gārhapatya, and the Āhavanīya. And four auspicious gifts come to him: the golden necklace (niṣka), the bowl (kaṃsa), the mule (aśvatara), and the elephant; he becomes overlord [among his own and among others, he who knows thus].
Of all these waters, the Himālaya is their udder, Soma is their calf, and Parameṣṭhin is their overlord. Whoso knows of these waters that the Himālaya is their udder, Soma their calf, and Parameṣṭhin their overlord — he becomes Parameṣṭhin, he attains the state of supreme sovereignty; he becomes overlord among his own people and among others — he who knows thus.
May Agni drive the fever away from here; may Soma, the pressing-stones, and the Maruts of pure might — may the vedi, the barhis, and the blazing kindling-sticks blow the demons away by that same power.
This one — the Ruru who burns with scorching heat, who renders all forms yellow-green — to him, to you, O Takman, the tawny, the reddish-brown, the fervid, the mighty: homage be!
Seek out a travelling companion, O Takman, and being thus appeased, show us mercy! Come now — go to where your dwelling-places are, among the never-satiated Dasyus.
The man who is speckled, reddish like one covered in blemishes — the all-powerful fever, drive it downward and away!
Downward I dispatch it, turning my mind toward the fever. O destroyer of Śakambhara, go back again to the great Vṛṣas!
Go, having departed, to the Mahāvṛṣas, to the Mūjavats — make that your home! We declare vows for Takman: these are other territories for him.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The Mūjavats are his home; the Mahāvṛṣas are his home. By that people among whom you, O Takman, were born, among those Balihikas you shall roam below!
O Takman, ward off the serpent, the tongueless one, the lame — drive them far away! Seek out the slovenly slave-woman; pierce her through with your thunderbolt!
Go to the mountain — you are mountain-born; in the mountain your buffalo's home lies! Seek out the coarse slave-woman; shake her violently, O Takman, like a reed!
You who are the chill, and also the fierce burning, together with your cough: your dreadful missiles, O Takman — with those, do encompass and wound us not!
O Takman, together with your brother Balāsa and your sister Kāsikā, and with Pāman your kinsman-rival — vanish utterly, both of you, toward the Maraṭas!
To the Gandhāris, to the Mūjavats, to the Kāśis, to the Māgadhas — we pass along Takman as one passes a dear treasure to the people!
Not among the Arkavindas, not among the Arvidālas, not among the quail-haunted river Annadī — we declare the vows for Takman: these are other territories for him.
The thousand-eyed immortal one takes no delight in another's territory. Takman has now been duly sought — he will go to the Balihikā!
Go to yonder Mūjavats, or yet farther beyond them! Do not come back to us again from there — this I speak to you, O Takman!
Roam only to the beyond, in the farthest of far regions — so that you may not come to our end, so that you may not burn us again!
As this broad Pṛthivī, like a mature woman, has taken the embryo to herself — so I place the embryo in you; to that end I invoke you for your protection.
Gathered from the mountain, from the womb of heaven, limb by limb — the seed of the god upon god I have set, like a leaf on a bough.
May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms; may Prajāpati pour in the seed; may Dhātṛ place the embryo in you.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Place the embryo, O Sinīvālī; place the embryo, O Sarasvatī! O Aśvins, you two wreathed with lotuses, place the embryo in her here and now!
May King Varuṇa place the embryo in you; may the god Bṛhaspati; may Indra and Agni place the embryo in you; may Dhātṛ place the embryo in you.
You are the embryo of the herbs; you are the embryo of the forest-lords; you are the embryo of all that exists — so, O Agni, place the embryo here!
That by which the herbs become pregnant, that by which the beasts become pregnant — by that embryo of their embryos, may you become pregnant!
We cut loose your knot; may Dhātṛ place the embryo in you. Let a son mount into the womb; let him be born to birth!
For she shall give birth in her greatness — the womb has come together here. Now, like Soma readied for drinking, may the embryo settle in its proper season!
O Dhātṛ, with your finest form — in the two birth-passages of this woman — place a male son, to be delivered in the tenth month!
O Bhaga, with thy most excellent form — in the womb-cavities of this woman — place a male son [there], for her to bring forth in the tenth month.
Mount [her], O Skanda; put forth thy virile power; place the embryo in the womb. A bull-like [son], possessed of bull's vigour — we lead thee [to her] for offspring.
What king Varuṇa knows, what the god Bṛhaspati knows, what Indra the Vṛtra-slayer knows — that embryo-making [power], drink [of it].
Open thyself, O [thou who art] of the Bārhastyasāman; let the embryo lie down into thy womb. The gods shall give thee a son, a drinker of soma, covered with wool on both sides.
With the seasonal [rite] of Soma I approach thee for the making of an embryo. From that may a son be born to thee, to accomplish [great] heroic deeds.
Be born, O Agni, from the aśvattha [tree], for this [man's] sovereign power and vigour — fierce, from the timber-source, who mounts upon the trees.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Even overwhelming the [opposing] obstacle, we generate thee, O Agni. Drive away from me rivals already born and those yet to be born.
The fire-drills have been fashioned from the wood of the aśvattha tree that is to be climbed. From that [fire], born for thee, was Vīḍujambha Agni generated for [the rite of] fire.
That [Agni] born — Jātavedas, immortal — I establish [on the hearth]: the purifying, brilliant fire, for [our] aid, the vanquisher of poison.
Stretch thy bow; put on thy armour; smite [thy] enemies — I fashion thy heroic powers. Let those who are thy rivals submit here; become thou the sole bull [among them].
We make thee the bull among thy kinsmen, the vanquisher of rivals, the slayer of enemies, the sovereign, the lord of cattle.
Thou art the ocean, the foremost of waters; thou art Indra among the gods, the slayer of Vṛtra. We make thee a tiger, a lion, the subduer of those who attack.
Cast [thy] rivals down as Indra [casts down] the Dasyus; crushing rivals as the fierce wind [does]. Let them wither — as [wood dries] away from a forest fire — thou hast turned [them] away from thyself.
Cut them down — let them wither when [thou hast] cut them; leave no remnant of them whatsoever. Having pierced all thy rivals, become thou the sole bull [among them].
Be thou fierce; be thou strong; be thou pre-eminent in speech. Be thou first among those who battle; afflict and drive down thy rivals.
Rivalless, a slayer of rivals — like Indra, uninjured, undiminished — let all thy rivals be beneath thy feet, trodden down.
Let thy rivals wither, their roots dug out; I call forth the fire from their bodies. I deposit their vital breaths into the oblation-offering — thus are the bonds made for them.
An oblation that increases [thee], that overpowers, that destroys rivals — we prepare it for [thy] sovereignty, for thy [use], and for the defeat of [thy] rivals.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The man — whether one of our own or a stranger — who bears hostility toward us: like a kindling-wood layer consumed [by fire], let nothing of him remain.
[The formula] "Rivalless" — [applied to] two [verses].
By thee, O herb, the Ātharvaṇas first smote the demons; by thee Kaśyapa smote them, by thee did Agastya destroy them.
By thee we drive away the Apsarasas and the Gandharvas. O Ajaśṛṅgī, by thy fragrance destroy all demons.
Let the Apsarasas go to the river, breathing as if into a wilderness — Gulgulū, Pīlā, Naladī, Aukṣagandhī, Pramandinī.
Where the immortal ones dwell within the waters of the ocean — Turū, Nīlī, Turvaśī, Puṇḍarīkā — thither go, O Apsarasas; ye have been recognized.
Where the golden swing of the Gandharvas is bound in the sky — [remainder lost].
The assembly-place of the Gandharvas and Apsarasas called Ānarta — [remainder lost].
Where the aśvattha trees and the nyagrodhas, laden with great golden ornaments, stand crested — [remainder lost].
Where your dice — green, white, tawny, kakara — sound together: thither go, O Apsarasas; ye have been recognized.
This creeper of Śikhaṇḍin, lord of the Gandharvas, master of the Apsarasas — may it split his testicles; may his phallus also depart.
This herb has come, potent among plants — Ajaśṛṅgī, Arāṭakī with sharp horns: let it drive them away.
Depart hence, O Apsarasas and Gandharvas, to where your homes are. Let Tīkṣṇaśṛṅgī, Arāṭakī, and Ajaśṛṅgī drive you away.
The wife knows you, O Apsarasas; ye Gandharvas are the husbands. Step away from this man, O immortals; do not follow a mortal.
Fearsome are Indra's missiles, a hundred iron-tipped shafts for him. With these let it drive away the Gandharvas, the invulnerable, the Avakāda-dwellers.
Those who dwell in the water-reeds, shining and blazing with malign heat — all the Gandharvas, O herb, push them forth, lead them away.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Those Apsarasas who roam as a swarm, maddening men, afflicting them with burning, making the sage go naked and laugh in vain, the wives of the Gandharvas — may Ajaśṛṅgī lay them low.
Making the man turn pale, assuming all manner of forms — like a dog at one moment, like a monkey at another, a youth with hair all about — the Gandharva, having become pleasing to look upon, follows after the woman: him from here we drive away.
He who sacrifices a vaśā-cow to the gods and cooks it incompletely without proper oblation — he is bound in the snare of Death, of the gods, and of Yama.
They call the vaśā-cow the dakṣiṇā, the solar Aditi, forming her speech into a common harmony. The seven seers established this speech, Sarasvatī graciously ordering it.
This vaśā they call speech itself as vaśā; three vaśās are deposited together in the common place. Of those three I offer one into Agni with the mind; may the Lord of Beings make her sweet for us.
May Savitṛ make her sweet for us; may the progenitor of cattle make her sweet for us. Sacrifice, O Agni, knowing all the sacred ordinances; may the Lord of Beings make her sweet for us.
This is the third portion of the vaśā-cow; thou art the mistress of vaśā. The embryo has entered into thee for the sake of greatness. Yearning thyself, go to the yearning gods; may the desires of the sacrificer be fulfilled.
This cow, steadfast with her water, sustaining vigor, in whom Indra and Varuṇa flash their brilliance — the heroic and the unheroic attend upon her; she has come here; the steadfast beast has entered into virile power.
The vaśā-cow gave birth to the steadfast wise one; the vaśā gave birth to the yearling calf touching heaven. The vaśā gave birth to the young one for the distribution; the vaśā gave birth to the conqueror of riches.
The sprinkling-water that fell around the sacred grass, south of the altar, charged with vital power — the vaśā-cow lowed above it in full presence; her marrow became her armor-garment.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Homage to your greatness and to your eye, O Vaśā and Ṛṣabha — this I do with the mind. Go together to the gods by auspicious paths; harm us not with divine wrath.
The bull mounted the vaśā-cow as she stood upon the threads of fate. Who today knows that embryo — in what manner he has disposed it?
One encompassed form entire; one is called King by name; one is lord of form, its very form; one is the form of those who act aright.
Prajāpati, Parameṣṭhin, Mṛtyu, Viśvānara, and Svarga — from this sacrifice, from this vaśā, were they born.
In whose house the vaśā were received as an oblation fashioned by the gods — the treasure to be sought of her is like a daughter's to her husband.
Let no one approach her even once; let no lame creature be in his house — for the vaśā, like an ill-omened maiden, brings ruin upon the knowing man who disregards her.
He should not withhold her from Brāhmaṇas, nor cause her name to be dishonoured; he should not turn back one who has gone forth — in whose cattle the vaśā may be.
Neither gods nor men shall restrain her vaśā; because she followed the will through brahman — therefore has she become the vaśā.
Making the will her own, the auspicious one has arrived at the station proper to the sovereign; being born beyond the unsacrificed sacrifice, she who measures out the measure of the rite.
The Maruts who possess Indra — they have partaken of the fourth portion in the vaśā; the Ādityas and Rudras have the fourth portion, the Vasus the fourth, in the vaśā.
The seers know the Ādityas as sharers of the fourth portion in the vaśā; then her body, as the one path, became arranged as the four quarters.
The vaśā beheld the path, the back of the firmament belonging to those who know heaven; the Ādityas followed after her, and the seers rich in austerity.
Step by step the Ādityas and the Aṅgirasas arranged the Yajus; those who praise followed after the vaśās — therefore is that called the iḍā-Sāman.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The vaśā is Iḍā; the vaśā is Anumati; they call Sarasvatī the vaśā; the vaśā they reckon as Virāj; Speech is the vaśā, the Earth is the vaśā.
The vaśā is the guide Sinīvālī; the vaśā is Uṣas; Nirṛti is the vaśā; Death entered into the vaśā — yes, Death entered the vaśā.
Agni, Speech, Water, Eye, Mind, Wind — the sovereign vaśā is the vaśā. Who knows that body of hers wherewith she has stepped forth as the one?
Her whom the seers, the wise ones, behold in unison with eye, mind, and heart — of her is the lord of the creation of cattle; the vaśā is sovereign: this creation has no boundary-garment.
Who knows the udder of the vaśā? Who knows her amnion and caul? Who knows her teats? Who, indeed, knows that which she yields when milked?
I know the udder of her; I know her amnion and caul; I know her teats — and I know that which she yields when milked.
I would not protect her; yet should she be given, and should she be mine — for I know her teats, her milk, her amnion and her caul.
Skin, womb, covering-garment, caul, pallid amnion, navel, and turban are hers; let the sovereign vaśī suckle the mother to old age — for he who is fashioned by brahman-spells is truly her kinsman.
Now shall I proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra, the first deeds the Vajra-bearer performed: he smote the serpent, then pierced open the waters; he cleft the flanks of the mountains.
He smote the serpent that lay sprawled upon the mountain; Tvaṣṭar had fashioned for him the resonant bolt of heaven. Like lowing cows flowing swiftly, the waters straightway descended to the sea.
Exerting himself as a bull he chose Soma; he drank of the pressed draught at the three Kadrū-pressings; Maghavan took up the missile, the thunderbolt, and smote that first-born among serpents.
When, O Indra, thou smotest the first-born among serpents and then destroyed the māyās of the māyā-wielders, bringing forth the sun, the sky, and the dawn — then, verily, thou foundest no enemy to match thee.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Indra smote Vṛtra, the greater of obstructors, the shoulderless one, with the great death-weapon, the thunderbolt; like the branches of a tree split by an axe, the serpent lay stretched along the earth.
For like one drunk with ill-madness he challenged the great hero, the overpowering, the pressers-juice-drinker; the enemy of Indra could not cross the meeting-point of his death-blows — crashing together, he was crushed.
Footless and handless he gave battle to Indra; Indra struck the thunderbolt upon his back's ridge; the castrated one seeking to match the bull — Vṛtra lay strewn in many places, scattered asunder.
Like a broken reed he lay there prostrate; the waters pass over him, rising and climbing in their minds. Over those very waters which Vṛtra in his greatness had encompassed, the serpent became one whose head is crushed underfoot.
The mother of Vṛtra was brought low — Indra seized the weapon away from her; the mother was above, the son was below; Dānu lies there like a cow with her calf beside her.
Among the currents that stand still, that find no resting-place, the body was laid in the midst of the flood-channels; the waters flow about the secret of the wolf — the enemy of Indra lay stretched in long darkness.
The waters, guarded by the serpent, stood blocked, mastered by the Paṇi-lord like cattle penned. The aperture of the waters that had been stopped up — he who smote Vṛtra swept that aside.
That became a horse-hair noose for thee, O Indra, wherein the one god struck back at thee with a tusk. Thou didst win the cattle, thou didst win the Soma, O hero; thou didst loose the seven rivers to flow.
Neither lightning nor thunder could restrain him; Yamī dispersed neither mist nor hailstorm against him. When Indra and the serpent fought, the Bountiful One conquered utterly over all adversaries.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Whom didst thou behold as the avenger of the serpent, O Indra, when fear entered thy heart upon slaying it? Like an undaunted eagle thou didst cross the realms of space where nine and ninety rivers flow.
Indra, vajra-armed, has departed — king of the halted, of the still, and of the horned one. He it is who reigns as king over all peoples; like a wheel-rim he has encompassed them all.
He who, born first of all, was full of mind — the god who surpassed the gods in power of will; at whose vehemence the two world-halves trembled, by the greatness of whose manly might — he, O people, is Indra.
He who steadied the earth as it was shaking, who calmed the mountains that were stirred to fury; who measured out the atmosphere more broadly, who propped up the sky — he, O people, is Indra.
He who, having slain the serpent, set the seven rivers free; who drove forth the cattle, having broken open the lair of Vala; who kindled fire within the two stones, undefeated in battles — he, O people, is Indra.
By whom all these movable things have been set in motion; who cast the Dāsa colour downward into concealment; who, like a dicing-master winning, seized the prize — the Ārya's prosperities — he, O people, is Indra.
Of whom they ask in dread, "Where is he?" — and of whom they even say, "He does not exist" — he diminishes the Ārya's prosperities like a gambler's stake. Place faith in him — he, O people, is Indra.
He who is the impeller of the weak, of the lean; who aids the imploring brahman-poet; the fair-lipped one who is the protector of him whose pressing-stones are yoked and whose Soma is pressed — he, O people, is Indra.
Whose are the horses in every direction, whose the cattle, whose the settlements, whose all the chariots; who begot the sun, who begot the dawn, who is the leader of the waters — he, O people, is Indra.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Whom the two battle-cries, meeting in conflict, call upon — both the farther and the nearer, both enemy hosts — even while they have mounted the same chariot, they invoke him separately — he, O people, is Indra.
Without whom people do not conquer; whom those fighting invoke for aid; who has become the counterpart of all the world; who shakes the unshakeable — he, O people, is Indra.
He who slew all those perpetually bearing great sin, all those who remained unawakened; who does not yield to the insolent their arrogance; who is the slayer of the Dasyu — he, O people, is Indra.
He who found Śambara dwelling in the mountains in the fortieth autumn; who slew the serpent gathering its strength, lying prostrate in the flood — he, O people, is Indra.
He who ranged around Śambara with his missiles, who did not drink the pressed draught of Vṛka; who within the mountain did not rejoice over that abundant folk performing sacrifice — he, O people, is Indra.
He who, the seven-rayed bull, the mighty one, loosed the seven rivers to flow; who, vajra-armed, kicked aside Rauhiṇa as it climbed toward the sky — he, O people, is Indra.
Even heaven and earth bow down to him; even the mountains tremble from his vehemence; who is a Soma-drinker, collected within, vajra-armed, who holds the vajra in his hand — he, O people, is Indra.
He who with his aid protects the one pressing Soma, who protects the one cooking the offering, who protects the one reciting the hymn, who protects the one who has toiled; whose sacred formula is the strengthener, whose is the Soma, whose is this bounty — he, O people, is Indra.
Even for him who presses and cooks though refractory, thou dost grant the prize — thou indeed art true. We, thy beloved at all times, O Indra, possessed of good heroes, shall speak forth at the assembly.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Born, he gazed about in the lap of his parents; he knew not the womb of a further begetter. Gathering strength, he perceived his might and the ordinances of the gods — he, O people, is Indra.
He who, bay-horsed, desires the Soma in these very things; from whom all the worlds tremble; who slew Śambara and who slew Śuṣṇa; who is the sole hero — he, O people, is Indra.
May Indrāgnī be auspicious to us with their aids; may Indrāvaruṇa, to whom oblations are given, be auspicious to us; may Indrāsomā be auspicious for our well-being and bliss; may Indrāpūṣaṇa be auspicious to us in the winning of spoil.
May Bhaga be auspicious to us, and may our praise be auspicious; may Puruṃdhī be auspicious to us and may riches be auspicious; may the laud of Truth, well-pressed, be auspicious to us; may Aryaman, born of many, be auspicious to us.
May Dhātṛ be auspicious to us, and Dhartṛ be auspicious to us; may the broad-stretching one be auspicious to us with her bounties; may the vast Rodasī be auspicious, may the stone be auspicious to us; may the invocations of the gods be auspicious to us.
May Agni, whose face is light, be auspicious to us; may Mitrāvaruṇā be auspicious, and the Aśvins auspicious; may the good deeds of the righteous be auspicious to us; may the vigorous wind blow auspiciously upon us.
May Dyāvāpṛthivī be auspicious to us at the first invocation; may the atmosphere be auspicious for our beholding; may the plants and the forest trees be auspicious to us; may the victorious Lord of the realm of dust be auspicious to us.
May Indra, the god together with the Vasus, be auspicious to us; may Varuṇa of excellent praise be auspicious with the Ādityas; may the refreshing Rudra be auspicious to us with the Rudras; may Tvaṣṭṛ with the goddesses hear us here with auspiciousness.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
May Soma be auspicious to us, may brahman be auspicious to us; may the pressing-stones be auspicious to us, may the sacrifices be auspicious; may the measured chants of the heavenly melodies be auspicious to us; may the pressing-ladle be auspicious to us, and the vedi be auspicious.
May Sūrya of wide sight rise auspiciously for us; may the four directions be auspicious to us; may the steadfast mountains be auspicious to us; may the rivers be auspicious to us, and may the waters be auspicious.
May Aditi be auspicious to us with her ordinances; may the Maruts, fond of the sun, be auspicious to us; may Viṣṇu be auspicious to us, and Pūṣan be auspicious to us; may our future be auspicious, and may Vāyu be auspicious.
May the god Savitṛ, who protects, be auspicious to us; may the shining Dawns be auspicious to us; may Parjanya be auspicious to us for our offspring; may the Lord of the field, the beneficent one, be auspicious to us.
May the Lords of Truth be auspicious to us; may the horses be auspicious to us and the cattle be auspicious; may the Ṛbhus, of good deed and skillful hand, be auspicious to us; may the Pitṛs be auspicious to us at the oblations.
May the All-gods, the Viśvedevas, be auspicious to us; may Sarasvatī be auspicious along with inspirations; may those that accompany the oblation and those that accompany the gift be auspicious; may the celestial, the terrestrial, and the aquatic be auspicious to us.
May Aja Ekapād, the god, be auspicious to us; may Ahir Budhnya be auspicious, and the ocean; may Apāṃ Napāt, the swift one, be auspicious to us; may Pṛśni, the god-guarded one, be auspicious to us.
May the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus delight in this brahman-prayer being fashioned anew; may the celestial and terrestrial ones hear us, those born of cattle and those worthy of sacrifice.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Those divine priests who are worthy of sacrifice, who are adorable as Manu's, immortal and knowing the Ṛta — may they grant us wide renown today; do you all ever protect us with blessings.
May that be so, O Mitrāvaruṇā, may that be so, O Agni; may this that is recited be auspicious and blissful for us; may we attain the path and firm footing; homage to the vast sky, to its abode.
Fire moves having entered into fire — this one is the supreme king, the son of the seers; to him I offer with an oblation of ghee; may the due portion of the gods not be withheld.
Yoked, carry forward from the east, O Jātavedas; O Agni, know what is being performed here; you are the physician, the maker of the remedy; through you may we win cattle, horse, and man.
So do you act, O Agni Jātavedas, knowing through this oblation, O youngest one; whichever Piśāca has devoured this man, may it fall from his enclosure.
Whichever one has deceived and devoured this man, may it fall from his enclosure; so do you act, O Agni Jātavedas, in accord with all the gods.
Pierce out its eyes, pierce out its heart, cut out its tongue, crush its teeth; whichever Piśāca has devoured this man — O Agni, youngest one, smite that one in return.
Whatever has been taken from him, dispersed, carried away, devoured from his own self, and whatever by Piśācas — that, O Agni, knowing it, do you bring back; stir up again the breath of life in his body.
Whichever Piśāca has injured you in the drinking of water, in porridge, in the stirred drink, or in what is licked — may the Piśācas pay penalty with their own selves and offspring; may this man be free of disease.
Whichever Piśāca has injured you in milk, in flesh, in food cooked without plowing, in grain — may the Piśācas pay penalty with their own selves and offspring; may this man be free of disease.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Whichever Piśāca has injured this man in raw food, in well-cooked, in mixed, in half-cooked — may Indra the mighty slay it with his thunderbolt; may the bold Soma split open its head.
Whichever flesh-eating Piśāca sorcerer has injured you by day or by night while lying down — that, O Agni, knowing it, burn up and destroy; place it in the lap of Nirṛti.
By the might of Soma and Indra, of Varuṇa the king, by the power of Viṣṇu and the impulse of Savitṛ, by the priestly office of Agni — I drive away the piśācas by the sacred word of Jātavedas, the youngest.
O Agni Jātavedas, smite with your powers the flesh-eating, blood-drinking piśāca, the slayer of the mind. May this sacred formula find favour with the generous one; may he live long, may he be free of disease.
May breath return to you, may life return; may sight return to you, may hearing return. Drive away from us all misfortunes; may we rejoice through a hundred winters, possessing all heroic sons.
Restore mind to him, restore life, restore strength. O Agni, increase in him both the out-breath and the in-breath, that he may live.
O Sūrya, grant him sight again; O Vāyu, stir his breath back together. O Agni, restore his body and his flesh, make them whole.
O Jātavedas, bring together again what has been consumed and what has been borne away. Set his limbs in order; may this man swell back to fullness.
O Jātavedas, may this man swell as the shoot of Soma swells. O Agni, make him abundant, fit for the sacred rite, free from disease, that he may live.
"May the Maruts sprinkle me" — so runs the single verse.
With the sacred formula I release Jātavedas, Agni the priest, the ageless one who touches the chariot. Knowing all the birthplaces of the gods, may Agni carry the oblation, each portion to its proper share.
The male sorcerers, the yātudhānas, and the female sorcerers, the yātudhānīs — with the mighty vajra of Indra I smite them down, driving them away to the nether regions.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Him whom we curse and who curses us, him whom we hate and who, the piśāca, hates us — that flesh-eater, O Agni, burn him down here with a great weapon, O Jātavedas.
He who has seized someone, or the Apsarā who has devoured his substance, the sorcerer who conspires with a crafty device — he whose demon is the owl-phantom, the bhṛmala — him [burn down here, O Jātavedas].
He who has taken, or who has consumed another's ancestral property — the thief, the dog-demon, and those who conspire together; he who has fallen upon the stake of the barring-place with intent to gamble, the flesh-eating piśāca who craves raw flesh and lusts for carrion — he whose demon is the owl-phantom, the bhṛmala — him [burn down here, O Jātavedas].
He who rides with a man in the chariot — the flesh-eating, malicious yātu, the piśāca — him, with Vaiśvānara yoked together with Sūrya — him [burn down here, O Jātavedas].
He who haunts our tribute-hunt, who has beset our tillage with sorceries, and who has cursed us — may Rudra the bowman shatter his life — him [burn down here, O Jātavedas].
May the sorcerer find no one to show him mercy; may all the quarters of space be lightless for him. May both heaven and earth burn him with heat — burn him down here, O Jātavedas.
Those luminous, scorching, and shining flames of yours, O Agni, those bodies of yours that burn in counter-fire — with those protect my vital points on all sides; may the yātudhānas not deceive you, O watcher over men.
May the divine Waters bind shut the mouths of the piśācas, so that this self of mine may fall back upon them, unassailable.
Always in flower, always in fruit, always under Indra's protection — may the piśācas die forever; may not one of them survive.
Those yātudhānas who fly about and prowl by day and by night — may Night protect me from them; to Day I entrust my self.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
This amulet I bind upon you for long life and for vigour — darbha grass, crusher of rivals, scorcher of the hearts of those who hate.
Scorching the hearts of those who hate, burning the minds of enemies — you, O darbha, the ill-willed one, scorch them all utterly as the gharma cauldron scorches.
Scorching all around like the gharma, O darbha, burning down those who hate, O amulet — split apart the hearts of rivals as Indra splits the resisting Vala.
Split apart, O darbha, the hearts of rivals, of those who hate, O amulet. As one strips away the crust of the earth, so send their heads flying asunder.
Split apart my rivals, O darbha; split apart those who array armies against me. Split apart all who bear me ill will, O amulet; split apart those who hate me.
Cut through my rivals, O darbha; cut through those who array armies against me. Cut through all who bear me ill will, O amulet; cut through those who hate me.
Hew down my rivals, O darbha; hew down those who array armies against me. Hew down all who bear me ill will, O amulet; hew down those who hate me.
Shear through my rivals, O darbha; shear through those who array armies against me. Shear through all who bear me ill will, O amulet; shear through those who hate me.
Tear to pieces my rivals, O darbha; tear to pieces those who array armies against me. Tear to pieces all who bear me ill will, O amulet; tear to pieces those who hate me.
Pierce through my rivals, O darbha; pierce through those who array armies against me. Pierce through all who bear me ill will, O amulet; pierce through those who hate me.
Pierce, O Darbha, my rivals; pierce for me those who array armies against me; pierce for me all the malicious of heart; pierce for me the haters, O amulet.
Bore through, O Darbha, my rivals; bore through for me those who array armies against me; bore through for me all the malicious of heart; bore through for me the haters, O amulet.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Shatter, O Darbha, my rivals; shatter for me those who array armies against me; shatter for me all the malicious of heart; shatter for me the haters, O amulet.
Crush, O Darbha, my rivals; crush for me those who array armies against me; crush for me all the malicious of heart; crush for me the haters, O amulet.
Churn down, O Darbha, my rivals; churn down for me those who array armies against me; churn down for me all the malicious of heart; churn down for me the haters, O amulet.
Compress, O Darbha, my rivals; compress for me those who array armies against me; compress for me all the malicious of heart; compress for me the haters, O amulet.
Scorch, O Darbha, my rivals; scorch for me those who array armies against me; scorch for me all the malicious of heart; scorch for me the haters, O amulet.
Burn, O Darbha, my rivals; burn for me those who array armies against me; burn for me all the malicious of heart; burn for me the haters, O amulet.
Smite, O Darbha, my rivals; smite for me those who array armies against me; smite for me all the malicious of heart; smite for me the haters, O amulet.
What in you, O Darbha, constitutes death-by-old-age — that is your armour at the vital points; having made this one armour-clad with it, smite the rivals with heroic powers.
A hundred armours are yours, O Darbha, a thousand heroic powers are yours; all the gods have given you over to be borne by him unto old age.
They call you the armour of the gods; they call you, O Darbha, the lord of brahman-power; they call you the armour of Indra — you are the protector of kingdoms.
The Darbha that destroys rivals, that scorches the heart of the hater, the amulet that augments sovereign power — I make it a guardian of your person.
When the ocean roared forth and Parjanya roared with the lightning — from that was born a golden drop, from that was born the Darbha.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Concealed for me is the vast mid-air; concealed for me are the mountains and the fires. Let not this sorcery of theirs succeed — I strike them back with the pratisara amulet.
Tapas and toil I place as a double concealment around me; I set the brahma-sacrifice as a concealment within me. […]
May Agni and Soma become a double concealment for me; I make heaven and earth my armour. […]
Concealed for me is the sāman that has been intoned; concealed for me is Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati. […]
Concealed for me is the queen of serpents together with my heroes; concealed for me is the sacrificial man. […]
Concealed for me are the six broad realms arrayed together; concealed for me are the Sādhyas and the Āptyas. […]
Concealed for me are the wise seers; concealed are the Sun and Mātariśvan. […]
Concealed for me are the flowing rivers; concealed for me are the flowering plants. […]
Concealed for me are the tethered cattle; concealed is every bird that flies. […]
Concealed for me are the arrows of the brāhmaṇas; concealed for me are the forest trees with their roots. […]
Concealed before me are the divine couches; concealed for me is the jagatī among the metres. […]
