Concealed for me are the twelve oceans; concealed for me are the stars at dawn. […]
Concealed for me are the dhiṣṇya fires; concealed for me are the seasonal rites of the seasons. […]
Concealed for me are the four cardinal directions; I hold within myself both the past and the future. Let not this sorcery of theirs succeed — I strike them back with the pratisara amulet.
I smite the oblation you have made — you who have wrought this dreadful act against me. Both your arms I bind behind your back; I bind shut your mouth.
I bind your two arms; I bind shut your mouth. With the wrath of the god Agni I have slain the oblation of you who wrought this dreadful act against me.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Having risen, Indra wheels his chariot a hundred yojanas; bearing his sharp-edged arrow, he crushes the serpent broods.
Stiff they lay — the serpents slain, those that creep with their bellies — their tails curling up, as a dog gnaws a lump of meat.
Evil one, evil-formed one, why did you sting my companion? You did not see me coming — me, the true antidote to poison.
We move about as crushers of serpents, with scrota drooping like those of bulls. We strike the embrace of the pīlā plant against the spotted snake; we drive it against the post.
All those who have sat here attending to this, dispersed like the wind from here and there — come now, all of you declare: the serpent's venom is without potency!
Threefold is your resting place, O wicked one; three-tufted is your lair. The wind strikes you without cutting you off; it rains upon you without cutting you off.
With the mongoose remedy we crush the serpents. The small tree named māṃścatur — it has made them devoid of venom.
The venom of the dark serpent is without potency, as is that of the light one and of both together. The festering sores of the roaring one — those we drive away from here.
This is what the Paidva herb was born for; this is its turning and unfolding. This roaring creature's venom goes to destruction.
Let the winds blow in all directions; let the rains rain on all sides. Flow forth your venom in all directions, like a cistern with a hundred streams.
From here Indra wheels forth the chariot garlanded with green; upon it he rides, licking as he crushes the brood of the serpent.
With that whereby thou, O Indra, didst smite the Dasyus, with that whereby thou didst crush Vṛtra — with that, O Śatakratu, do thou devour the offspring of the serpent.
The earth exulted in response, heaven responded, the sun responded, when Paidva, the horse-born one, with his cry swept away the serpents.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
When Paidva, the horse-born one, swept away the serpents with his cry, they lay along the earth like ropes with their fangs bitten off, festering.
The waters do not decay, nor does immortality wane, nor did Indrāṇī become a widow — let the poison not cleave to thee, as an arrow to a stone.
Indra and Agni, Mitra and Varuṇa, Tvaṣṭṛ, Aditi, and Bhaga — I invoke the swift Paidva: may this man of mine come to no harm.
Born straightway, he neighed and shook off the caul; by the cry of the victorious horse the serpents were slain one by one.
This hymn of praise to the worthy Jātavedas we fashion together with devotion, as a chariot; for his guidance over us is auspicious. O Agni, may we never suffer harm in thy friendship.
He for whom thou dost procure by sacrifice prospers; unhindered he dwells, acquiring excellent manly strength; he hastens onward — no affliction reaches him. O Agni…
We bring fuel; we prepare oblations for thee, attending upon thee season by season. O Agni, guide our thoughts further along the way of living…
May we be able to kindle thee; may we direct our thoughts aright — in thee the gods eat the oblation poured out. Do thou bring hither the Ādityas, for thou art their heat, O Agni…
Thou art the Adhvaryu and the ancient Hotṛ; the Praśāstṛ, the Potṛ; by birth the Purohita. Wise one, knowing all priestly offices, thou dost fulfill them, O Agni…
As guardian of the quarters the creatures move about — both the bipeds and the quadrupeds — through the nights. Thou art the brilliant intelligence of the Dawn, the great one, O Agni…
Thou who art of fair aspect on all sides and of like appearance, even when far away thou blazest forth like lightning. Even through the darkness of night dost thou see, O divine Agni…
May the chariot of the one who presses soma be foremost among the gods; may our praise be hard to overcome. Know this, and cherish our words, O Agni…

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
With thy weapons smite away those of evil speech, hard to overcome; whosoever are devourers, whether far or near. Then make an easy path for the sacrificer who sings thy praise, O Agni…
When thou dost yoke the ruddy red steeds to thy chariot, wind-driven — thy roar is like that of a bull; then thou dost impel the forests with thy smoke-banner, O Agni…
Even birds were afraid at thy roar, when thy sparks that feed on grass scattered abroad. Let there be an easy road for thy chariots, O Agni…
Thou dost sustain the will of Mitra and Varuṇa; the wrath of the Maruts — wondrous — is turned away. Be gracious to us; may their mind return in favor, O Agni…
Thou art the divine Mitra of the gods, wondrous; the dear Vasu of the Vasus at the sacrifice. May we dwell in thy most wide-spreading protection, O Agni…
That is thy good gift: kindled in thine own house, fed with soma, most gracious to old age — thou dost bestow treasure and wealth upon the pious offerer. O Agni, may we never suffer harm in thy friendship.
He to whom thou hast given rich wealth, O giver of goodly goods — sinless thou, O Aditi, in thy wholeness — him whom thou dost urge on with thy auspicious might: may we be possessed of offspring and of thy bounty.
Do thou, O Agni, knowing the way of good fortune, extend here the life of us, O divine one. May Mitra and Varuṇa grant us that, and Aditi, Sindhu, Earth, and Heaven.
What is the garment of Indra, what of Agni, what the raiment of Viṣṇu, of Tvaṣṭṛ, of Varuṇa? What of Bṛhaspati and of King Soma — clad in what shall the Maruts let the rain fall?
What are the elements of Rudra? What is the great garment of Vāyu, of the swift ones? What do Pūṣan, Brahmaṇaspati, and all the gods bear and sustain?
What is the common garment of the gods, wherein their harmony was established? Where does Night settle to rest, and where does Day — where does this cloud that gathers and disperses come to be?

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
By what means do the waters bear up the sky? Who is the guide that leads with equal rising? Of the wind, of the lightnings, of the thunderer — I ask of thee the paths of the waters and of Agni.
I ask thee of Pṛṣatī and of Rohiṇī; I ask thee of the calf together with its mother. I ask thee directly of Indra, and of the lord of assemblies among the assemblies.
Who assigned the names of birds, who of cattle, who of serpents among those who were the divine folk? Who bestowed the name upon this living creature — declare that to us.
How many ascents cause one to mount to the light, by which the Rohita mounted to heaven — bearers of kingship, bearers of dominion, bearers of riches, givers of riches, those for whom grain is wealth?
Who strides forth fourfold in his greatness? Whom do the seers guard with unwearied vigilance? I ask thee directly of the Puruṣa — how many are the limbs of Death? Dost thou know them?
That thunderbolt which the bull of all peoples, Indra, fashioned, rivalling the serpents — wherewith the bounteous one crushed Vṛtra — declare that to us, if indeed thou knowest it.
Who assigned the names of mountains, who bestowed the names of forest lords and plants? I ask thee of the navel of the world; I ask thee of the cow — which ones directly?
The divine couches, the divine treasuries — where are they here? Declare them to us if thou knowest them. I ask thee how many are the altars of oblation, from which Agni, the immortal, knowing it, carries the offering poured by mortals on behalf of mortals.
He who in dream comes alone with darkness, seizing the limbs and the eye of a man — he departs at dawn with the darkness again; he goes toward the light — where, tell me, does he settle?
The lord of vows, the overlord, the maker of sweetness, the lord of honey — I ask thee of all the gods; and those who feed on the unoffered oblation — how many are they?

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Who gazes round upon this from the mid-air, from whom at first vital power arose? That great one — from whom did he fear, becoming fearless? From the corner of whose mouth, when yoked, did blood flow forth? Where indeed is that?
Thus some go forth, and thus some others — southward, westward, northward, eastward some advance. The meeting point of all of them here together — he, having become one, moves about knowing all.
A mote of light there was; it came together out of the mind. It spread abroad; it held an embryo. That embryo grew; grown, it said: "Wife!" To her Prajāpati offered oblation, saying "Thou who art firmly established" and "Thou who movest firmly." Prajāpati fashioned two bowls: "Part asunder; do not scorch me — looking upon the great world" — and from them he was born. Of that one born, Heaven-and-Earth were the two flanks, the two oceans were the two hollows, Sun-and-Moon were the two eyes, the Virāj was the head. From that one thus born all evils flee; all evils flee from him who knows this.
Indra, knowing, carried the divine waters with both arms for Varuṇa; all the Ādityas consecrated him, that fierce king, for the great battle. May those waters, the rājasūya waters, be favorable to us.
[The four verses beginning with] 'Of golden hue' — [rubric indicating four verses of the Golden-Hued Waters hymn to be recited here].
The divine waters, honey-sweet, yielding strength, the rājasūya waters that bring well-being — those with which Mitra and Varuṇa were consecrated — [may those waters be favorable to us].
Those bright ones, sent forth by Varuṇa, move onward — divine waters that bear the golden spring; those that purify in concert with the sacred utterance — [may those waters be favorable to us].
The waters that carry from the ocean up to heaven, and from heaven release themselves upon the earth; those with which the sovereign Maruts roam — [may those waters be favorable to us].

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Those that bear immortality, that carry sweet honey, those that the seers seized in the companionship of the gods; those by which Indra was led beyond his foes — [may those waters be favorable to us].
Those that fill wealth to the brim for the mortal who is devout and generous, who desires the gods; whose milk is inexhaustible among inexhaustible things — [may those waters be favorable to us].
Those that have golden ornaments, that bear banners, purifying themselves — the milk-cows that flow toward the ocean; those that Parjanya carries in the atmosphere — [may those waters be favorable to us].
When the Rathantara and the Bṛhat sāmans are sung, they invigorate lordly power and extend life; those by which the swift steeds are made to course in the three contests — [may those waters be favorable to us].
Those in whose company Indra the Vṛtra-slayer, lord of riches, drank the pressed Soma; those that the seven seers, the inspired poets, purify — [may those waters be favorable to us].
The seven seers consecrated Bharata; they established the realm in him, rich in sacrificial fees; the gods endowed Manu with vital breath for his offspring — [may those waters be favorable to us].
Those with which the wise ones sprinkle the eastward-facing sacrifice; those with which they purify the honey-mixed Soma; those by which all this stirring universe lives — [may those waters be favorable to us].
Those whose drops have become full of honey; those that swell with ghee-rich agreement and with sweetness; those waters that Soma leads forth by the sacred word — [may those waters be favorable to us].
Those at whose feet the strength-giving ghee flows; those that purify themselves in the wake of Soma's outpouring; pregnant ones, with young calves, rich in ghee — may those waters, the rājasūya waters, be favorable to us.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Inspired thoughts were born; those that know the way to heaven came forward through the sacred word to the places of the well-spoken hymns. The rājasūya waters gave forth their streams of milk; the god Savitṛ impelled all the worlds.
Soma the king, Bhava the king, Paśupati lord of beasts, Varuṇa the steadfast in vow — those gods who were present at the rājasūya, let them bestow upon you sovereign power, long life, and might.
He stood up, he rose, the inspired sage was born; he stepped over his foes, he wielded his arms in battle; he thrust Nirṛti far away toward the distant quarters; and with the sun he mingled, with its rays.
I beheld you descending, as if from heaven to earth; I beheld Rudra, the blue-throated, the crest-bearing, as he cast his shaft.
The dreadful one climbed down from heaven and stood established upon the earth. O people, behold this one — the blue-throated, the deeply crimson.
This Rudra, the healer with cooling medicines, the destroyer of no man's hero, comes hither. He has made your trembling to vanish utterly; may your feverish agitation depart.
Homage to you, O Bhava, in your brilliance; homage to you, O Bhava, in your wrath. Homage to you be unto both your arms, and homage also to your arrow.
That arrow which you hold in your hand to shoot, O lord of the mountain — make it auspicious, O Giriśa; do not harm my people.
With auspicious speech we address you, O Giriśa; so that for us all this world may be free of consumption and of glad spirit.
Your arrow that is most auspicious, your bow that has become auspicious, your quiver that is auspicious — with that grant us ease, that we may live.
That form of yours, O Rudra, which is auspicious, which is not terrible, which does not reveal evil — with that most tranquil body, O Giriśa, shine upon us.
That one yonder who is copper-red, tawny, and deeply crimson — and these Rudras here on all sides, stationed in the directions by thousands — from their wrath we seek protection.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
I beheld you descending, the blue-throated, the deeply crimson; the herdsmen too beheld you, and so did the women fetching water; all beings too beheld you — homage to you, to you thus seen.
Homage be to the blue-crested one, the thousand-eyed, the swift; and likewise to his host of attendants — to them too I have rendered homage.
Homage to your weapon, to the bow unstrung, to the bold one; homage I have rendered to both your arms, and to your bow.
Release the bowstring from both tips of the bow; and the arrows that are in your hand — scatter those away, O blessed one.
Having unstrung the bow, O thousand-eyed, O hundred-quivered one, shattering the heads of the arrow-shafts — come to us as benign, as bringer of joy.
The bow of the crested one is without its string, and he is free of arrows, quiverless; his arrows are without venom, benign is his quiver.
May the missile of your bow encompass us on all sides as a protection; and your quiver — place it far off from this one.
The bolt that was in your hand, the bow that was yours, O most bountiful — with that weapon guard us on all sides, keeping us free from disease.
The well-flanked, wish-yielding hundred-cooked-rice-offering has come to us, swelling with milk; milking forth vital strength, without stumbling, it prolongs the life of the sacrificer.
I seize her who is fit for sacrifice, who is eager, who brings well-being, who is replete with vitality, free from disease, worthy of meditation; may my whole world be among the gods — believing, I cook the hundred-rice-portion.
Bind and apply the goddess, the muñja-grass-girt hundred-rice-offering — for she is the wish-yielding one; do not injure her with the stone in your exuberance: she passes to the gods beyond the enemy.
Seize with the sacred formula this all-divine hundred-rice-offering — a hundred sins are hers to absorb; pressing with the stone as with a mountain, cause him to ascend above to the heavenly world.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Boldly cutting and slicing it into pieces, driving away evil, mix it with the skin-ladle; anointed by means of this daughter of Virāj, may she milk desire upon desire for the sacrificer.
Even as you cut joint by joint, do not tarry; make the portions for me separately; she who formerly was human, the hundred-rice-offering of many forms and golden hue, has gone to the gods.
The two-footed, two-handed man, the great subduer, bears the tree-piece with its knife-tip at the front; with it, skilled, he shall carve apart the joints of the inviolable one — sunder the divine hundred-rice-offering into a hundred parts.
Cut this reddish piece from the skin well, and having measured it, divide it into a hundred parts; releasing all the portions together, bestow abundance of wealth upon the sacrificer.
With the Ṛc-verse I place the pot upon the fire; I set you upon the earth, above the earth; bearing the flesh in the waters, do not tremble; may the Piśācas not slay you with their weapons.
Rise upward, do not collapse; spread out the inner atmosphere; having crossed beyond all the Rakṣasas — then ascend to heaven.
Go to heaven, O hundred-rice-offering; become the path for a thousand; become ten thousand, become a hundred thousand — be inexhaustible: thus you shall mount the heavenly world.
They partake of the hundred-rice-offering in a hundred ways; he who gives her ascends a hundred rungs; the Vāmadevya and the Naudhasa are her two wings — established on the third vault, she abides above the firmament.
The hundred-rice-offering, arranging itself in a hundred ways, fashions a hundred forms as she goes to the sky; may that goddess, easy to invoke, grant us shelter, and likewise grant ease to those in such condition.
The hundred-rice-offering, measured out with the twelve-day rite, has created a hundred Pṛṣṭha-hymns as she traverses the sky; encompassing all sacrifices beyond, may she establish the giver in abundance of wealth.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Go toward the soma-pressing sacrificers who have offered oblations, O hundred-rice-offering; having pervaded all sacrifices, become the pathway to the fulfillment of desire.
Go forward, O hundred-rice-offering; with sacrifice pass beyond those who have not sacrificed; you have climbed up to the gods, to where you shine on high in the triple heaven.
The first hundred-rice-offering has the nourishment-footed one as its base; truth is indeed your middle, immortality is your crown; O goddess, you fill both the worlds.
Order indeed are the hips, and the thighs in the body; power indeed are the arms, and that serves for strength; the belly follows the due course, and further the flanks — the hundred-rice-offering has reached all the worlds.
The first hundred-rice-offering is endowed with sight; the sun is indeed your eye, and the moon also; in accord with all the gods and with the seasons, you, O goddess, shall satiate the giver with satisfaction.
A hundred are her milkings, a hundred her calves; they distribute her, cooked, in a hundred shares; the seven worlds established in heaven — these you have won, O first of the hundred-rice-offerings.
Measured in hundreds, surpassing a thousand, as you go forth you have conquered the worlds, foremost O Śataudanā. She has attained the Sarvavedasa rite and the Vājapeya; all worlds the Śataudanā has encompassed.
Indra partook of the Śataudanā first, graciously disposed toward the seven ṛṣis; by her he seized the strength and vigor of the asuras, by her he ascended the heights of the celestial worlds.
Here Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Atri, Bharadvāja, Gotama, and here Vasiṣṭha — these with Kaśyapa as the seventh, let them partake first of this cooked Śataudanā.
Luminous is the foremost Śataudanā; proceeding toward the heavenly light she fashions the three luminaries. Her givers live in prosperity; wherever they are, they rejoice in common festivity with the gods.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The great Śataudanā, whose wings are the meters, going toward heaven has brought forth the three chants. They have found the year, the overlord of seasons, as her lord.
Surpassing the Agniṣṭoma and the Atirātra, O Śataudanā — having attained all the sacrifices, spread wide through the fire-altar built in layers.
Surpassing what belongs to the Aśvamedha and the Dvādaśāha, O Śataudanā — having attained the three-night rite with the press-day, she equals the Vājapeya.
Those who have sacrificed with thousands of offerings, those who have presented oblations in the Agnihotra, those who have sacrificed with all sacrifices — all of these the Śataudanā attains.
Auspicious I make your joints, O blessed one; auspicious too are the portions of flesh that are consumed. Whatever bone the sacrificial slaughterer has broken — that which is disjointed in you, let Tvaṣṭṛ restore.
Whatever worlds have been won by sacrifice, whatever meters have been obtained — all those worlds does he attain who gives the Śataudanā.
Vibrant, a maiden, youthful, dwelling within the house — Night belonging to the divine Savitṛ and Bhaga; unharmed as a horse, easy to invoke, her splendor gathered, she has filled heaven and earth with her greatness.
Deep, she has descended over all things; tireless, she has ascended to the highest peak. Eager Night spreads out along the benign ridge, like Mitra with her own powers.
O Night, worthy of heroes, deserving of praise, blessed, nobly born — come hither; be well-disposed; may I be here with cheerful mind. Protect us with the riches born of heroes, the ample wealth in horses and in cattle.
Eager Night, you have assumed the splendor of the lion, of the piśāca, of the tiger, of the leopard; the redness of the horse, the wizardry of man — shining abroad, you take on many forms.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Propitious Night and Sun by day — the mother of frost, easy to invoke, be good to us. O blessed one, heed this hymn of praise whereby I honor you in all directions.
O Night of brilliant radiance, take pleasure in our praise as a king takes pleasure. May we be possessed of all heroes, may we be possessed of all wealth, as you shine forth continuously, one Dawn after another.
You indeed bear the name Śamyā; those who would despoil my wealth — here let Night drive those away; then shall no thief be found, then shall no enemy be found.
You are auspicious, O Night, like a pressed cup; youthful, you uphold all that is of the form of the cow. Seeing with full eyes, touching my forms, you have released the divine golden ornaments belonging to the Ādityas.
Whosoever today comes as a thief, a mortal of sinful life, an enemy — encountering him, may Night strike off his throat, strike off his head.
His feet go not forward as they go, his hands do not reach as they stretch. Whosoever approaches in filth — crushed, he departs. He departs indeed, he departs; he has departed onto the dry stump.
O Night, make the serpent blind, motionless as smoke, headless. Strike out the eyes of the wolf; strike the thief into the wooden trap.
O Night, whatever bullocks of yours are sharp-horned and swift-footed — with them carry us across today, ever carrying us beyond all difficult passages.
Night after night, passing through unharmed in body, may we cross over; may our enemies not cross, as those who cannot swim through the deep.
As a millet grain falling down, cast upward, is found no more — even so, O Night, cast down the one who plots evil against us.
Drive away the thief, the plunderer of dwelling, the cattle-stealer, and the robber; and also him who, having tied a rope about a horse's head, would lead it off.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Whatever iron-rich wealth they distribute today, O Night of great blessing — come, make us resplendent with it; thereafter you approach others.
Hand us over to Dawn entirely guiltless, O Night. May Dawn give us a share of the day; the day belongs to you, O Night of brilliant radiance.
From all the quarters it blows together, resonant with heaven; from thence may Mādhava protect us with sweetness. May Agni the god, hard to cross, undeceivable, guard this sovereign power and protect us.
May the Rathantara protect us with its sāman-chants, all-formed with the Gāyatrī metre. By the twelve-day sacrifice the praise-hymn of the days — may the ocean of speech fill this might.
Fierce the conquest of the quarters, sustainer of life, pure on the bright day of might. With Indra as overlord, may he fill us from thence; may he uphold in me this sovereign power from all sides.
The great kingship, bearing the warrior-power, with grown virility, adorned with the strength of the Triṣṭubh, of fierce heroism — may Indra guard this lustre with praises through the fifteenfold, together with the wind and the ocean.
The eastern quarter, sharing in glory, itself glorious; all the gods, the luminous one on the days of the rainy season — let this sovereign power be hard to cross, its might unconquered, overpowering, one that overpowers.
In the Vairūpa sāman I declare this — may I be able; with the Jagatī metre I make it enter among the clans. All the gods by the seventeenfold — this fierce sovereign power, accompanied by flood-waters.
May the supporting quarter uphold this sovereign power; among those who hope for refuge may the might be as Mitra. May Mitra and Varuṇa, discerning on the autumnal days, grant great shelter to this sovereign power.
In the Vairāja sāman rests my wisdom; the virile force and might gathered through the Anuṣṭubh. May Mitra and Varuṇa protect this sovereign power, Mitra-like, with moist-giving strength, unto overlordship.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The universal sovereign of the quarters, the powerful one whose sāmans are of might — may the season of winter fill us through its extension. May the Bṛhatī and Śakvarī, born from healing, and the ghee-bright one protect this sacrifice of ours.
The heavenly one of good milking, rich in milk for us — may the divine goddess of the quarters, the ghee-bright one, protect us. You are guardian before and behind; O Bṛhaspati, yoke the southward speech.
O mistress of existence in the twenty-one-fold praise, in the wind pervading all — sing out for us. May the direction rich in ghee, O Savitṛ, unto overlordship; the direction rich in milk be our delight.
The upward quarter, the delight of the directions, of the plants — may Savitṛ impel us through the year, through the day. Rich in the Paṅkti of sāmans and metres — may the one who has no born enemy be comfortable to us.
The pillar of heaven, the support of the earth, the mistress of this world, wife of Viṣṇu — may she who quickens, all-pervading, of good oblation, be comfortable to us in the lap of Aditi.
The firm quarter, wife of Viṣṇu, not terrible, mistress of this — she who was thought of through might: may Bṛhaspati, Mātariśvan, and Vāyu, the joining winds, sing out for us.
He who is our father, our begetter, our disposer, who engendered among the existent what truly exists — he, desiring wealth through blessing, has entered into the first covering, into the boon.
Turn toward us, O Earth, together with the sacrifice, together with milk. May Agni, urged onward, the drinker of the final share, descend.
Whatever is bright in thee, O Agni, whatever is pure, whatever is radiant, and whatever is fit for sacrifice — that we bring to the gods.
Refreshment and vigour — I take these hence from the womb of sacrifice, from the abode of the great one. May it enter into our cattle, into our offspring; I cast away languor, debility, and disease.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
You are the prolonger of life, you are called the inspired medicine. Therefore, O Añjana, you are for our peace — made into that which brings well-being.
The jaundice that arises again and again, the splitting of limbs, the visalpaka fever — let the añjana drive out entirely your every disease from your limbs to the outside.
The añjana, born from the earth, auspicious, life-giving to man — may it produce what is not ruinous, swift as a chariot, free from sin.
O Prāṇa, protect breath; O breath, be gracious to the living. O Nirṛti, free us from the bonds of dissolution.
You are the womb of the Sindhu, the flower of lightnings. The wind is breath, the sun is sight, the milk of heaven.
O divine Añjana, O Traikakuda, protect me on all sides. Neither the external herbs nor the mountain ones surpass you.
He released the strong middle portion — the destroyer of demons, the disperser of disease. Driving away all diseases, destroying them, the overpowering one expelled them from here.
Much falsehood, O King Varuṇa, has a man spoken. From that, O you of a thousand powers, free us from transgression on every side.
What we have said — \"O inviolable waters,\" \"O Varuṇa\" — from that, O you of a thousand powers, free us from transgression on every side.
May Mitra and Varuṇa follow after you, O Añjana. Having followed you far, may it grow again for enjoyment.
As one debt is discharged by another debt, carry the sorcery back to the house of its maker. O collyrium, O evil-hearted one of the eye-spell, shatter even the ribs.
Whatever ill-omen of evil dreams rests upon us, upon our cattle, or within our house — let that evil-hearted one who has gone home to his mother release it back to the dear one who sent it.
This mountain-born collyrium, grown mighty with the vigour and vitality of the waters, born from Agni upon Jātavedas — four-hero-bestowing — let it make all the directions and the sub-directions auspicious for you.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The collyrium that bestows four heroes is bound upon you; may all the directions be free from fear for you. Stand firm as the desirable Savitṛ stands; let these peoples bring tribute to you.
Apply one, fashion one amulet, bathe with one, drink one of them. May the four-hero-granting collyrium guard us from the four Nirṛtis, from the bonds of seizure.
May Agni guard him with the means sacred to Agni — for breath and outbreath, for life-span, for radiance, for vital force, for brilliance, for well-being, for good estate. Svāhā.
May Indra guard me with the means sacred to Indra — for breath and outbreath, for life-span, for radiance, for vital force, for brilliance, for well-being, for good estate. Svāhā.
May Soma guard me with the means sacred to Soma — for breath and outbreath, for life-span, for radiance, for vital force, for brilliance, for well-being, for good estate. Svāhā.
May Bhaga guard me with the means sacred to Bhaga — for breath and outbreath, for life-span, for radiance, for vital force, for brilliance, for well-being, for good estate. Svāhā.
May the Maruts guard me with their hosts — for breath and outbreath, for life-span, for radiance, for vital force, for brilliance, for well-being, for good estate. Svāhā.
O Agni, O god, giver of life-span, filling him with old age, ghee-faced and ghee-backed — drinking ghee and the lovely immortal essence of the cow, lead this man to old age as a father leads his son.
Bestow long life upon him, O Jātavedas; firmly place offspring in him, O Tvaṣṭṛ, from on high. Grant him the full swelling of riches, O Savitṛ — may this man of yours live a hundred autumns.
Establish this man in life-span and radiance, O Agni; make his seed dear, O Varuṇa, O King Mitra. Grant him shelter as a mother, O Aditi; may he be vigorous unto old age, O All-Gods.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
May Agni further extend your life-span; may Soma further establish your nourishment. May Indra with the Maruts speak on your behalf; may Aditi together with the Ādityas grant you shelter.
The Revatī stars fashioned your pervasion; the Kṛttikās shaped you. The active ones stretched you out; the prayers, the Avāgnāyī constellations, commingled you in weaving.
A thousand threads they set along the borders; eighty threads the women spread in the middle, fearless. O divine women, for the deity Savitṛ as a garment — great indeed was the greatness of these goddesses.
Stand upon this stone; become firm as stone itself. Crush down those who wish harm; overpower those who array their forces against you.
With that by which the gods encompassed the divine Savitṛ — with that same means, O Bṛhaspati, encompass and establish this man for sovereignty.
Encompass this Indra and establish him for long life and great sovereignty — so that you may lead him to old age; long may he remain wakeful in sovereignty.
Encompass this Soma and establish him for long life and great hearing — so that you may lead him to old age; long may he remain wakeful in hearing.
Invest him, invest him with radiance; make death come only at old age, extend his life-span long. Bṛhaspati gave forth this garment to be put on by King Soma.
Go well to old age; put on the garment; be one who overcomes the curse of the young cows. Live a hundred autumns, brilliant in radiance; clothe yourself in the full swelling of riches.
Put on this garment all around for well-being; become one who protects against the curse of the sowers. Live a hundred autumns in fullness; lovely and living, may you distribute riches abundantly.
At every yoking we invoke the most fervent Indra; at every contest, as friends, we call him for aid.
Golden-hued, unaging, rich in heroes, dying only at old age — enter into your offspring thus. So has Agni declared; so too has Soma declared; so Bṛhaspati, Savitṛ, and Indra.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
With this uppermost thread, the new garment fit for tying — preceding in course, manifold in form and ornament, with auspicious aspect, coeval in aging, rich in heroes — with this may the gods extend his life-span.
He whose skirt the Brāhmaṇas take hold of — loosening the waistband, extending his life-span — may the gods delight in that man's invocation of the gods; may well-being attend him always.
Take up a different garment; clothe yourself in it — I cut away this caul that clings to you. May the seers clothe you for old age; may Sūrya and Bhaga extend your life-span.
Him whose first garment I remove — may all the gods protect you, that one. May many brothers, well-grown, growing in prosperity, be born after you, O well-born one.
Unsmit, be unsmit; firm, unite with firmness. Crush down those who wish harm; overpower those who array their forces against you.
Mitra is the overseer of the earth. May he protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
Varuṇa is the overseer of the waters. May he protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
Vāyu is the overseer of the atmosphere. May he protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
Sūrya is the overseer of the sky. May he protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
Candramā is the overseer of the lunar mansions. May he protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Vasu is the overseer of the years. May he protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
Saṃvatsara is the overseer of the seasons. May he protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
Agni is the overseer of the forest lords. May he protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
Indra is the overseer of actions. May he protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
Savitā is the overseer of impulses and procreations. May he protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
Viṣṇu is the overseer of the mountains. May he protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
Tvaṣṭā is the overseer of forms. May he protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
Rudra is the overseer of cattle. May he protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
Soma is the overseer of the milky substances. May he protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
Parjanya is the overseer of the plants. May he protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Samudra is the overseer of the rivers. May he protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
Hiṃkāra is the overseer of the Sāmans. May he protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
Sarasvatī is the overseer of speech. May she protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
Pūṣan is the overseer of the paths. May he protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
Gāyatrī is the overseer of the metres. May she protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
Bṛhaspati is the overseer of the gods. May he protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
Prajāpati is the overseer of creatures. May he protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
Yama is the overseer of the ancestors. May he protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this bodily invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
The fathers — the most distant, the nearer, then the grandfather — may they all protect me in this sacred utterance, in this rite, in this priestly office, in this divine invocation, in this intention, in this blessing. Svāhā.
O gods of the gods — gods, super-gods among gods — pass beyond! The first among the second, the second among the third.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Three times eleven, the all-gods, the universal fires — great and mighty ones, do not seize me. May I be capable of this which I now perform. Svāhā.
His countenance becomes like that of a thunder-cloud when, clad in armour, he goes into the lap of battle. With body unpierced, conquer thou; may the greatness of the armour carry thee through.
With the bow let us win cattle; with the bow let us win contests; with the bow let us win fierce battles. May the bow turn the enemy's desire away; with the bow let us conquer all armies.
Hissing repeatedly, she draws close to the ear, embracing her dear friend. Like a woman she whispers to him stretched upon the bow — this bowstring carries him safe through the assembly of battle.
Moving together like a woman at the assembly, may she nourish him in her lap as a mother nourishes her son. These two bowstrings, quivering and in accord, shall pierce the foes and repel the enemies.
The father of many, his offspring are many; descending into battle he creates wide space. The quiver, its fastenings, and all the armies — bound upon the back, he conquers when sped forth.
Standing in the chariot, the skilled charioteer drives the horses forward wherever he desires. Marvel at the greatness of the reins; the reins hold the mind in check from behind.
Making fierce clamour, the bull-handed warriors, spurring on the horses together with the chariots, destroy the enemies by advancing upon them with their forelegs, crushing the foes without wavering.
"Chariot-bearer" is his oblation-name — there where his weapon is laid and his armour rests. Upon that prosperous chariot may we be seated, all our days gladdening our hearts.
Sweet in assembly are our forefathers, bestowers of vigour, taking refuge in difficulty, mighty and profound; of brilliant host, strong in arrows, irresistible, heroic in battle, broad-ranged, overcoming hordes.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Brahman-knowing forefathers, partakers of Soma — may Heaven and Earth be auspicious and free of distress for us. May Pūṣan, increaser of cosmic order, guard us from evil-going; protect us — let no evil-voiced one have power over us.
May Bṛhaspati guard us from behind and from above, from below, from the one who would do us harm. May Indra guard us from the front and from the midst; may he, the friend, make wide space for his friends.
The eagle's feather she wears; her tooth is the fawn; bound with cowhide sinew she flies forth when sped. Where men surge together and scatter — there may these arrows grant us shelter.
The eagle is her garment; clarified butter her mouth; mind her gold; the arrows are the winged ones. Let them not strike us as they swoop from yonder — sped hence, O Savitṛ, may they conquer.
Like a serpent with its coils it winds about the arm, warding off the bowstring's stroke. The hand-guard, knowing all the ways of movement, a man shall guard a man from death.
They strike the ridge of their backs; they smite upon their haunches. O horse-whip, urge them on; plant the horses firm in the battles.
Vigour gathered from Heaven and Earth, might assembled from the forest trees, the swelling power of the waters — brought round with cowhides: with oblation worship the chariot as Indra's thunderbolt.
Thou art Indra's thunderbolt, the battle-face of the Maruts, the womb of Mitra, the navel of Varuṇa. So, O divine chariot, enjoying this our gift of oblation, receive thou the offered portions.
O Forest Lord, be thou of firm limb; be our friend who carries us forward, possessed of good heroes. Bound with cowhides, O chariot, make thyself firm; may he who mounts thee conquer what is to be conquered.
Cause Earth and Heaven to resound; let the wide-spread world take note of thee, in many places. O war-drum, in unison with Indra and the gods, drive the enemies away — ever farther away.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Roar aloud; lay power and might into us; thunder forth, pressing back misfortunes. Drive away ill-omen, O war-drum, from hence; thou art the fist of Indra — make thyself strong.
May they conquer going forward; may they conquer here in this fearful fray; may the banner-bearing war-drum resound aloud. May our horse-winged men take flight together; O Indra, may our chariot-warriors conquer.
May Indra prepare the footing for the chariot; may those whom Maghavan has mounted be victorious. Like a cowherd he yokes together with cattle; born unhurt, the foremost, he who would conquer.
Like the thunder of Parjanya is the roar of its breath; like that of Indra and Agni its clamour rings out. A warrior of a thousand, winning a hundred, winning ten thousand — O chariot, be gracious here.
The wings of an eagle, the arms of a deer, the fist of Indra, the battle-face of the Maruts — bound with cowhides thou art; make thyself firm.
He lifts his arms together, stretching them as one; both his flanks he adorns, fearsome in his gleaming. He drives forth the bright mantle with his powers; he casts off the new garments from the mothers.
Fierce are thy rims, fierce are thy tires, fierce are the pins of the great chariot. The tongue-shaft and the bamboo reeds, thy bendings are fierce; Agni is the eye, the forward-runner of the chariot. Grinding down the non-allies, go thou against the foes.
The spokes and the hubs — that is thy strength, O axle; fierce are thy two boxes together with those who sit in them. The leather thongs of the pins, the box-sheaths, the standing place, the fastening, and thy seat — all are firm.
Strength is the stall; one limb is the fawn — stride forth; press on into the great realm. The reins have slain Vṛtra with this one; fierce is he with lordship and progeny.
Mount, O conquering one; with swiftness overcome the rivals; a warrior of a thousand, grinding down, go against the foes. Perform heroic deeds in the span of the back-ridge — thus: welcome this very chariot of his.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
May the eight eyes of the seers bow in unison; may the illumined horses run straight. May the pillar-post support thee like a father — as it revolves, hold him in thy lap; may his life-span be extended.
Sewn by the seers, he is fastened in the chariot; born in the mind of the bow, keeper of the bow. These broad-middled ones, fashioned by the seers, are to be cast before the horses for their welfare — may the gods grant thee shelter through them.
We invoke Agni, the lords of the forest, the healing plants, and the creeping herbs; Indra, Bṛhaspati, and Sūrya — may they release us from distress.
We invoke the divine Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, and Pūṣan; Tvaṣṭṛ, the foremost, we invoke — may they release us from distress.
We invoke the king Varuṇa, Mitra, Viṣṇu, and also Bhaga; Aṃśa and Vivasvat we invoke — may they release us from distress.
We invoke the Gandharvas and the Apsarases, the twin Aśvins, and Brahmaṇaspati; the god whose name is Aryaman — may they release us from distress.
We invoke Vāta, Parjanya, the atmosphere, and the directions; all the quarters too we invoke — may they release us from distress.
Day and night we invoke here; both Sūrya and Candramās; all the Ādityas we invoke — may they release us from distress.
May Day and Night release me from the curse, and also Dawn; may the celestial Soma release me — he whom they call Candramās.
The five kingdoms of plants, with Soma as their chief, we proclaim — hemp, darbha-grass, barley, and sahas — may they release us from distress.
The seven domestic animals and whatever wild beasts roam the forest; the birds and the winged ones we invoke — may they release us from distress.
We invoke here Bhava and Śarva, the fierce one and he who is lord of cattle; the arrows of theirs that we know of — may they release us from distress.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
We invoke the sacrifice and the sacrificer, the ṛc-verses, the sāmans as healing powers; the yajus-formulas and the hotṛ-priests we invoke — may they release us from distress.
We invoke the seasons and the lords of the seasons, the seasonal plants and the yearly ones; years, full years, and months — may they release us from distress.
We invoke the sky, the lunar mansions, the earth, the yakṣas, and the mountains; the oceans, the rivers, and the streams — may they release us from distress.
The seven seers we invoke here, the divine waters, and Prajāpati; the Fathers with Yama as their chief we invoke — may they release us from distress.
All the gods we invoke here, true to their bonds, those who grow great through sacred order; together with all their consorts — may they release us from distress.
The Ādityas, the Rudras, the Vasus, the divine Atharvans among the gods; the Aṅgirases, those of inspired wisdom — may they release us from distress.
Those gods who dwell in heaven, and those who dwell in the atmosphere; those mighty ones who are established upon the earth — may they release us from distress.
These gods — rise up eastward from the south, you mighty ones from the east and from the north; all gods assembling together — may they release us from distress.
We invoke the arāyas, the rākṣasas, the serpents, and the puṇyajanas; the hundred and one deaths we invoke — may they release us from distress.
The five divine directions and the twelve divine seasons; those who are the fangs of the year — may they always be benign to us.
We invoke the beings and the lord of beings and him who is master of all beings; all beings in their entirety we invoke — may they release us from distress.
As far as the sky extends, as far as the earth extends, as far as the sun moves around — so far do you, O potent plant, protect all around, O Arundhatī.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The uninjured one digs you up; for the sake of freedom from injury I dig you up. May all of our two-footed and four-footed creatures be without disease.
You are the sister of the gods; you are the companion who moves with the Maruts. Whatever living man you reach, that person shall not suffer harm.
Arundhatī is your name; you are in the third heaven from here. There is the stalk of immortality — by means of that we call to you.
Benign to you be the heart-pleasing waters; benign to you the spring-fed streams. Benign be Vāyu, benign Bṛhaspati; may Sūrya warm you with benevolence.
May Indra and Agni be benign to you; may Night be laid down in benevolence. Benign to you be the plants in the earth; benign too may the healing herbs be to you.
Among many plants I have found you, O potent herb; O Arundhatī, I have brought you hither — "may she bring us safely across" is what they say.
As if striving to reach a living man, may Arundhatī shine forth; this divinely luminous healing goddess cures even him who is afflicted by wind-sickness.
Sprinkle it upon us, do that — he shall indeed be free of disease. As healer of wind-sickness the divine Arundhatī has come.
Fear not — you shall not die; you shall indeed be free of disease. As healer of wind-sickness the divine Arundhatī has come.
The Arundhatī-plants speak together like cows going out to graze. Go to this afflicted one; make him free of ailment, free of ailment.
Do thou, O herb, make this man of mine one who dies only of old age. For thou art Arundhatī, queen of all herbs.
For thou art Trāyamāṇā, life-giving, full of potency. O Arundhatī, I have brought thee hither — 'from this one deliver him,' so I say.
For one pierced by a poisoned weapon, and for the evil and its evil venom — O Arundhatī, thou art the poison-destroyer of that poison.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
For one bitten by a snake and by that evil — [Arundhatī, thou art the poison-destroyer of that poison].
For one struck down by a wind-demon and by that evil — [Arundhatī, thou art the poison-destroyer of that poison].
And by Bhava — [for one struck down by that evil, Arundhatī, thou art the poison-destroyer of that poison].
And by Śarva — [for one struck down by that evil, Arundhatī, thou art the poison-destroyer of that poison].
And by Rudra — [for one struck down by that evil, Arundhatī, thou art the poison-destroyer of that poison].
And for one struck down by Paśupati — [that evil, Arundhatī, thou art the poison-destroyer of that poison].
And for one struck down by the fierce deity Ugra — [that evil, Arundhatī, thou art the poison-destroyer of that poison].
And for one struck down by Mahādeva — [that evil, Arundhatī, thou art the poison-destroyer of that poison].
And for one struck down by Īśāna, and for the evil and its evil venom — O Arundhatī, [thou art the poison-destroyer of that poison].
Whatever poison is in the earth, whatever poison is upon the plants — [Arundhatī, thou art the poison-destroyer of that poison].
Whatever poison brahmins collect from herbs for a woman — [Arundhatī, thou art the poison-destroyer of that poison].
Whatever sharp, keenly-virulent poison brahmins compound — [Arundhatī, thou art the poison-destroyer of that poison].
He who has been struck down by death, by those through whom he is struck, he who has been bitten by sharp-fanged creatures — O Arundhatī, thou art the poison-destroyer of that poison.
Rouse thyself, rise up free of disease! Ascend to the highest realm. Thou dost live by a vessel of water — come hither to the city of the living.
O Apsarases, I split asunder your liver, I split asunder your urinary organ; the Caṇḍāla, the Arjuna, and the Vavṛtra — these of yours I split asunder.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The universal-folk Apsarases, the five-tribal, the great-golden-ornament, the crest-bearing — all those bubble-roaming spirits have been slain by Indra's thunderbolt.
With the base of the mortar, smite the blind-one, the dark-one — drive them away; strike down the calf-drinker.
From afar I saw these ones flying toward me, and from the sky too — those who bewitch the oblations of the gods; Indra smote the Apsarases.
Struck down, away with them from here — like female sorcerers driven from a threshing floor! Go to that man over there; away she goes to the ocean.
Let the celestial ones go to the sky; let the lake-dwellers go to the lake; whatever hiding-place belongs to Uluṅgula, to that very place let the Āsurī spirits go.
O Āskandikas, O Viskandikas, dance away in the direction of the far distance — together with the spotted dog.
The spotted one, the golden-giving, the celestial dog who roams everywhere — his name have I seized, for the sake of uninjured wholeness for this man.
Today, O Viraṇī, dance away in the direction of the far distance! I shall crush your dreadful backbones and your vertebrae too with sacred power.
Thirty-one horse-possessing ones, four Guṅguvas as well; ten propitious ones, ten Śṛtās, twenty-five long-haired ones — to these Uluṅgulukā Apsarases I have made obeisance.
Those [Apsarases] who swing upon the swing, clinging like mālavā creepers along the span — [the rest of the verse is not preserved].
Those who move in the east together with the rays of the Sun — [the rest of the verse is not preserved].
Those who move from below together with a cart and its canopy — [the rest of the verse is not preserved].
Those who move from the west together with blind darkness — [the rest of the verse is not preserved].
Those who move from the north together with rain and lightning — [the rest of the verse is not preserved].

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Those who gaze upward from below, with sidelong eye, of strange deeds — [the rest of the verse is not preserved].
Those who look down from above, wearing blue [garments] with [their] markings visible — [the rest of the verse is not preserved].
Those who roam through the atmosphere together with the wind and the storm-blast — [the rest of the verse is not preserved].
Those [who are] the four rivers.
From you, O Rudra, the most beneficent [remedies] are born; for you have become the bounteous one for us, for refreshment and healing. Drive away the disease-afflictions from us, drive away the anguish; chase far from us the diseases that spread in all directions.
You are the foremost of the gods, O Rudra, the most mighty of the mighty, O strong-armed one; rejoicing with a gracious mind you have become [what you are as] the son of Rudra.
Rouse up heroes for us with your medicines; may you, O bounteous lord accompanied by the Maruts, become wide [in your favour] for us. Carry us across to the far shore of distress in well-being; ward off all terrors from us.
You, O bull, are the greatest in sight [and in glory]; to this Rudra, the fierce and bountiful, the lord of heroes, we offer our prayer — that you may be auspicious to us for the biped and auspicious for the quadruped.
Where, O Rudra, is that hand of yours among these — the merciful, the healing, the cooling one — that removes the divine affliction?
Let the wasting disease, let Nirṛti go forth from us; let disease depart like an army put to rout. Away, away — leave behind your ancient haunts!
Worthy [of worship], you bear the strung bow; worthy, [you wear] the gleaming necklace of all forms. Worthy, you rule over all this moving [world]; nothing is far from you, nothing is beyond your reach — be present now; you behold all the earth on every side.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Homage to you, O lightning; homage to you, O thunder; homage to you, O thunderbolt, with which you hurl [destruction] in every direction.
O fierce king among the gods, may our people not be harmed; we destroy the rākṣasas and the disease-afflictions from us with the sacred word.
With the sacred word we destroy here whatever afflicts the limbs; the splinters of disease, and also the festering sores — these we lead away from here.
I lead you both, O Paśupati [and his consort], strengthening [you] with ghee and clarified butter. Him whom we hate and who hates us — his dwelling shall you two destroy.
Speak forth, O Paśupati [pair], on behalf of my biped and quadruped. Where the two who gave birth [have] struck, from there let my mother not be harmed.
The auspicious body that belongs to you two, O Rudra [pair]; the disease-inflicting forms that you two possess; the life-giving bodies that you two have — with those be merciful to us, you two.
The keepers of vows do not transgress their vows, speaking truth, quickening the sacred rites, [attending] the assemblies — he to whom these two worlds, both, are joined in mind and in heart.
He is Prajāpati of creatures; he duly protects and gives rain. He knows the jewel-medicine fetched from among the gods; with that be merciful to us, you two — for the sake of living, not of dying, and for the sake of unimpaired wholeness.
The virtuous ones sit united together for strength indeed. Whatever vital power belongs to them — it grows; the shining [firmament] shines.
Those two great shining [realms] of yours, in the atmosphere and also in heaven — through those two come to us, [keeping] all our heroes unharmed.
All our heroes, unharmed, have taken their stand in the shining [realm]; may the refreshing wealth in heaven — [that which goes] to those who cast [offerings] and that which is in the waters — come to us.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
I call upon Indra and Agni, the foremost pair; I summon the beneficent Maruts; I summon all the gods — may they protect this oblation of mine.
You, O Agni, first won immortality; as a god, you first conquered divinity. Your heart was established in heaven — O Jātaveda, grant us those auspicious waters.
Fire moves within fire, having entered — this one is the son of the seers, the overlord. For him I offer oblation with ghee; let him not cut off his share among the gods.
O Jātaveda — you gods who dwell in heaven, who are on the earth, who are in the wide mid-air, who are within the mountains, the hills, and the waters — keep lightning away.
Make friendship by the directions, O Jātaveda; make friendship by the quarters, O wise guardian. Do not harm our crops with the celestial fire with which the Maruts go forth in rivalry.
Flashing and thundering, you advance like a bull, roaring loudly. Fearsome Parjanya, this is your chariot — may it grant us shelter.
The Maruts who stretch out lightning and thunderbolt from above the flood — may they let them drop harmlessly for the sake of our all-desirable crops.
To those Maruts who brandish lightning and thunderbolt from the mid-air, from the wind, and from heaven — homage be to them, to their might.
May they pass by, well-marshalled, gentle, and most auspicious, along their path. O Indra, do not strike down our barley — with this rite we make you our ally.
Darbha grass, foremost of plants, with a hundred stalks, was born. Dispatched by the gods, this bull has come for our well-being, in accord with the Maruts.
You are the anger of the bull-eyed Asura; thus does Karṇa Kauvidā know you in this manner. Do not overwhelm me for twelve days — I ward it off.
My sword is of sharp iron, well-whetted by Indra and Agni. With it I drive away the troublesome thing: "Let it not go against my crops" — "Let it not strike my grain."

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
O Maruts, protect us from the small hailstones of heaven. With a branch of the Udumbara tree — with the far-seeing one — we drive away the thunderbolt.
O Maruts, show us favor against the bright hailstones of heaven. With a branch of the Udumbara tree — with the far-seeing one — we drive away the thunderbolt.
Pass from whirlwind to whirlwind, from mountain over mountain. Confined as you are to the hill, shatter trees — not barley.
With a tether, with a binding, with a restraint made of barley-straw I bind you fast. Confined as you are to the ridge, shatter grass — not barley.
Your name is Uśatī; Salindā is your name. Go to another of these — go to the one we hate.
Follow the stream flowing away yonder, follow the current going away yonder, run down following what moves away. From here we drive you away with potent sacred utterance.
Become water, become moisture, become the water of waters. Having become smaller than the smallest, go now into the lowest darkness.
Be gentle, be auspicious, be more auspicious than auspicious. Having become more yielding than foam, approach this grain crop.
Homage to you, O lightning, O thunder. Homage to you, O Agni — we place your missile far off; do not harm our bipeds, do not harm our quadrupeds.
We repel you, O overpowering one, with power; we block you with power. This great Indra-born force, resting in heaven above the earth — step onto the unploughed ground; O Indra, do not strike our barley.
Those waters that rise up from the ocean, those that come from springs, from rivers — may the serpent born of lightning, dwelling within, drive the thunderbolt away from here.
Homage to Antaka, to Mṛtyu — let this man remain here together with his vital breath. In the portion of Sūrya, in the realm of immortality, may your in-breath and out-breath take their delight here.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Bhaga has seized him upward, the radiant Soma has seized him upward; the Maruts, the gods, have raised him up — Indra and Agni have raised him for well-being.
Here is your vital force, here your breath, here your life-span, here your mind. With the divine word we bear you up out of the nooses of Nirṛti.
Rise up and do not fall down; loosening the foot-fetter of Death, do not sever yourself from this world, from the sight of Agni and Sūrya.
May Vāyu, Mātariśvan, blow for you; may the waters rain down their immortal gifts upon you; may Sūrya warm your body with well-being. Let Death be compassionate toward you — do not perish.
Your going is upward, O man, not a going-down; may your living make your vitality complete. Mount this immortal, pleasant chariot, and then in old age speak forth at the assembly.
Let not your mind go thither; let it not be lost. Do not stray from the living in intoxication; do not follow the Pitṛs. May all the gods protect you here.
Do not fix your gaze upon those who have gone, those who lead to the far realm. Ascend, come from darkness to light — we take hold of your hand.
Śyāma and Śabala, the two dogs of Yama, the road-guardians sent forth — come hither; do not stare away, do not stand there with your mind turned backward.
Do not travel this path — it is dreadful, the one by which they lead those who went before; so I declare it. Darkness lies yonder, O man; do not fall forward upon it. Fear lies beyond, but safety lies this side of you.
May the fires that dwell within the waters guard you; may that fire which men kindle guard you. May Vaiśvānara, Jātavedas, guard you. May the heavenly one not scorch you along with the lightning.
May Earth guard you, may Dyaus guard you; may Sūrya and Candramās guard you. Let the flesh-eater not assail you — keep away from Saṃkasuka from afar.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
May the mid-air with its divine weapon guard you; may Awareness and Counter-awareness guard you. May the Sleepless One and the Ever-wakeful guard you; may the Watcher guard you, and the Vigilant.
Let them guard you, let them protect you, let them shield you from distress. Homage to them; svāhā to them.
For the living, in the community, may Vāyu, Indra, Dhātṛ, the protecting Savitṛ establish you. Let not the breath forsake your strength — we call after your vital spirit.
Let neither the jaw nor the snap of teeth find you; let not the darkness; let not the tongue of the sacrificial grass cause your destruction — how could you perish? May the Ādityas and Vasus raise you up; may Indra and Agni raise you for well-being.
O gods, let this man be here only; let him not go from here to yonder. We ferry this one across from Death with a thousandfold heroic power.
I have ferried you across from Death; may the life-sustaining ones blow strength into you. Let not the disheveled-haired woman weep over you; let not she who wails with grief lament for you.
I have fetched you back; I have found you. You have returned, renewed. With every limb intact, all your sight, and all your life-span I have found for you.
Heaven has seized you upward, and Earth, and Prajāpati has seized you upward. The plants whose queen is Soma have ferried you across from Death.
As far as your light extended, darkness has retreated from you. Away from you we blow Death, Nirṛti, and wasting disease.
Grasp hold of this hearing of immortality; may your old age be unbroken. I bring back your vital force and your life-span. Do not go to the dust, to darkness — do not perish.
Come back to the light of the living, to the world; I carry you to a hundred autumns. I make your life-span ever longer and more extended. Let the nooses of Death, the curses, be released.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
From Vāyu I have recovered your breath; from Sūrya I have recovered your sight all around. Whatever mind is yours, in you I hold it steady. Awaken with all your limbs; speak, converse with your tongue.
With the breath of bipeds and quadrupeds I blow upon you as upon a fire just kindled. Homage to your eye, O Mṛtyu; I have paid homage to your breath.
Let this one live; let him not die — we stir this one back into life. I make the healing remedy for him. O Mṛtyu, do not slay this man.
The Jīvalā, the Naghāriṣā, the living herb — the protecting, enduring, powerful Arundhatī — these I invoke here for his inviolate well-being.
Speak favorably; do not seize him — release this one. Belonging to you entirely, let him who lives all his years be here. O Bhava and Śarva, show mercy, grant shelter; thrust evil away and bestow life.
May the weapon of the gods enfold you protectively. I ferry you across; I have carried you over from the dust of Death. Driving the flesh-eating fire away from afar, I place a boundary around you for the sake of life.
O Mṛtyu, speak favorably for this one; be gracious to him — let him go up from here. Uninjured, with all his limbs intact, well-formed, let him attain the enjoyment of the self through old age for a hundred years.
O Mṛtyu, the dusty downward path of yours — I have turned it away from him. Guarding this man from that path, we make the brahman a coat of armor for him.
I make for you breath and vital breath; let old age and death make long life and well-being. The messengers of Yama dispatched by Vaivasvata, all those who roam about — I drive them far away.
Far away — malice, dissolution, the seizing demon beyond, flesh-devouring Piśācas; whatever evil being there is, every Rakṣas — that we smite away like darkness.
From immortal Agni Jātavedas, long-lived and cognizant of all births, I take breath for you, as for Manu — so that you may be unharmed and immortal in fellowship. This I do for you; may this be fulfilled for you.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
May Heaven and Earth be auspicious to you, resting upon you without scorching heat, shining with splendour. May the sun warm you auspiciously; may the wind blow auspiciously upon your heart. May the heavenly, milk-rich waters flow auspiciously over you; may the plants be auspicious to you.
I have lifted you up from the lower region toward the higher earth. There let both Ādityas — Sun and Moon together — guard you.
The garment you put on for wearing, the girdle you fasten about yourself — we make that auspicious for your body; may it be unharmful in contact with you.
When, with a razor of fine keenness, the barber shaves off hair and beard — making the face beautiful, let it not rob this one of life.
Auspicious to you be rice and barley — not causing weakness, not causing oppression. These two repel disease; these two release from distress.
Whatever you eat, whatever you drink — the grain, the produce of tillage, the milk — what is to be eaten and what is not to be eaten: all food I make free of poison for you.
To both Day and Night together we entrust you. From the greedy devouring demons — protect this one of ours on all sides.
May there be for you a hundred, ten thousand years of life; two ages, three, four. May Indra and Agni, may all the gods consent to this without anger.
For autumn, for winter, for spring, for summer we entrust you. May the rainy seasons be gentle for you — those in which the plants flourish.
Death rules the two-footed; Death rules the four-footed. From that Death, lord of cattle, I lift you up. May he not slay you.
Unharmed, you shall not die; you shall not die — fear not. Truly, they do not perish there; they do not go to the lower realm of dust.
Truly everything lives there — cow, horse, man, beast — where this sacred formula is performed as a protective enclosure for life, for bliss.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
May it guard you on all sides from the sorcery of kindred folk, from those of equal standing. Be one who does not wither; be immortal, one who outlives; may your vital forces not abandon your body.
May all the gods sustain you with immortality; may Paśupati be your advocate. May Savitṛ make you free of sickness; may breath enter you for the sake of life.
The hundred-and-one deaths, the fatal nights that are not to be outlived — from those let the gods release you, above and beyond Agni Vaiśvānara.
I kindle the strong slayer of Rakṣases; I approach the shelter of the most widely spread Friend. Agni, whetted and kindled with rites — may he protect us from harm by day, by night.
Touch with your flame those who grow strong with iron fangs, O Jātavedas, when kindled. With your tongue seize the fool-gods; having consumed the flesh-eaters, close your mouth upon them.
O bearer of both kinds, apply your fangs — fierce and whetted — upon the lower and the upper. And roam through the atmosphere, O Agni; crush the sorcerers with your jaws; fall upon them.
O Agni, pierce the skin of the sorcerer; may the fierce thunderbolt strike him down with heat. Shatter his joints, O Jātavedas; the flesh-eating fire, hungering for raw flesh, picks him apart.
O Agni, bending your arrows with sacrificial rites, smearing your shafts with speech and with thunderbolts — with those, pierce the sorcerers in their hearts; shatter the arms of those who oppose us.
Wherever you now see him, O Jātavedas, O Agni — standing still or moving about — or a sorcerer flying through the atmosphere: pierce him through with darkness, wholly, you who are whetted.
And shatter the sorcerer with your spears when seized, O Jātavedas; and when he is about to fly. Strike first, O blazing Agni; may the raw-flesh-eating female spirits, shrieking, devour him.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Declare here, O Agni, which one he is — the sorcerer who hears this. Seize him, O youngest one, with fuel; surrender him to the sight of the man-watching eye.
With your keen eye, O Agni, guard the sacrifice; lead it forward eastward to the Vasus, O wise one. Blazing against the fierce Rakṣases — may the sorcerers not deceive you, O watcher of men.
O watcher of men, look upon the Rakṣas among the settlements; shatter his three foremost points. Shatter his ribs, O Agni, with your heat; cleave the root of the sorcerer into three.
Thrice let the yātudhāna come within thy snare; he who smites the truth with falsehood, O Agni — him, crackling with thy flame, O Jātavedas, cut down before the eyes of him who praises thee.
What curse the two together hurl today, O Agni, what harsh word the chanters generate — the arrow that is born from wrath and from the mind: with that pierce the yātudhānas in the heart.
Smite away the yātudhānas with thy heat; smite away the rakṣas with thy blaze, O Agni; smite away the foolish demons with thy flame; smite away those who would drink up the vital force as thou blazest forth.
Let the gods today cut off the crooked one; let the hurled curses fly back upon him; let the arrows strike the word-thief in the vital spot; let the yātudhāna enter thy noose from every side.
From of old, O Agni, thou dost crush the yātudhānas; the rakṣases have never conquered thee in battles. Burn down the flesh-eating fools along with their companions; let them not escape from thy divine weapon.
The yātudhāna who defiles himself with human flesh, who does so with the flesh of horse or cattle beast, who carries off the milk of the inviolable cow, O Agni — hew off the heads of those with thy blaze.
Whoever, gazing upon men, is a yātudhāna and would drink the year-long milk of the dappled cow, or the colostrum — whoever among them would satisfy himself therewith, O Agni, pierce that one head-on with thy flame in the vital spot.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Let the yātudhānas drink the poison of the cows; let those evil ones be cut down for Aditi. Let the god Savitā give them over utterly; let them forfeit their share in the plants.
Do thou, O Agni, guard us from below and from above, from behind, and protect us from in front. Let those ageless, most scorching flames of thine, blazing, burn the evil-proclaimer.
From behind and from before, from below and from above, guard us with the poet's wisdom, O Agni the poet. As a friend guards a friend against old age, O Agni, thou art immortal — guard us mortals.
That eye, O Agni, fix upon the chanter — the hoof-smashing one with which thou seest the yātudhāna. Like Atharvan, with the divine light, burn down completely that unwise one who harms the truth.
Around thee, O Agni, we place our thought as a stronghold, O wise one, O powerful one — bold-hued, day by day the slayer of the Bhaṅgurāvat demons.
Agni blazes forth with great light; by his greatness he makes all things manifest. He overcomes the divine māyās and the evil ones; he sharpens his two horns to pierce the rakṣas.
Agni drives away the rakṣases, brilliant in radiance, immortal; pure, cleansing, worthy of invocation.
O Agni, protect us from affliction; ward off, O god, those who would harm us. Ageless, burn them with thy most scorching flames.
Those two ageless horns of thine, O Jātavedas, sharp-gleaming, whetted by sacred utterance — with those two pierce through the kimīdin who is hard-hearted, who would destroy, the yātudhāna who faces thee, O Jātavedas.
Burn together the Bhaṅgurāvat rakṣas with thy poison, O Indra; O Agni, with thy brilliant radiance, with flames whose tips are burning hot.
Burn down, O Agni, the yātudhāna and the kimīdin as a pair. I whet thee with hymns; be vigilant, O wise one, undeceived.
Smite down, O Agni, the blaze with thy fiery wrath, from every direction. Shatter the strength, the heroic power, of the yātudhāna rakṣas.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Crush down utterly this one who dwells on the path, O Indra, O guardian, with the fools who destroy yātudhānas. Let these two yātudhānas as a pair, O Agni, lie dead and scattered in every direction, slain by thy blaze.
Let Bṛhaspati guard us from behind and from the north, from below against the evil-doer. Let Indra guard us from in front and from the middle; let him, as a friend, make things more spacious for his friends.
O Indra and Soma, scorch the rakṣas, press it down, cast it down, O ye two bulls who increase darkness. Smite it away, the senseless one; burn it utterly, smite it dead and thrust it away; sharpen yourselves against the devourers.
O Indra and Soma, let burning heat go against the evil-proclaimer, against evil, like a cauldron full of fire. Lay irresistible hatred upon the brahman-hater, the flesh-eater, the fierce-eyed kimīdin.
O Indra and Soma, pierce the evildoers through into the pit, into the darkness that has no handhold. So that not one of them may rise up from there again — let that be your power, full of wrath and might.
O Indra and Soma, hurl down from heaven your stone-blows, heated in fire. With your burning, ageless weapons of death, pin the devourers in their ribs; let them go voiceless.
O Indra and Soma, hurl the death-bolt from heaven; bring the crusher from the earth upon the evil-proclaimer. Hew out the solar timber from the mountains with which you two crush down the waxing rakṣas.
O Indra and Soma, let this thought encompass you on all sides like a girth around prize steeds. The oblation-invocation I send forth to you with insight — invigorate these sacred formulations, as a king invigorates his men.
Remember it back with your vigorous courses — slain, the rakṣas of treachery, the Bhaṅgurāvat demon. O Indra and Soma, let there be no easy passage for the evildoer, for that deceitful one who would ever assail me.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Whoever denounces me as I go about with a guileless mind, denounces me with false words — may he be seized like water by a gleaming vessel; may the speaker of falsehood be shown to be a speaker of falsehood, O Indra.
Those who scatter naive speech about with their courses, or who corrupt what is auspicious with their practised powers — let Soma give them over to the serpent, or let him place them in the lap of Nirṛti.
Whoever would harm the sap of our food, O Agni — of horses, of cattle, of bodies — let that enemy, that thief, that committer of theft, go forth diminished; let him be abandoned here with his body and his progeny.
May he be cut off — body and offspring — and may all three earths lie beneath him. His glory withers away, O gods, whoever seeks to harm me by day and whoever seeks to harm me by night.
To the person of discernment it is well known: the words of truth and falsehood touch each other. Of these two, whichever is true, whichever is the more upright — that one Soma protects; the false he strikes down.
Soma does not drive forward the crooked, nor the kṣatriya who bears false office. He slays the rakṣas; he slays the speaker of falsehood — both lie in Indra's snare.
If indeed I am one who makes a god of falsehood, or if I invoke the gods in vain, O Agni — why then art thou angry with us, O Jātaveda? Let them who speak treachery cleave to Nirṛti without purpose.
May I die this very day if I am a yātudhāna, or if the breath of a man has been scorched by me. But let him who calls me a yātudhāna falsely be scattered apart with his ten heroes.
Whoever says to me 'thou art a sorcerer, a yātudhāna,' whoever, being a rakṣas himself, says 'I am pure' — may Indra smite him with a great blow; may he fall the lowest of all living creatures.
She who moves abroad at night like a screech-owl, concealing her treacherous body — may she fall down into endless pits; may the pressing-stones smite the rakṣas with their thunder.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
