Spread out, O Maruts; search through the settlements; seize the rakṣases, crush them together. Those who take the forms of birds and fly through the nights, or those who have set deception within the divine sacrifice — crush them.
Here they come flying, the dog-roving ones; the deceivers seek to deceive Indra, the undecievable. Śakra sharpens his weapon against the slanderers; now will he loose his thunderbolt against the sorcerers.
Roll forth the stone of heaven, O Indra; sharpen it well, O Maghavan, whetted by Soma. From the east, from the west, from below, from above — smite the rakṣases with the mountain.
Indra became Parāśara against the yātu-sorcerers, against those who churn away the oblation. Śakra indeed advances like an axe through a forest, splitting the rakṣases by the hundreds like vessels.
Slay the owl-sorcerer and the screech-owl-sorcerer; slay the dog-sorcerer and the kokay-bird-sorcerer; slay the eagle-sorcerer and the vulture-sorcerer — crush the rakṣas, O Indra, as with a pressing-stone.
Let no rakṣas, none possessed by yātu-sorcery, press upon us. Drive away the coupled Kimīdins. May the Earth protect us from earthly distress; may the Atmosphere protect us from the heavenly.
O Indra, smite the male yātudhāna and also the female who injures through sorcery. Let those with broken necks, the god-bereft, weep; may they not behold the sun as it rises.
Keep watch, keep vigil — O Indra and Soma, be awake! Hurl the weapon of death upon the rakṣases; hurl the thunderbolt upon the sorcerers.
The brown ones and the bright ones, the red ones and the dappled ones, the dark ones, the black plants — to all these healing herbs we now speak out.
May they protect this man from the yakṣma disease sent by the gods — those whose father is Dyaus, whose mother is Pṛthivī, and whose root has become the ocean.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The divine waters are foremost among the healing herbs. They have driven out the sin-laden yakṣma from your limb by limb.
I address the spreading plants, the clumping ones, the single-stemmed, the creeping herbs. I call you — the filamentous, the jointed, those with spreading branches — those plants that belong to all the gods, the potent, the life-sustaining for man.
By that power of yours, O herbs, which overpowers, by the virile force and strength that is in you — with that, release this man from this yakṣma disease.
I invoke Jīvalā, Naghāriṣā, the living herb, and Arundhatī the uplifting, the flowering one, the honey-sweet one.
May the wise, the knowing ones come here at my word, so that we may carry this man across, beyond misfortune.
The food of Agni, the embryo of the waters — those that grow anew as punarṇavās: may those steadfast, thousand-named healing plants be gathered and brought here.
The herbs that dwell in hollows, whose nature is water, the sharp-horned ones — shaking off all misfortune, they drive it away.
Those that release bonds, the wide-opening ones, the fierce ones that destroy poison, and those that destroy the balāsa affliction, those that destroy rakṣases, that neutralize kṛtyā witchcraft — may those herbs come here.
Benign be to you the herbs, the purchased ones, the mightier plants, the creepers that have been invoked with praise; may Sarasvatī, the eldest of the waters, protect our cattle, our horse, our man, our beast.
Honey-sweet the root, honey-sweet the tip of these plants has become; honey-sweet the middle of the creepers; honey-sweet their leaf, honey-sweet their flower — born of sweetness, they are a taste of immortality; they yield ghee and food for the herd of cattle led by the bull.
However many, however numerous these herbs that grow upon the earth — may they, with their thousand leaves, release us from the distress of death.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The tiger-amulet, the gem of plants, the guardian that wards off curses — may it drive far away from us all diseases and all demons.
As the roar of a lion, as the blazing of fire scatters what was gathered against the herbs — the wasting disease of cattle and of men, chased off by the plants, shall flow away like a navigable river into a river channel.
Loosed forth from Vaiśvānara, the all-consuming fire, the herbs spread themselves over the earth from here — they whose king is the lord of the forest.
The creepers that I know and those that I see with my eyes, those unknown ones that we may come to know, those in which we know healing to be gathered — may all herbs, complete and entire, heed my utterance.
The Āṅgirasa plants, the universal-healing creepers that grow on mountains and on level grounds — may those herbs, full of delight, benign, be a blessing to our heart.
The aśvattha, the darbha among the creepers, King Soma the immortal oblation; rice and barley are two healers, the two immortal sons of heaven.
Rise up, you herbs, as it thunders and roars — when Parjanya, rich in seed, waters you, O speckle-mothered ones.
By that immortal power we bring this man across to safety; and I make a remedy so that he may live a hundred years.
The boar knows the healing plant; the mongoose knows the medicinal herbs; whatever herbs the Gandharvas and the serpents know — let those herbs come here.
Those that the suparṇas know, the heavenly Āṅgirasa plants that the raghaṭa bird knows; those that the birds, the haṃsas know, and all the flying creatures; the herbs that the deer know — those I call hither to give him aid.
As many herbs as the inviolable cows graze upon, as many as the goats and sheep graze upon — of that many kinds of universal-healing herbs I bring a full measure toward you.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
In as many herbs as human healers know a remedy — may herbs of that many kinds, brought to you, bestow shelter upon you.
Those that are in flower, those that have given birth, those bearing fruit, and those without fruit — like mothers uniting together, let them give milk to him for the sake of his unharmed wholeness.
I have raised you out of the five-fettered snare, and out of the ten-fettered snare as well; I have lifted you out of Yama's foot-fetter — with the herbs I have brought you safely across.
The first chariot belongs to Indra; the next chariot belongs to the gods; Varuṇa's is truly the third. The last chariot is that of the serpents — it has come near to the post; let it then strike.
The darbha grass is the flame, the tender shoot; it is the shield of the horse, the shield of the man; it is the cross-bar of the chariot — the venom of the serpents is made powerless; indeed it is a mighty ward.
O white one, strike down with your fore-hoof and with your hind-hoof alike; like a piece of wood that has been soaked in water, the venom of the serpents is made powerless — indeed it is a mighty ward.
Araṃghasa, having plunged and emerged again, spoke once more: like a piece of wood that has been soaked in water, the venom of the serpents is made powerless — indeed it is a mighty ward.
Paidva slays the kaṣarṇīla serpent; Paidva slays the white one and the dark one; Paidva has shattered the head of the ratharvyā, of the spotted snake.
O Paidva, go forth first; we shall follow after you. Drive the serpents away from the path along which we shall travel.
Here Paidva was born; here is his domain. These are the hoofprints of the steed, of Vājinīvat, the serpent-slayer.
What is shut let it not spring open; what is open let it not shut tight. In this field there are two serpents, a female and a male — both of them are rendered venomless.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Venomless are the serpents here, those near and those far away. With a club I strike the scorpion; the serpent that has come I strike with the staff.
This is the remedy of Aghāśva, for both kinds of serpent and for the constrictor as well; Indra and Paidva have restrained for me the serpent that seeks to do evil.
We meditate upon Paidva, the steadfast one, the firmly-abiding one; these spotted serpents behind us sit blazing forth.
Their life-breath extinguished, their venom destroyed, slain by Indra the wielder of the vajra — Indra has struck them down; we likewise have struck them down.
Slain are the tiraścirāja serpents, crushed are the spotted pṛdākus; strike down the darvī, the karikrata, the śvitra, the dark asita lurking in the kuśa-grass.
A Kirāta maiden, a young girl companion, digs up the healing herb with her golden spades upon the ridges of the mountains.
Here has come the young healer, the variegated, the unvanquished; he is indeed the crusher of the svaja serpent and of both species of scorpion.
Indra has crushed the serpents for me, and Mitra and Varuṇa, and both Vāta and Parjanya.
Paidva has crushed the serpents for me, and the spotted pṛdākus as well — the svajas, the tiraścirājas, the kasarṇīlas, the daśonaśīs.
Indra first slew the progenitor of your kind, O serpent; of those crushed ones, what then could remain as the essence of them?
For I have seized the heads together, as Pauñjiṣṭa seizes the skull-bowl; having crossed to the midst of the Sindhu river, I wash away the serpent's venom.
Let the rivers carry away the venom of all serpents; slain are the tiraścirājas, crushed are the spotted pṛdākus.
I choose out the herbs, as one chooses fertile fields with skill; I lead them like swift mares — O serpent, let your venom go forth out of you.
Whatever venom is in fire, in the sun, in the earth, in the herbs — the kāndā-venom, the kanikla — let it go forth; let it become your secretion flowing outward.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Drive it out from limb to limb, protect the heart from it; then let the fiery power of the venom depart downward from you.
O Agni, protect Vimada; lead this one back, restore him to life, O Jātavedas. May we not fall into your wrath through wrongdoing; let not the serpent slay our man with its venom.
Those serpents born of fire, born of herbs, those that have come into being from clouds and lightning — their many and diverse broods: to those serpents we would offer reverence.
You are named Taudī, or else you are named Ghṛtācī, O maiden; from beneath your foot, from between your feet, I take the venom-antidote.
The venom stood far off; venom wailed at venom and shrank away; Agni drove out the venom of the serpent, Soma led it away; the venom followed after the biter — the serpent became deathless.
Whence were those two born? Which is that half? From which realm, from which of the two earths? The two calves of Virāj arose from the primordial waters — I ask you: by which of the two was she milked?
He who made the waters cry out by his greatness, having fashioned a triangular womb lying there — the wish-fulfilling calf of Virāj has made the bodies turn away from sight in the hidden depths.
Those four great ones, of which the fourth releases speech — let the wise brahman know this through ascetic power: that in which the one is yoked, and that in which the one alone abides.
The sāmans are fashioned around the Bṛhat; from the sixth, five are built above it; the Bṛhat is fashioned from the Bṛhatī meter — from what, moreover, is the Bṛhatī measured out?
The Bṛhatī is fashioned around the measure, built upon the mother's measure; for Māyā was born from Māyā, and Mātali arose from Māyā.
Above the image of Vaiśvānara is the sky; as far as Agni has pressed apart the two world-halves — from thence, from the sixth, the stotra-hymns proceed; they rise up hence toward the sixth day.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
We seers, six of us, ask you this, O Kaśyapa — for you have harnessed what is fit to be harnessed and what is capable of yoking; they call Virāj the father of Brahman — reveal her to us according to the seasons, among our companions.
She when dislodged, the sacrifices were dislodged after her; she when standing firm, they stand firm in attendance upon her; in her cowpen, at her bringing-forth, the yakṣa trembles — she is Virāj, O seers, in the highest heaven.
The breathless one advances through the breath of breathing beings; Virāj follows after Svarāj from behind; Virāj, touching all things, beautiful in form — some see her in you, others see her not in you.
Who truly knows the twofold nature of Virāj, who knows her seasons, who again knows her ordered pattern? Who knows her strides, drawn forth in manifold ways, who knows her abode and how manifold are her dawns?
She is verily that one who first shone forth; she moves within the waters, having entered therein. The bride has conquered, the newly-come, the mother; great are the powers of greatness abiding within her.
The two Dawns, adorned with meter as their wings, course together following the same womb. The wife of Sūrya moves in union with him, perceptive, blazing with light, unwasting, rich in seed.
Three have come along the path of Ṛta; three heats have come following the generative flow. One quickens offspring, one quickens nourishment, one guards the kingdom of those devoted to the gods.
The Agnīṣṭoma they established as the fourth; the seers, arranging the wings of the sacrifice, bringing the Gāyatrī, Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, Anuṣṭubh, and Bṛhat-arkā — bringing heaven for the sacrificer.
Five dawnings, following them five milkings, the cow of five names, following her the five seasons; the five directions ordered by the fifteenfold — all these, headed as one, face toward the one world.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Six born-and-existent firstborns of Ṛta, and six Sāmans bearing the sixfold day; the plow of six yokings follows the Sāman upon Sāman — six, they say, are Heaven-and-Earth, six the broad expanses.
Six, they say, are the cold months, and six the hot — tell us which among the seasons is the surplus one. Seven fair-winged seers settled down; seven meters follow, and seven consecrations.
Seven oblations, and seven kindling-woods indeed, seven honeys, and seven seasons verily; seven ghee-portions have come round to existence — seven hotar-priests sacrifice seasonally. These I have heard called the seven vultures.
Eight are the stations of the firstborn of Ṛta; eight the divine priests-of-Indra; Aditi of eight wombs, of eight sons — the oblation approaches toward the eighth night.
Deeming this the better way, I have come hither; in your friendship I am auspicious. May there be for you an intention propitious, of common birth; knowing all, may it accompany us entirely.
The young cow milked for Indra alone — a heifer milking her first milk of beestings; then fourfold she satisfied the four: the gods, the humans, the asuras, and the seers.
Eight portions are Indra's, six are Yama's, seven sevenfold belong to the seers; the waters, humans, and plants — these five have poured themselves out in sequence for them.
Who then is the cow? Who the sole-seer? What the Sāman? What the blessings? The disease that grows alone upon the earth, alone in season — which one, then, is that?
One is the cow, one the sole-seer, one the Sāman and one the direction of blessings; the disease that grows alone upon the earth, alone in season — it exceeds not beyond.
Homage to Prāṇa, in whose power all this universe is held — who, existent, is lord of all, in whom all things are established.
Homage to you, O Prāṇa, as roaring thunder-cry; homage to you as the thunderclap; homage to you be as lightning; homage to you, O Prāṇa, as rain.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
When, O Prāṇa, upon the arrival of the season you thunder over the plants, they burst forth with vigor, they take on the embryo, and thereupon they bring forth abundantly.
When, O Prāṇa, with thunderclap you thunder over the plants, then all that exists upon the earth rejoices at that moment.
When Prāṇa thundered over the world with rain and thunderclap, the cattle rejoiced then — 'Great indeed shall this be for us.'
The plants, rained upon abundantly, spoke together with Prāṇa: 'Life force has truly extended out for us; all of us it has made fragrant.'
Homage to you, O Prāṇa, as you breathe forth; homage be to you as you breathe back. Homage to your westward movement, homage to your eastward movement — this homage here to all of you.
Homage to you coming near, homage be to you departing afar; homage to you, O Prāṇa, standing still, and homage to you seated.
That form of yours which is dear, O Prāṇa, or that which is yet dearer to you, O Prāṇa — and whatever medicine is yours, bestow that upon us for the sake of living.
Prāṇa clothes his creatures as a father his beloved son; Prāṇa is verily the lord of all — both of what breathes and what breathes not.
Prāṇa is death; prāṇa is immortality; the gods attend upon prāṇa. Prāṇa indeed establishes the truth-speaker in the highest world.
Prāṇa is Virāj; prāṇa is the directress; all things attend upon prāṇa. Prāṇa is Agni, the moon, the sun; they call prāṇa Prajāpati.
Prāṇa and apāna are rice and barley; the ox is called prāṇa. In barley indeed prāṇa is lodged; apāna is called rice.
The person breathes out and breathes in while yet within the womb. When thou, O Prāṇa, dost quicken him, then he is born forth from thee.
They call prāṇa Mātariśvan; wind indeed is called prāṇa. In prāṇa verily are the past and the future; in prāṇa is all things gathered together.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The plants of Atharvan, those of the Āṅgirases, the divine ones, and those born among men — all plants rejoice when thou, O Prāṇa, dost quicken them.
When Prāṇa has rained upon the great earth with rain, the plants rejoice, and likewise whatsoever creeping herbs there are.
Whoever knows this thy prāṇa and that in which thou art established — may all things bring tribute to him in yonder highest world.
As, O Prāṇa, all these creatures here bring tribute to thee, so may they bring tribute to him who has heard thee, to those who have heard.
He moves within the womb among the gods; having come into being he is born again. He — the past, the future, the world, the yet-to-be — as a father has entered the son by his powers.
The swan does not wrench up even one foothold as it flies up from the water. If, O friend, he were to wrench it up, then there would be neither today nor tomorrow, neither night nor day, nor would anything whatsoever be discerned.
Eight-wheeled it rolls, single-rimmed, with a thousand syllables, onward in front and backward behind. By its half has this whole universe come into being; what then is that half — what is its sign?
He who is lord of this universe of all beings, who moves all things — among the others, to the swift-bowed one: to him, O Prāṇa, be homage to thee.
He who is lord of all the beings of this universe, who moves all things — may Prāṇa, unwearied, wise with brahman, protect me.
Standing upright he keeps watch among the sleeping; he does not lie crosswise. Of his sleeping among the sleepers no one has ever heard.
O Prāṇa, do not turn away from me; thou shalt be no other than me. Like the embryo of the waters, for life I bind thee within me, O Prāṇa.
This bull of a thousand, rich in milk, bearing all forms upon his flanks, teaching welfare to the giver and the sacrificer — he, son of Bṛhaspati, has stretched the thread of the dawn-cows.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
He who at the first became the measure of the waters, lord over all like the divine earth — the father of calves, the master of the inviolable cows, may he place us in thousandfold nourishment.
A male, pregnant, ancient, rich in milk — the bull bears the barrel of treasure. May Agni Jātavedas carry him, offered up by the paths that lead to the gods, to Indra.
This is the portion of the gods, the binding-bond, the essence of waters, of plants, of clarified butter. Śakra chose the drop of Soma; the great stone-presser became what is his body.
Father of calves, lord of the inviolable cows, and moreover father of the great bellowing bulls — the calf is the afterbirth; the beestings are the first milking; curds, clarified butter — that indeed is his seed.
Thou bearest a full vessel of Soma; Tvaṣṭṛ, the begetter of forms, the progenitor of cattle — may thy generative powers be propitious; grant us those yonder ones, O self-powerful one.
The vigor of Indra, the arms of Varuṇa, the shoulders of the Aśvins — this is the hump of the Maruts.
He bears the oblation-butter; clarified butter is his seed; thousandfold nourishment — that they call the sacrifice. Wearing the form of Indra, may this bull, given by the gods, come to us benignly.
Rich in milk, thou stretchest out the divine clans; they call thee Indra, they call thee Sarasvant. A thousand at a single bestowal does he give who sacrifices a bull to a brahmin.
Bṛhaspati, Savitṛ has established thy mind; thy breath of life has been brought from Tvaṣṭṛ and Vāyu. With mind I offer thee into the atmosphere; Heaven and Earth have become thy sacrificial grass.
He who moves among the gods like Indra, lowing loudly among the kine — let Brahmā praise with a blessing the limbs of that bull.
His flanks belonged to Anumati; his haunches belonged to Bhaga; his knee-joints — Mitra declared: "These two are mine alone."

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
His rump belonged to the Ādityas; his haunches belonged to Bṛhaspati; his tail belonged to the god Vāta — with it he fans the herbs.
His chest was Jāmiśaṃsa's; the vessel of Soma was set there; when they assigned portions to the bull, they declared his hooves to be the Utthātu.
His entrails belonged to Sinīvālī; his hide they declared to be Sūryā's — when all the gods assembled and apportioned the bull.
The gods gave his hoofs to Saramā and to the tortoises; his belly contents they sustained for the insects and for the dung-beetles.
With his two horns he drives away the demons; with his eye he smites the enemy; with his two ears he hears what is auspicious — he who is the inviolable lord of kine.
He performs a hundredfold sacrifice; the fires do not afflict him; all the gods quicken him who offers oblation to the bull, O Brāhmaṇa.
Having given a bull to a Brāhmaṇa, one makes the mind more spacious; may he behold the thriving of the inviolable ones in his own cattle-pen.
May there be cattle; may there be offspring; and may there be bodily strength — may all the gods consent to all of that for the giver of the bull.
This one, drinking in vigor, bears a wealth endowed with consciousness; this one milks the good-milking cow ever accompanied by her calf, milks the amenable one, the wise one, in front of the sky.
Of tawny form, sustainer of vigor from the sky, the might of Indra, all-formed, has come to us; bestowing offspring upon us and wealth, may we abide, having drawn near to the increase of riches.
We place this young one here among you; roaming in delight with him, follow the amenable cows; do not harm us, O well-favored ones by your nature — attend upon us with the increase of wealth.
Let the Upaparcana come hither; let it mix within this cattle-pen — the seed of the bull, O Indra, that is your virile power.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
This amulet-stone bound as a counter-charm is tied upon the hero for a hero's sake; possessed of virile force, a slayer of rivals, a warrior-hero, a protector, most auspicious.
This gem is a rival-slayer, a fine hero, full of might, a prize-winner, overpowering, formidable; may the warrior come forward, deflecting and corrupting sorceries.
With this gem Indra, the wise one, slew Vṛtra; with this he caused the Asuras to be overthrown; with this he conquered both heaven and earth; with this he conquered the four directions.
This Srāktya gem, a repeller, a counter-charm — the gem full of vital force that crushes enemies: may it guard us from all sides.
That Agni has declared, that Soma has declared, Bṛhaspati, Savitā, and Indra have declared it — may those gods, as your priests, drive back with counter-charms the sorceries directed against you.
Within himself he concealed heaven and earth, and the day, and the sun, and also this Brahmaṇaspati — may those gods, as your priests, drive back with counter-charms the sorceries directed against you.
Those persons who fashion armor with the Srāktya gem — like the sun mounting the sky, the sovereign drives away sorceries.
With the Srāktya gem, as with a sage endowed with wisdom, I have conquered all armies; I smite the enemies, I slay the Rakṣases.
Whatever sorceries are those of the Āṅgirasas, whatever sorceries are those of the Asuras, the sorceries that are self-made and those that are brought by others — may all of them pass away to the far distance, beyond the ninety navigable waters.
May the gods bind the gem as armor upon him — Indra, Viṣṇu, Savitā, Rudra, Agni, Prajāpati, Parameṣṭhin, Virāj, Vaiśvānara, and all the seers.
Thou art the foremost of plants, as the bull among cattle, as the tiger among beasts of prey. That one whom we sought and declared — him they called a counter-snare.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
He indeed becomes a tiger, and also a lion, and also a bull; he shines forth in all directions, he who bears this amulet.
The Apsarases do not smite him, nor the Gandharvas, nor mortal men; he shines forth in all directions, he who bears this amulet.
Kaśyapa fashioned thee, Kaśyapa set thee in motion; Indra, bearing thee fearlessly among men, conquered by thee the one who clings close.
The gods fastened this amulet, the crusher of rivals, as armour. He who seeks to slay thee with sorceries, he who seeks to slay thee with consecrations, he who seeks to slay thee with sacrifices — smite him back, O Indra, with the hundred-jointed thunderbolt.
This is indeed the amulet that turns back, mighty and victorious; may it guard offspring and wealth — all-protecting, of great auspiciousness.
Make us free of rivals from below, free of rivals from above; O Indra, O hero, place before us a light free of rivals, and behind us as well.
The broad, fierce armour belonging to Indra and Agni — which all the All-Gods together cannot pierce — let that great armour protect thy body from every side, so that thou mayest live long, reaching old age.
The divine amulet has mounted thee for my unharmed continuance. Enter ye into this post, O ye who guard the body, triple-shielded, for vigour.
May Indra deposit heroic power in this; enter ye, O gods, into this. For long life, for a hundred autumns — so may he live long, reaching old age.
May Indra bind the amulet upon thee — ever conquering, unconquered, drinking Soma, the bull who creates fearlessness; may he protect thee always, by day and by night, from every side.
Let Indra churn, the churner, Śakra the hero, the breaker of strongholds — so that we may slay the army of enemies by the thousands.
Let the stinking rope, the blower-upon, make yonder army stinking; seeing before them fire and smoke, may they place fear in their own hearts.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Let the Rough-named one make those ones rough; the slayer smites them with slaughters. Like arrows, let them quickly shatter, caught fast in the great net.
Crush down yonder ones, O Aśvattha; gnaw yonder ones, O swift Khadira. Like the snapping of tāja-reeds let them break, caught fast in the great net.
The atmosphere was the net, the great directions were the net-poles; having covered the army with that net, Indra swept away the Dasyus.
Great is thy net, O great Indra, O hero, worth a thousand, possessed of a hundredfold power; with that net, O Maghavan, press down the enemies through all the everlasting years.
Great is thy net, of the great Śakra possessed of troops; with it Indra slew a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand of the Dasyus, having covered their army.
This great world was the net of the great Śakra; with that Indra-net and with darkness I cover all those yonder ones.
Exhaustion, fierce-whirling distress, and inescapable affliction, weariness and languor and bewilderment — with these I cover all those yonder ones.
I deliver those yonder ones to Death; they are bound by the nooses of Death. The sinister messengers of Death — to them I hand these over, having bound them.
O messengers of Death, lead those ones away; O messengers of Yama, submerge them. Let them be slain beyond the thousands; the weapon of Bhava crushes them.
The Sādhyas go lifting one net-pole with vigour; the Rudras a second, the Vasus a third — one is lifted by the Ādityas.
Let all the gods come pressing down from above with vigour; let the Aṅgirasas come striking in the middle, smiting the army with weapons.
Trees, the offspring of trees, plants, and herbs — bipeds and quadrupeds I urge on so that they may smite yonder army.
Gandharvas and Apsarases, gods, serpents, beings of holy people, and the Fathers — seen and unseen ones I urge on so that they may smite yonder army.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
These nooses of Death are yoked — having stepped into which, thou art not released; let this snare smite that army by the thousands.
The gharma-vessel blazes with fire; this oblation is the slayer of thousands. O Bhava of the speckled arm, and O Śarva, smite that army yonder.
Let them fall upon the searing heat of Death, upon hunger, exhaustion, slaughter, and fear. O Indra with thy two eye-nets, and O Śarva, smite that army yonder.
Defeated, flee with trembling, O enemies, conquered and routed by the brahman-power; of these, driven forward by Bṛhaspati, let not one be released.
Let their weapons fall away; may they not be able to fix an arrow to the string. Then, of these greatly terrified ones, let arrows smite their vital spots.
Let both Heaven and Earth roar together upon them; let the atmosphere together with the deities roar upon them. May they find neither kinsman nor firm footing; striking one another, let them go to Death.
The four directions are the mule-mares of the divine chariot; the oblation-portions are its hooves; the atmosphere is its upward shaft.
Heaven and earth are its two wings; the seasons are the reins; speech is the outer road of the chariot.
Day and night are the two wheels; the months are the spokes; the year is the axle-base.
Virāj is the pole; the two fires are the front of the chariot; Indra is the left-standing one; the Moon is the charioteer.
From here conquer, conquer thoroughly, conquer, conquer altogether — svāhā!
For Madhukaśā was born from heaven, from earth, from the atmosphere, from the ocean, from fire, from the winds. Having waited upon her, all creatures clad in immortality rejoice with their hearts.
Men behold her movement upon the earth, severally, pondering her in many ways. For Madhukaśā was born from fire and the winds — the fierce granddaughter of the Maruts.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Great and all-formed is her milk; they call it the seed of the ocean. Whence Madhukaśā comes forth rejoicing — there is the breath of life, there immortality is lodged.
Mother of the Ādityas, daughter of the Vasus, the breath of creatures, the navel of immortality — golden-hued Madhukaśā, radiant with ghee, moves as a great splendour among mortals.
The gods gave birth to the whip of honey; her womb became all-formed. The mother nourishes him newly born and tender; he, once born, clothes all the worlds.
Who truly knows them? Who has declared them — her two breasts that flow in a thousand streams, imperishable, milking out vigour without ever shrinking?
Who truly knows it? Who has discerned it — that vessel of her heart, the imperishable Soma-receptacle? May a brahman of sound understanding rejoice therein.
She who moves to the rites with the hiṅkāra-call — great, sustaining life, resounding loudly — lowing repeatedly toward the three ritual heatings, she bellows her cry, she yields milk with her streams.
The waters approach her as she is full-uddered; the mighty bulls approach her; the self-rulers approach her. They rain, they cause it to rain — in that the waters know desire and nourishment.
Your thunder is your voice, O Prajāpati; as bull you cast your vigour down upon the earth. For Madhukaśā was born from fire and the winds — the fierce granddaughter of the Maruts.
As Soma at the morning pressing becomes dear to the Aśvins, even so let the Aśvins hold radiant lustre within my self.
As Soma at the midday pressing becomes dear to Indra and Agni, even so let Indra and Agni hold lustre [within my self].
As Soma at the third pressing becomes dear to the Ṛbhus, even so let the Ṛbhus hold radiant lustre within my self.
May I be born in honey, may I think in honey. I have come to you, O Agni, rich in milk — unite me with lustre.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Unite me, O Agni, with lustre; unite me with offspring; unite me with long life. May the gods know this of me; may Indra know it together with the seers.
[Colophon:] "That which is on the mountains" — this is a five-verse sūkta.
As the honey-makers gather honey upon honey, even so let the Aśvins hold strength and vital force within me.
As bees smear this honey upon the honeycomb, even so let the Aśvins hold lustre and blazing energy within me.
O Aśvins, lords of auspiciousness, anoint me with the honey of the bee, so that I may speak lustrous speech among the people.
As bull you cast vigour upon the earth; with the honey-whip from heaven you have anointed the earth. All creatures live by her once she is born; therewith does she nourish the remaining vigour.
The earth is the shaft, the atmosphere the womb, the sky the lash, lightning the lustre. Thou art the lash of honey, dripping ghee, the golden drop.
Thou art vast, thou art eminent, thou art water, thou art sky, thou art great. Make me water, make me sky, make me great.
Thou art the ocean, undiminished, unbounded, winning thousands — let a thousand come to me. Whosoever truly knows the seven honeys of the honey-lash, and the seven honey-bearing ones —
— he wins the honey-rich world; the honey thereof becomes unassailable. When it thunders in the cloud-rift, it is Prajāpati himself who manifests thereby for his creatures.
Therefore one should stand with the sacred cord worn to the east, saying: 'O Prajāpati, be thou aware of me.' Prajāpati becomes aware of him, and his creatures become aware of him — so knows he who thus knows.
That which skilled healers fashion as a bride at the wedding procession — all-formed, wrought by hand — let us drive them away from the very core.
The sorcery-effigy endowed with a head, full of sap, possessed of ears, fashioned and assembled by the sorcerer, all-formed — back and away we dispatch it; let it reach the one who made it.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Whether made by a Śūdra, made by a king, made by a woman, or made by brahmin-sages — like a wife repulsed by her husband, let it reach the maker, its own kinsman.
With this herb — just this one — do I act.
Let the sorceries fall upon the sorcery-maker, the curses upon the curser. Back and away we dispatch them; let them reach the one who made them.
The westward-facing Āṅgirasa is our overseer and domestic priest. Turn back the sorceries westward, and smite that sorcery-maker.
He who told thee 'Go forth!' in a contrary and hostile utterance — turn back upon him, O sorcery; do not seek us who are guiltless.
He who fitted together thy joints with skill, as a master does with a chariot — go to him; there is thy path; this person here is unknown to thee.
Those knowing sorcerers who have smeared thee upon the sorcery-image — we know this sorcery-bane, the return-path counter-charm; with it we bathe thee.
If we have approached a woman ill-fated, bathed in misfortune, whose calf is dead — let all evil depart from me; let no wealth fail to abide with me.
Whatever name they seized of thine — whether when giving to the Fathers or at the sacrifice — from all that pollution, from every sin, may these herbs release thee.
From divine sin, from ancestral name-seizure, from pollution fully contracted — may the plants release thee by their power, by the brahman, by the ṛk-verses, by the milk of the sages.
As the wind dislodges the dust from the earth and the cloud from the atmosphere — even so let all ill-being depart from us, driven away by the brahman.
Depart, O thou braying and bound one, like a she-ass. Seek out the makers from here, driven away, expelled by the mighty brahman.
This is the path — along it I lead thee, O sorcery; we dispatch thee back toward the one who sent thee. Travel along it as a all-formed, misshapen draught-animal travels without a cart — go, consuming.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Thy light faces away, thy path faces backward; make thy course elsewhere, not toward us. Cross beyond the ninety navigable streams, pass over the difficult crossings and the swirling rapids — harm us not; be gone.
Like wind crushing and felling a tree — crush and fell them; spare the cow, the horse, the man of these folk. O sorcery, turning back from here, rouse the makers to childlessness.
The sorcery they wrought for thee upon the sacrificial grass, the stake they buried against thee in the cremation-ground or in the field, or by which the more cunning ones assailed thee in the Gārhapatya fire — being innocent and simple, from all that we destroy and free thee here.
The enmity brought near, tracked down, buried, the treacherous deed — we have discerned the makers. Let it return whence it came; there let it turn about like a horse; let it smite the offspring of the sorcery-maker.
Iron swords there are in our house; we know, O sorcery, how many joints thou hast.
Rise up and begone, O sorcery-charm dispatched by an unknown one — what do you seek here? I shall cut off your neck and feet, O kṛtya; flee away!
May Indra and Agni, the two lords of creatures, protect us; may Soma the king, the supreme sovereign who bestows grace, and the lords of cosmic order be gracious to us.
Let Bhava and Śarva hurl the divine lightning-bolt of the gods against the evil-doer, against the maker of the kṛtya, against the worker of ill.
Whether you have come as a two-footed or four-footed kṛtya, assembled and fashioned in all forms by the sorcerer — having become an eight-footed beast of ill omen, go back the way you came!
Smeared and anointed, arrayed in her own cry, carrying all evil — begone! Seek out, O kṛtya, your maker, as a daughter seeks her own father.
Begone, O kṛtya, do not linger — lead back your step as if to one who has been pierced. He is the quarry and you the hunter; he who sent you does not deserve to destroy you.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The mortal is his own death — he who, through heedlessness, fashioned with his own two hands destruction for himself.
The later one smites with his arrow the one who sat before, having reclaimed it; and in turn the later one strikes back against the one who is slaying the former.
Hear this word of mine and return to where you came from; go back again to the one who fashioned you.
The slaying of the innocent is truly dreadful, O kṛtya; do not smite our cow, our horse, our man.
Wherever you have been deposited, from there we rouse you up and drive you forth; become lighter than a leaf.
If you are shrouded in darkness, covered over with a net — we dissolve you all, O kṛtyās, and send you back again to the maker.
Crush the offspring of the one who has gone forth, who made the kṛtya, who performed root-sorcery; O kṛtya, do not spare him — smite yonder maker of the kṛtya!
As the sun is freed from darkness, casts off the night, and surpasses the beacons of dawn — so I cast off all ill-being and evil, as an elephant shakes off dust.
The ties that are measured at the top, measured across, and measured around — the knottings of the all-sheltering house we now unloose.
Whatever noose has been bound in you, O all-sheltering one, and whatever knot has been made — I, like Bṛhaspati, undo that binding by the power of the sacred word.
He who drew tight, who compacted and made a firm knot in you — knowing your joints, we loosen them as if with a blade, together with Indra.
The knottings of the clamps, of the peg-fastenings, and of the encircling embrace — all the bindings of yours, O wife of the house-lord, we now unloose.
The lashings of your bamboo rafters, and of the binding-grass, and of the wing-beams — all your bindings, O all-sheltering house, we now unloose.
The hanging nets within you that they have pierced through for some purpose — those we now loosen for you. Be auspicious, O wife of the house-lord; do not afflict the body with what is unbound.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The hall of the oblation-press, the fire-shed, the seat and dwelling of the wives — you are the seat of the gods, O divine house.
The axle-pin, the peg, what is spread wide, what is thousand-eyed and turned on all sides — what is fastened and bound down we now unloose by means of sacred speech.
He who receives you in his keeping and he by whose effort you have been built — both of them, O wife of the house-lord, may they live to old age.
Let her who is firm, well-bound, and fully adorned go to meet him there — of her, we unloose you limb from limb, joint by joint.
You shelter Agni within, together with men and cattle; O fruitful one, O prolific one — we cut asunder your bonds.
Rich in vigor, rich in ghee, measured and fixed upon the earth — the hall bearing all food: do not harm the one who receives you.
He who first measured you out and gathered together the forest-trees — Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati fashioned you, O hall, for progeny.
Homage to him, homage to the giver — and we make obeisance to the lord of the hall; homage to Agni who moves within, and homage to you, O Man.
Homage to the cattle and horses that are born in the hall. By the expanse that lies between heaven and earth — by that expanse do I receive this hall of yours.
That which is the intermediate space, the measure of the luminous realm — that I make the womb for treasures; for that for which I praise the hall, be it so.
Covered with grasses, clothed in thatch, like Night the hall is the resting-place of the world; measured, it stands upon the earth, like a great elephant, footed firm.
She who is measured with two sides, four sides, six sides — the eight-sided, ten-sided hall, wife of the house-master: Agni lies within her like a child in the womb.
I undo what is bound of your wicker-work, uncovering what is covered over; what has been pent up by Varuṇa, may Mitra release it at dawn.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Nest upon nest, sheath within sheath compressed — therein does the mortal take birth, from whom all the world is born.
Four-cornered, furnished with a circuit, measured and built by the sages — Indra and Agni, those two immortal lords of Soma, protect the hall.
Do not hurl your bonds back upon us; become light, O heavy burden. Like a bride, O hall, we carry you wherever we wish.
I carry forward these waters, disease-free, destroyers of disease; I settle into the dwelling together with immortality and with Agni.
Westward I, facing westward, approach you, O hall, unharmful; for Agni within and the waters — both are the foremost of the cosmic order.
Svāhā to the gods, svāhā to those worthy of svāhā — from the eastern quarter of the hall, homage to its greatness.
Svāhā to the gods, svāhā to those worthy of svāhā — from the southern quarter of the hall, homage to its greatness.
Svāhā to the gods, svāhā to those worthy of svāhā — from the western quarter of the hall, homage to its greatness.
Svāhā to the gods, svāhā to those worthy of svāhā — from the northern quarter of the hall, homage to its greatness.
Svāhā to the gods, svāhā to those worthy of svāhā — from the fixed (nadir) quarter of the hall, homage to its greatness.
Svāhā to the gods, svāhā to those worthy of svāhā — from the upper (zenith) quarter of the hall, homage to its greatness.
Svāhā to the gods, svāhā to those worthy of svāhā — from every quarter of the hall, homage to its greatness.
The head of the rival, the enemy, the ill-willed adversary who hates us — this I cleave off with might.
This amulet, born from the plowshare, shall make armor for me; satisfied with the oblation-drink, may it come with vital sap and with luster.
What the skilled carpenter struck away from you with the adze in his hand — from that may the living waters, pure themselves, purify you, O pure one.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
This amulet, garlanded with gold, milking forth inexhaustible wealth, bearing faith, sacrifice, and greatness — may the guest dwell in our home.
For him we carve out ghee, surā, honey, and food — let the amulet, having gone to the gods, discern for us ever greater prosperity, as a father does for his sons.
The amulet — the plowshare-piece dripping with ghee, fierce khadira-wood — which Bṛhaspati bound on for might: with that strike down your enemies.
Agni fastened it back on — for the sake of clarified butter and vital sap; it milks ghee for him, ever more, day after day. With that strike down your enemies.
The amulet — the plowshare-piece dripping with ghee, fierce khadira-wood — which Bṛhaspati bound on for might: with that [strike down your enemies].
Indra fastened it back on — for might and heroic power; it milks strength alone for him. [With that strike down your enemies.]
Sūrya fastened it back on; with it he conquered these quarters; it milks luster alone for him. [With that strike down your enemies.]
Soma fastened that amulet upon him — for wealth, for vital sap, verily. It milked greatness for him (…).
The Moon, bearing that jewel, conquered the citadels of the Asuras, the golden strongholds of the Dānavas. It milked lustre for him (…).
King Varuṇa fastened upon him that amulet, the well-being-granting one. It milked sovereignty for him (…).
Tvaṣṭṛ fastened that amulet upon him — for progeny, for heroic vigour. It milked beauty of form for him (…).
Savitṛ, bearing that jewel, conquered the heavenly realm with it. It milked gracious speech for him (…).
The Waters, bearing that jewel, flow on for ever, inexhaustible. It milked immortality for them (…).
With that jewel the two Aśvins guard this farmland. It milked milk for the two healers (…).
The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for swift Vāta — it milked sacred speech for him (…).

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The gods, bearing that jewel, conquered all the worlds in battle. It milked conquest for them (…).
May the deities place this jewel upon you to be worn; may it milk prosperity for you indeed. Again and again, day after day, with it do you smite your foes.
The intermediate quarters fastened it; the cardinal directions fastened that amulet. The jewel brought forth by Prajāpati has laid my enemies low.
The seasons fastened it; the seasonal divisions fastened that amulet. The year, having bound it, shines sovereign over all existing beings.
The Atharvaṇas fastened it; the Ātharvaṇas fastened that amulet. The Aṅgirasas, having bound it, split open the strongholds of the Dasyus.
Dhātṛ fastened that amulet; with it he fashioned all existing creatures. With it do you smite your foes.
The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the gods as protection against the Asuras — that jewel has come to you together with cattle, with goats and sheep, with food and with offspring.
(…) they have come with a stream of honey and ghee, with sweet drink, together with splendour.
The amulet which Bṛhaspati bound for the gods as protection against the Asuras — that jewel has come to you with vital power, with lustre, with might, with prosperity, with wealth, together with splendour.
He whose milk these three worlds attend as something milked — may that jewel protect you from above for pre-eminence.
May that jewel of hundredfold capacity quicken you for pre-eminence — that jewel upon which gods, Pitṛs, and human beings continually depend for their sustenance.
O amulet that augments the sacrifice, I have fastened you, auspicious one, upon this man — him do you, O jewel of hundredfold capacity, quicken to pre-eminence.
Without rivals, slayer of rivals, it has laid my rivals low. May this jewel, born of the gods, make you superior over your adversary.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The jewel of thousandfold power, auspicious — I fasten it upon you together with sacred formulation and lustre. May this plough-jewel mount upon you together with the gods.
As the seed sprouts in the fertile field when ploughed with the ploughshare, so may progeny, cattle, and food upon food flourish in him.
O Agni, being pleased, welcome this fire-wood duly gathered, welcome the oblation. May we find in him — in Jātavedas — through sacred formulation, benevolence, well-being, sight, breath, offspring, and cattle.
You are Kṣā and you are Kṣamā; in your mouth are Being and Auspicious-Being. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two of yours we bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are Bhūmi and you are Bhūti; in your mouth are the World and Fair-Flourishing. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are Pṛthvī and you are Pṛthivī; in your mouth are What-Shall-Be and What-Shall-Not-Be. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are Kṣemyā and you are Kṣiti; in your mouth are Bliss and the Vault-of-Heaven. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
You are the Firm One and you are the Yielding One; in your mouth are Luminous-Space and Heaven. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are the Immeasurable and you are Nirṛti; in your mouth are Mitra and the Benevolent-One. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are the White-Backed One and you are the Shaking One; in your mouth are Finding and the Act-of-Finding. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are the Well-Fed One and you are Suhiti; in your mouth are Acquisition and Fair-Acquisition. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are Vapsā and you are Vapsatī; in your mouth are the Well-Speaking and the Forth-Speaking. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
You are the Apsaras and you are Sadānvā; in your mouth are Own-Wealth and Well-Endowed-Wealth. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are Pṛśni and you are Pṛṣatī; in your mouth are Giving and Bestowing-Forth. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are All-Sustaining and you are All-Form; in your mouth are Giving and Giving-Forth. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are the Swallowing One and you are Garargṛt; in your mouth are a Multitude and the Gathering-Multitude. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are the Heavy One and you are the Bearer-of-Weight; in your mouth are Milking and the Act-of-Milking. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
You are Diti and you are Aditi; in your mouth are Milk and the Milk-Filled. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are the Aged One and you are the Aging One; in your mouth are Vigor and the Vigorous-One. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are Foundation and you are the One-Who-Stands-Firm; in your mouth are Vital-Force and Fiery-Splendor. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are the World-Possessing One and you are the World-Maker; in your mouth are Renown and the Seeker-of-Renown. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are the Vast One and you are the Powerful-Origin; in your mouth are Action and the Perfecting-Action. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
You are the Low One and you are the Upturned One; in your mouth are Growth and Abundant-Growth. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are Rohiṇī and you are Surohiṇī; in your mouth are Food and the Eating-of-Food. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are Sarā and you are Sarasvatī; in your mouth are Sacred-Power and Lordly-Might. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.

To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
You are Mahas and you are Mahasvatī; in your mouth are Desire and Satisfaction. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two be our bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
You are the All and all this here is yours; in your mouth are the All-World and all the Gods. To those two of yours we are subject; to those two of yours we bow; by those two be gracious to us, speak over us, breathe upon us. As a mother to a son, as a father to a son — this one here am I; release him not, O Seizer; lead this man forth, freed from the bonds of possession.
Whatever offence against the gods, O gods, we have committed — from that, O Ādityas, do you release us by the power of ṛta.
By the power of ṛta, O adorable Ādityas, release us here; for though you, the bearers of the sacrifice, were willing to instruct us in sacrifice, we fell short.
Offering oblation with the ladle and ghee — though all of you gods were willingly instructing us, we sacrificers rich in fat-offerings could not fully attain.
Whatever sins we have committed knowingly or unknowingly — from that guilt, release us here, all you gods acting in concert.
Whether waking or sleeping I have done wrong upon wrong — from that, both what has been and what is yet to be, may they release me, as from a wooden post.
As one released from a wooden post, as one who has sweated and bathed away impurity — let them release me, purified with the purifying ghee, from all sins.
What a boundary the ploughmen made at the beginning by driving in stakes — without proper knowledge and without learning — that I offer into Vaivasvata the king; may our sacrificial rite now be sweet.
May Vaivasvata prepare the remedies; may he, having a share of sweetness, unite us with sweetness. Whatever sin sent by a mother has come upon us, or whatever offence a father has committed in anger — may it be healed.
If this sin has come upon us injuriously from mother, from father, from brother, or from a son — may the wrath of all those fathers who attend upon her be propitious.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Whatever debt remains unpaid, whatever I owe — that by which I move under Yama's authority — from this, O Agni, I become free of debt; while yet living I render back all sin.
Even here and now, we make this return; we, the living, carry back this debt to the living. Whatever grain was consumed after being borrowed — may Agni make me free of that debt.
May we be free of debt in this world, free of debt in the next, free of debt in the third vault of heaven. May we dwell free of debt on all paths — those of the gods and those of the fathers.
Whatever guilt we committed with our hands seeking to anoint the dice — that, O Ugraṃpaśyā and Ugrajit, you two Apsarases, grant us release from that debt today.
O Ugraṃpaśyā, sustainer of the realm, whatever guilt arising from the play of dice — grant us release from that. Let not the one seeking our debt come to us; may he arrive at Yama's world, fettered with cords.
Him to whom I owe a debt, whose wife I approach, whom I approach as a supplicant — O gods, may they speak no word superior to mine; O divine wives, O Apsarases, this has been pondered by you.
When gambling, I incur a debt; when intending not to give, O Agni, I also make a pledge. May Vaiśvānara, our most excellent overlord, lead us upward to the world of the well-performed deed.
May Vaiśvānara purify us with purifiers, since I run toward the quarter of pledged obligation. Whatever sin is there in begging mentally without knowing — that I press away.
Let us make known to Vaiśvānara this pledge of the debt that I declare among the deities; may he fully understand the unravelling of these bonds, and then may we come together with what is ripened.
Whatever harm we have done to the atmosphere, to the earth or to heaven, to mother or to father — from that sin may Agni Gārhapatya release me.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Earth is our mother, Aditi our birth-source, the atmosphere our brother against our calumny; may Father Heaven be auspicious from the ancestral realm — do not, having approached a kinswoman, fall us from the world.
Where the good-hearted and the well-performed rejoice, having shed the disease of their own body — whole in limb, uninjured, in heaven — there may we behold both our parents and our sons.
May Viṣāṇā loosen and release from you all the bonds — highest, lowest, and those of Varuṇa — by which you are bound with wood, by which with rope, by which you are bound to the earth, and by which with a spoken vow.
The two auspicious stars named Vicṛtau have risen; may they reach here and bestow of immortality — that which releases the bound.
Open wide, make room; you release the bound from their bonds. Like an embryo thrust forth from the womb, dwell upon all the paths.
Knowing him, may the wise Prajāpati, first-born of ṛta, receive him; may we follow the unbroken thread that has been given by us, beyond old age.
Some follow along the stretched thread, for whom a path has been given through ancestral rite; some, having no kin, hand on and extend — if they have learned to give, that is their heaven.
Take hold of it in succession, grasp it in succession; those who have faith attend upon this world. Whatever charitable deed of you two has entered the fire — for its safekeeping let the couple take refuge together.
Gods are fathers; fathers are gods. Who I am, that I am; that one here — I am he.
He cooks, he sacrifices, he worships for this man. May the desired be auspicious to me; prosperous, pacified, propitious — from that keep the barley grain safe for me.
O king, stand firm in the vault of heaven; may this offering stand firm there. Know our charitable deed, O king; be well-disposed, O divine one.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Away from us we thrust the Brāhmaṇīsandhā, we drive off the obstructing torrents; may Indra and Agni, united in treasure, release us from the flood.
Homage to you, O Brāhmaṇīsandhā — go back whence you have come. He who hates us and him whom we hate, upon him I urge you forward; be you roused against him.
They call you a boundless ocean — those who do not lead rightly do not know you; but those who directly know your belly, your great mouth, your face, your rite of dismissal — they truly know you.
Her womb has been fashioned by Indra; hell is her nest. May the great ocean, the measurer of the atmospheric realm, grant us a place in the celestial world as well.
Of that odana: Bṛhaspati is the head, Brahman the face, the Sun and Moon the two eyes, the Bṛhat and Rathantara sāmans the two ears; Agni is the mouth, lightning the tongue, the Maruts the teeth, Pavamāna the breath.
The herbs are the body-hairs, the trees the head-hair, the ocean the urine, the two Aśvins the fore-feet; the caruvessel is the five-holed cooking-pot, the gharma is kindled here.
The eye is the pestle, Desire the mortar, Diti the winnowing-fan, Aditi the one who grasps the winnowing-fan, the Wind has winnowed it clean; the cows are the husked grains, the horses the broken fragments, the gnats the chaff, the kabru and phalīkaraṇa plants the dark iron, the red iron his flesh.
Tin is the ash, the white substances are the bones, green is the complexion, abundant is the fragrance; the threshing-floor is the vessel, the two camels the arms, the two wooden spoons the shoulders, the traces the intestines, the pole and the yoke-pin the cross-pieces, the yoke-beams the collar-bones.
Sacred truth is the hand-sprinkling, the channel-water is the pouring over; the seasonal rains are the cookers, Fire is the eater, the Brāhmaṇa is the receiver.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Of that odana: the Earth is the cooking-pot, Heaven the lid, the head the cloud, steam the mist; the Bṛhat is the spreading base, the Rathantara the ladle; the quarters are the flanks, the furrows the ribs, the sand the lower fat, the sesamum paste the under-layer, day and night the two strides of the odana.
Rain is the sprinkling-water, the Maruts have kindled it round about, the kiṣkara-grasses are the enclosing sticks; by the ṛc-verse the pot is placed upon the fire, by the priestly office it is dispatched, by Brahman it is received.
Whoever should thus know the greatness of this odana — he should not say it is small, nor say it is mere sprinkling-over, nor say this is nothing whatsoever.
As much as the giver might intend in his mind, that he should not overspeak; by the odana, the sacrificial word, all worlds are fulfilled.
In whom the ocean, heaven, and earth — the three — rest, lower and upper alike.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:

The theologians declare: 'You have eaten the rice-oblation facing toward it; you have eaten the rice-oblation facing away from it; the rice-oblations have eaten you.' With whose two feet did you eat it?

And if thereupon you were to eat it with a head other than the one with which you ate it before, he says to him: 'Your head shall fall apart.'
And if thereupon you were to eat it with a mouth other than the one with which you ate it before, he says to him: 'Your head shall go awry.'
And if thereupon you were to eat it with two eyes other than those with which you ate it before, he says to him: 'You shall become blind.'
And if thereupon you were to eat it with two ears other than those with which you ate it before, he says to him: 'You shall become deaf.'
And if thereupon you were to eat it with an oral cavity other than the one with which you ate it before, he says to him: 'Your speech shall depart from you.'
And if thereupon you were to eat it with a tongue other than the one with which you ate it before, he says to him: 'Your tongue shall be the first of you to die.'
And if thereupon you were to eat it with teeth other than those with which you ate it before, he says to him: 'Your teeth shall shatter.'

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
And if thereupon you were to eat it with vital breaths other than those with which you ate it before, he says to him: 'The breath of life shall abandon you.'
And if thereupon you were to eat it with a chest other than the one with which you ate it before, he says to him: 'You shall not succeed in cultivation.'
And if thereupon you were to eat it with a breadth other than the one with which you ate it before, he says to him: 'Rājayakṣman shall smite you.'
And if thereupon you were to eat it with a back other than the one with which you ate it before, he says to him: 'Lightning shall strike you.'
And if thereupon you were to eat it with a belly other than the one with which you ate it before, he says to him: 'Varuṇa shall smite you.'
And if thereupon you were to eat it with a bladder other than the one with which you ate it before, he says to him: 'You shall die in the waters.'
And if thereupon you were to eat it with two thighs other than those with which you ate it before, he says to him: 'Your two thighs shall fall off.'
And if thereupon you were to eat it with two knee-joints other than those with which you ate it before, he says to him: 'You shall become lame.'
And if thereupon you were to eat it with two feet other than those with which you ate it before, he says to him: 'A serpent shall strike you.'
And if thereupon you were to eat it upon a foundation other than that upon which you ate it before, he says to him: 'You shall become without firm footing.'
And if thereupon you were to eat it with two hands other than those with which you ate it before, he says to him: 'You shall slay a brahmin.'
I did not face toward it nor away from it; neither did I eat the rice-oblation, nor did the rice-oblation eat me. The rice-oblation itself ate the rice-oblation — with Bṛhaspati as the head.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
I did not face toward it nor away from it; neither did I eat the rice-oblation, nor did the rice-oblation eat me. The rice-oblation itself ate the rice-oblation — with brahman as the mouth.
I did not face toward it nor away from it; neither did I eat the rice-oblation, nor did the rice-oblation eat me. The rice-oblation itself ate the rice-oblation — with Sūrya and Candramās as the two eyes.
I did not face toward it nor away from it; neither did I eat the rice-oblation, nor did the rice-oblation eat me. The rice-oblation itself ate the rice-oblation — with the Bṛhat and Rathantara sāmans as the two ears.
I did not face toward it nor away from it; neither did I eat the rice-oblation, nor did the rice-oblation eat me. The rice-oblation itself ate the rice-oblation — with Agni as the oral cavity.
I did not face toward it nor away from it; neither did I eat the rice-oblation, nor did the rice-oblation eat me. The rice-oblation itself ate the rice-oblation — with lightning as the tongue.
I did not face toward it nor away from it; neither did I eat the rice-oblation, nor did the rice-oblation eat me. The rice-oblation itself ate the rice-oblation — with the Maruts as the teeth.
I did not face toward it nor away from it; neither did I eat the rice-oblation, nor did the rice-oblation eat me. The rice-oblation itself ate the rice-oblation — with the Seven Seers as the vital breaths.
I did not face toward it nor away from it; neither did I eat the rice-oblation, nor did the rice-oblation eat me. The rice-oblation itself ate the rice-oblation — with the earth as the chest.
I did not face toward it nor away from it; neither did I eat the rice-oblation, nor did the rice-oblation eat me. The rice-oblation itself ate the rice-oblation — with the atmosphere as the breadth.
I did not face toward it nor away from it; neither did I eat the rice-oblation, nor did the rice-oblation eat me. The rice-oblation itself ate the rice-oblation — with the sky as the back.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
I did not face toward it nor away from it; neither did I eat the rice-oblation, nor did the rice-oblation eat me. The rice-oblation itself ate the rice-oblation — with Varuṇa's belly as the belly.
I did not face toward it nor away from it; neither did I eat the rice-oblation, nor did the rice-oblation eat me. The rice-oblation itself ate the rice-oblation — with the ocean as the bladder.
I did not face toward it nor away from it; neither did I eat the rice-oblation, nor did the rice-oblation eat me. The rice-oblation itself ate the rice-oblation — with Mitra and Varuṇa as the two thighs.
I did not face toward it nor away from it; neither did I eat the rice-oblation, nor did the rice-oblation eat me. The rice-oblation itself ate the rice-oblation — with the knee-joints of ṛta as the two knee-joints.
I did not face toward it nor away from it; neither did I eat the rice-oblation, nor did the rice-oblation eat me. The rice-oblation itself ate the rice-oblation — with Savitṛ's feet as the two feet.
I did not face toward it nor away from it; neither did I eat the rice-oblation, nor did the rice-oblation eat me. The rice-oblation itself ate the rice-oblation — upon this very foundation did it eat.
I did not face toward it nor away from it; neither did I eat the rice-oblation, nor did the rice-oblation eat me. The rice-oblation itself ate the rice-oblation — with the hands of satya as the two hands.
They ate it; they mounted it; they attained it. It is from this very oblation that Prajāpati fashioned the thirty-three worlds out of worlds.
For its protection the gods created the sacrifices. Those thirty-three pure worlds created by Prajāpati — all of them are won and secured for him who knows this.
This rice-oblation indeed is all-limbed, all-souled, all-jointed, all-footed, all-backed. All-limbed, all-souled, all-jointed, all-footed, all-backed becomes he who knows thus.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
He who becomes a witness-observer of one who knows thus — that witness-observer obstructs his vital breath. Yet he does not obstruct the vital breath, and then all his wealth is wrested away.
And yet all his wealth is not wrested away — then one says to him: 'Thou shalt die, without foundation, without abode.' Without foundation indeed, without abode, does he die who becomes a witness-observer of one who knows thus.
By whom were the two heels of the man brought together? By whom was the flesh gathered? By whom the two ankles? By whom the fleshy toes, and by whom the apertures? By whom the two shin-bones raised up in the middle? Who is the foundation?
Why indeed did they make the two ankles lower, and the two knee-caps upper, in the man? Having fashioned them, they set the two shanks in place — where then? Who begot these two joints of the knees?
A fourfold frame is joined together, holding at its seams, a loose trunk above the knees. The two haunches and the thighs — who then begot them? By means of those two the body became well and firmly held.
How many gods, and which were they, who built up the foremost chest of the man? How many set the two breasts in place? Who formed the two collar-bones? How many fashioned the shoulders, how many the ribs?
Who brought together his two arms, saying, 'Let him perform heroic deeds'? Which god placed his two shoulders upon the trunk and set them there?
Which one fashioned his brain, his forehead? Who first shaped the nape-joint and the skull? Having built the built-up structure of the man's two jaws, which god was it who ascended to heaven?
Who pierced the seven apertures in the head — these two ears, the two eyes, the two nostrils, the mouth — whose greatness of conquest, in many places, both four-footed and two-footed creatures traverse?

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
He placed the tongue, widely extended, within the two jaws; thereupon he established mighty speech upon it. He rolls about in greatness in the sky, clothed in the waters — who indeed knows him fully?
Having stitched together his head and that which is the heart, Atharva sent the purifying breath upward from the brain, above the skull.
That head of Atharvan is a divine casket, firmly clasped shut. May that vital breath protect the glory, the food, and likewise the mind thereof.
The many pleasant and unpleasant things, sleep, oppression, torpor, delight, the vehement and its joys — all these does the man carry upward and bear forth.
Distress, ill-fortune, dissolution — whence now in the man is lack of wisdom? Attainment, full prosperity, non-growth, intelligence, utterances — whence do these come?
Who placed the waters in him — flowing in diverse directions, falling in abundance, born to run like rivers? The fierce red ones, the bloody, the coppery-smoky, the upward-flowing and downward-flowing and transverse ones within the man.
Who placed the in-breath in him, who the out-breath, and likewise the diffused breath? Which god established the equalizing breath upon this man?
Who placed form in him? Who greatness and a name? Who placed gait in him, who the distinguishing mark, who the deeds of conduct in the man?
Who placed seed in him, saying, 'Let the thread be extended'? Who poured wisdom upon him? Who placed the arrow in him, who the masculine vitality?
Who clothed him with a garment? Who ordained his lifespan? Who bestowed strength upon him? Who ordained his swiftness?
Who first, as the one, placed sacrifice upon this man? Who placed truth in him, who falsehood, who death, who immortality?
By whom were the waters spread out in sequence? By whom was the day made for brilliance? By whom was the dawn kindled? By whom was the evening-born given?

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
By whom was this earth covered over? By whom did he encompass the sky? By whom in greatness the mountains? By whom does the man perform his deeds?
By what does one dwell in the wake of the gods? By what did he bring forth the divine directions? By what this other constellation? By what is the existent called the ruling power?
By what does one attain Parjanya? By what the far-seeing Soma? By what does a man attain this Agni? By what does he measure out the year?
By what was this earth set in place? By what was the upper heaven established? By what was this atmosphere—both upward-reaching and transverse—spread wide and set in position?
By Brahman was the earth set in place; Brahman upheld the upper heaven; by Brahman was this atmosphere—both upward-reaching and transverse—spread wide and set in position.
By what does one attain the Vedic scholar? By what this Parameṣṭhin? By what sacrifice and faith? By what is mind established within him?
By Brahman one attains the Vedic scholar; Brahman is this Parameṣṭhin; Brahman is sacrifice and faith; by Brahman is mind established within him.
Who created these bones? Who assembled this flesh? Who gathered this skin and hair? Who put together this form?
Brahman created the bones; Brahman assembled the flesh; Brahman gathered skin and hair; Brahman put together the form.
Who created this eye? Who set the breath moving through the apertures? Who gathered this mind and speech? Who assembled this citadel?
Brahman created the eye; Brahman set the breath moving through the aperture; Brahman gathered mind and speech; Brahman assembled this citadel.
The eye does not abandon him, nor does the breath, before old age, for he who knows the citadel of Brahman—it is on that account that he is called Puruṣa.
To him who truly knows that citadel of Brahman enveloped in immortality, both Brahman and the Brahmic powers have given life-span, breath, and progeny.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Eight-wheeled, nine-gated is the unconquerable citadel of the gods; within it is a golden sheath enveloped in the light of heaven.
In that golden sheath with three spokes, set on three supports—that which abides within it, possessing the Self, that indeed the knowers of Brahman know.
The golden, resplendent, tawny citadel, enveloped in glory, unconquered—into it did Brahmā enter.
This varaṇa-amulet of yours has been fashioned as the destroyer of rivals; with it seize your enemies boldly, crush down those who scheme you harm.
Smite them, crush them down, attack them boldly—let the amulet be your vanguard going before you! The gods, day by day, warded off with the varaṇa the onslaughts of the Asuras.
The varaṇa—all-healing, thousand-eyed, green-hued, golden—has enclosed you in protection; you who strike your enemies down, overwhelm them first, those who indeed hate you.
This varaṇa shall ward off for you the widely spread sorcery, the man-made harm; this shall ward off all evil from you.
Let the divine varaṇa, lord of the forest, ward off this; the disease that has entered into him—that the gods have shielded against with the varaṇa.
