If on sleeping you behold an evil dream, if a beast runs off on an ill-omened track—from ill-boding sneezing, from an evil omen of a bird, let this varaṇa amulet ward off all.
From malice, from Nirṛti, from sorcery, and from fear; from the blow of a death mightier than death—from these, O Varaṇa, ward me off.
My adversaries and their kinsmen, shaken to pieces by the varaṇa—into the formless darkness, into the realm of non-being, let them go into the lowest gloom.
Whatever sin my mother has committed, whatever my father, my brothers, our own people—whatever transgression we have done—from that shall this divine lord of the forest ward us off.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Unharmed am I, unharmed in my cattle, long-lived, complete in all my being—me, thus, let the varaṇa amulet guard on every side, from all directions.
This varaṇa upon my chest — king, god, lord of the forest — may he bestow on me sovereignty, dominion, cattle, and vital force.
I bear this varaṇa, possessing life, one of a hundred autumns; may he drive away my enemies even as Indra drives the Dasyus like Asuras.
As the wind breaks aged forest trees with its might, so do thou shatter my rivals — those born before and those born after; may Varaṇa protect thee on all sides.
As trees withered by the wind lie cast down and felled, so do thou utterly destroy and lay low all my rivals — those born before and those born after; may Varaṇa protect thee.
As the wind and fire together consume all forest trees, so do thou consume all my rivals — those born before and those born after; may Varaṇa protect thee on all sides.
Do thou cut them off, O Varaṇa, before their appointed doom, before their full lifespan — those who seek to harm him among his cattle, and those who seek to harm his realm.
As the sun shines pre-eminent, as splendor is established in him, so do thou outshine all my rivals day by day; may Varaṇa protect thee on all sides.
As glory abides in the earth, as glory abides in Jātavedas — so may my varaṇa amulet confer on me fame and prosperity; may it anoint me with its brilliance, anoint me with its glory.
As glory resides in the Agnihotra, as glory resides in the vaṣaṭ-call — [so may my varaṇa amulet confer on me fame and prosperity; may it anoint me with its brilliance, anoint me with its glory].
As glory resides in the soma-drinking, as glory resides in the honey-mixture — [so may my varaṇa amulet confer on me fame and prosperity; may it anoint me with its brilliance, anoint me with its glory].

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
As glory resides in a maiden, as glory resides in this fully equipped chariot — [so may my varaṇa amulet confer on me fame and prosperity; may it anoint me with its brilliance, anoint me with its glory].
As glory resides in the moon and in Āditya the all-seeing eye of men — [so may my varaṇa amulet confer on me fame and prosperity; may it anoint me with its brilliance, anoint me with its glory].
As glory resides in Prajāpati, as glory resides in Parameṣṭhin — [so may my varaṇa amulet confer on me fame and prosperity; may it anoint me with its brilliance, anoint me with its glory].
As immortality is established among the gods, as truth is established among them — so may my varaṇa amulet confer on me fame and prosperity; may it anoint me with its brilliance, anoint me with its glory.
Of this brilliant, hoary Hotṛ — his middle brother is the devourer of food; the third brother is he of butter-bright back. Here I beheld the lord of the people who has seven sons.
Seven harness the one-wheeled chariot; one horse bearing seven names draws it. The three-naveled wheel is unaging and unchecked; upon it all these worlds are established.
Those seven who stand upon this chariot, the seven-wheeled — seven horses draw it; seven sisters sing forth together where the seven names of the cows are hidden.
Who perceived it first at its birth — the bone-possessing one that the boneless one bears? The breath of life, the blood, the self of the earth — where indeed is it? Who has gone to a knower to ask this?
Unwise, I ask with my mind not understanding — the hidden footprints of the gods lie in this. Upon the young calf the seers have spread seven threads, which are to be woven.
Unknowing yet questioning even the knowing seers here, I ask for understanding though I understand not — who propped apart these six expanses in the form of the unborn? What is that one thing?

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Let him declare here who truly knows it — the hidden track of this lovely bird. The cows milk milk from his head; clad in a covering they have fetched water with their feet.
The mother has embraced the father in truth; at the beginning she met him in thought, with mind. She, the shuddering womb-fluid, was buried within; reverencing, they approached to invoke her.
Yoked, the mother stood at the right-side pole; the embryo stood within the enclosures. The calf lowed, looking after the cow, the all-formed one, in the three journeys.
Bearing three mothers and three fathers, one stood erect; they do not wear him down. On the back of yonder sky they deliberate — an all-knowing speech that does not fill all.
The twelve-spoked wheel of Ṛta rolls around heaven, never subject to decay. O Agni, upon it stand paired sons — seven hundred and twenty.
They call the five-footed, twelve-formed Father full-bodied in the upper half of heaven; others above declare him, the far-seeing, fixed on the seven-wheeled, six-spoked [wheel].
As the five-spoked wheel turns round and round, all worlds are established upon it. Its axle glows with the immense burden; from of old the nave is never severed.
The ageless wheel with unbroken felly revolves; ten yoked [steeds] draw it upon the outstretched [sky]. Covered, the eye of the Sun moves through the atmosphere — upon it all worlds are fastened.
The seventh of those born together they call the only-born; six, they say, are the twin-born ṛṣis, offspring of the gods. Their oblations are distributed station by station; differing in form, they shine in the steadfast [realm].
Those who are women — men call them such; the seeing one with eyes perceives it, the blind does not discern. The son who is a seer recognises them; he who knows them would be the father of his own father.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Below the farther, above the nearer, bearing the calf on her hoof, the cow has arisen. Facing downward, to which side has she gone? Where does she calve? — for she is not in this herd.
Who knows his father below the farther, above the nearer — who, acting as seer, could here declare whence is born the divine mind?
Those moving hither — them they call moving yonder; those moving yonder — them they call moving hither. O Soma, those things which you and Indra made: yoked to the pole they carry [the load] through the atmosphere.
Two fair-winged companions, yoked together as friends, cling around the same tree. One of the two eats the sweet pipal berry; the other, eating nothing, only looks on.
In the tree where the honey-eating fair-winged birds nest and all bring forth their young — they say its sweet pipal berry is at the crest; he who does not know the Father will not attain it.
Where the fair-winged ones chant unblinking at the assembly for a share of immortality — the Lord, the guardian of all the world — that wise one has entered into the simple one right here.
That which in the gāyatrī was placed beyond the gāyatrī, and the triṣṭubh that was fashioned out from the triṣṭubh — and the verse that was set in the jagatī's jagatī — those who truly know that have attained immortality.
With the gāyatrī one measures the ark; with the ark the sāman; with the triṣṭubh the speech. With speech they measure speech — two-footed, four-footed — with the syllable they measure the seven voices.
With the jagatī [metre] he propped the celestial river; in the rathantara [sāman] he beheld the Sun round about. They speak of three kindling-sticks of the gāyatra; by that greatness it surpassed all in majesty.
I call near this good-milking cow; may the skilled-handed milker milk and draw from her. May Savitṛ press out for us the choicest pressing; the gharma kindled — of that I now proclaim aloud.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Making the hiṃkāra sound, mistress of the Vasus, seeking her calf she came near in thought. May this inviolable one be milked of her milk for the two Aśvins; may she increase to great good fortune.
The cow lowed toward her calf blinking its eyes; she made the hiṃ-sound at the calf's head, eager to be its mother. Lowing toward the brimming gharma vessel, she bellows her cry, overflowing with milk.
This is he who bellows, by whom the cow, covered all around, lows her cry, perched on the quivering [hide]. She, by her wisdom, laid low a mortal; becoming lightning, she hurled herself against the covering.
Lightning, slumbering on the back of the waters, though young, was devoured by the grey one. Behold the poetic power of the god in his greatness — today he died, yet yesterday he came together.
The breathing one lies still; the swift-footed, the living, the trembling, the steadfast — in the midst of dwellings. The living moves by his own powers among the dead; the immortal shares a womb with the mortal.
I saw the herdsman who does not rest, going hither and thither along the paths. Putting on convergent and divergent [forms] alike, he revolves again and again within the worlds.
He who made it does not know it; he who saw it — the sight has been hidden from him. Wrapped within the womb of the mother, he of many offspring has entered into dissolution.
Heaven is our father, our begetter, our navel here; kin to us is this great Earth, our mother. The womb lies between the two outstretched bowls; here the father placed the embryo in the daughter.
I ask you: what is the farthest limit of the earth? I ask you: what is the navel of the world? I ask you: what is the seed of the vigorous horse? I ask you: what is the highest heaven of speech?
This altar-ground is the farthest limit of the earth; this sacrifice is the navel of the world. This Soma is the seed of the vigorous horse; this brahman is the highest heaven of speech.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The seven half-embryos, the seed of the world, stand in Viṣṇu's law in the [four] quarters. Those wise ones, those far-seeing ones, encompass with their thoughts and minds; they surround on every side.
I do not discern what it is that I am; hidden, girded up, I wander with the mind. When the first-born of Ṛta came to me, then at last I obtained a share of this speech.
Going away, yet forward, seized by his own inherent power, the immortal shares a womb with the mortal. They two, ever going apart in opposite directions, perceive the one but not the other.
In the imperishable supreme heaven where all the gods have settled — he who does not know that, what will he do with the ṛc? Those who truly know that, they are seated here together.
Fashioning the footing of the ṛc by measure, with the half-verse they have fashioned all that moves. The triple-footed brahman manifests in many forms; by it the four quarters live.
May you become full of blessing from good pasture, and may we in turn be blessed. Eat the grass, O inviolable one, at all times; drink of the pure water, going about freely.
The gaurī has measured out and fashions the waters — she who is one-footed, two-footed, four-footed. Having become eight-footed, nine-footed, of a thousand syllables is the meter of the world; from her the oceans flow forth.
Then the footless goes first among those with feet — who of you two, O Mitra and Varuṇa, has perceived that? The embryo bears the burden even of him; it fulfils Ṛta and wards off what is not Ṛta.
Along the dark path the tawny fair-winged ones, clothed in waters, fly up to heaven. They turned back from the seat of Ṛta; and therewith they bedewed the earth with ghee.
Heaven by its swiftness, Earth by its breadth, the atmosphere by its greatness, the waters by their abundance — by the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, impelled forth, I pour thee out for the Brāhmaṇas.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
For the ṛṣis, for the seers' lineages, I pour thee out.
The most beloved, the best borne, the most filling, the most nutritious — the imperishable portion of vital strength, for the sake of imperishability I pour thee out.
May the Vasus pour thee out with the Gāyatrī metre.
May the Rudras pour thee out with the Triṣṭubh metre.
May the Ādityas pour thee out with the Jagatī metre.
This is for those who shout against us; this for those who rush against us; this for those who bear malice against us.
Just as a well of a hundred channels, a well of a thousand channels, fails not — so may this not fail us, like the ford of the Aśvins.
Whoever hates us in mind and whoever in speech, in the divine world or in the human — may Indra the god, the bounteous, the lord of Śacī, smite all of him with the great pressing-stone.
This garment, born among plants — O Soma, enter us again here with vital strength. Be firm, O Mother of arms, be bold; suffer no harm — Agni shall obtain this for you.
O divine Waters, for a share of vital strength I pour you in, imperishable ones, for the sake of imperishability.
O Jātavedas, with that body of thine that does not devour raw flesh, that heavenly form of thine, akin to austerity — with that form cook this odana offering; with it, O Agni, grant us great shelter.
Purified by the rays of Soma, O you who have eaten, be seated on the back of Āditya. Those among men who know the wooden vessel of thee, the odana, in the celestial world — for them may heaven be as great as the vessel. We know Earth as thy vessel, O odana.
May these waters, dripping with ghee, approach thee, O odana, augmenting thee with milk. Thou dost prop heaven, thou dost prop Earth and the atmosphere; with svādhā thou dost fill them.
As many grains of rice as are the foundations of thy cosmic order, so many sacrifices are the milkings of that order. So great may the svādhā be for me — the one whose back is ghee — milking vital strength mixed with honey in the vault of heaven.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The odana which I cook with faith, filling the vessel, delighting in the one whose back is ghee — may it not be exhausted for me, ever being eaten, in the world of Yama, in the highest heaven.
The odana, given together with the vessel and the sacrificial fee to Brāhmaṇas, establishes one in immortality. It has gone along the courses of the Sun, along his rays — ascending the back of heaven like a bird.
I release thee together with breath among the living, together with vitality, with milk, and with blessing. Go to the place of praise, to the world of those who have done good; may they eat of thee, seated to the south.
For thou goest on the same chariot as the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice; then go also to the recited Atirātra. Being of the measure of two nights, pervade the three-day rite; then ascend the four-night rite as though mounting a chariot.
Being consecrated by the four-night rite, advance; then go to the seven-night and the ten-night rite. Having encompassed the twelve-day rite on all sides, thrust away adversaries with the twenty-one-fold.
Having thrust away adversaries with the twenty-one-fold, then approach the forty-one-day rite, one at a time. Having become immortal through the thirty-three-fold, take hold of the odana of the three-month rite.
The year and the full year, in the realm of Bradhna in the highest heaven — O odana, become one with the vault of heaven upon vault of heaven.
May the Sādhyas lead this of mine forward from the front; the Ādityas, the Rudras, the Vasus, of one mind — may all the gods, united through the seasons, ever guard this with undivided attention.
The year, the full year, and the complete year — days and nights, months — O odana, follow upon the experience of the Sun, of Agni, of the Moon, the becoming of Vāyu.
Him whom the Pitṛs worship, whom the gods worship as purohita, through austerity and sacred knowledge — svādhā, vital strength, imperishability I offer into Vāyu the god, into Pavamāna, into Bṛhaspati.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Being consecrated fourfold, the odana — with vital strength the gods, with svādhā the Pitṛs, with bodily nourishment mankind, becoming food for the Brāhmaṇas — may it be ours in the highest heaven.
This path, O odana, the god-faring path, unobstructed by Death — by that path go. Undeceived, established by the virtuous through their own power, ordered by sacred knowledge, by the instruction of Yama — may it be ours in the highest heaven.
O odana, wherever thy homes are, go forth thither; let the waters go wherever is the place of the waters. Where the Brāhmaṇas know the womb of the odana — may that be ours in the highest heaven.
Offered into thy speech, may it be an oblation; offered into thy sight; offered into thy understanding, may it be offered into thy strength. Offered into thy hearing, into thy breath — offered into thy progeny, into thy immortality, and into thy desire, may it be offered.
Whether it belongs to Agni, or whether to Indra, whether to Marut, or whether to Viśvedeva — the Agni within thee whose name is Nṛmaṇas, the heart-dweller: into him may this odana be well offered; may it be ours in the highest heaven.
He who has entered mankind as Nṛmaṇas — the Agni of Agnis, the first, the sustainer of life.
That body of yours which departed from Death toward the fellowship of the gods, toward the world of the living — she who roams the waters, she who dwells in the depths, in her greatness: may this oblation-rice be well-offered to her; may it be ours in the highest heaven.
Without wrath, come back to our house, auspicious one, with gracious mind, not terrible — may the rain-grown [offering] go forth to meet you.
This our svadhā — the nine-fold mother — has become an immortal oblation among the immortals. Guard those [forebears] for us always, without negligence; they have come to us — watch over them, be wakeful.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Those who assail this deposit of ours — the current carried off into the realm of Yama — may king Varuṇa stand over their vital faculties with divine wrath. Those who sit together in this assembly: I give you this [deposit] in full, for the lord of sacrifice has come, having beheld it.
Those who scratch away and tear apart what has been given, who seize the sacrificial fee while it is being conveyed — let Indra the god, the bountiful, lord of Śacī, mighty Śakra, come burning them with the fire-kindler's flame. May Bṛhaspati, Varuṇa, Soma, and Indra make what I have given solely and wholly mine.
Headache, head-disease, earache, tertian fever — all the ailment in your head we charm out and away.
From your ears, from your ear-passages — the oyster-shell discharge, the bloody [flux] — [we charm out and away].
That [disease] which renders a man stupefied, which renders a man blind — [we charm it out and away].
On whose account wasting-disease (yakṣma) falls away from the nose and from the mouth — [we charm it out and away].
Head-disease, limb-disease, the disease that pervades all limbs, visalpaka — all the ailment in your head we charm out and away.
Whose terrible appearance makes a man tremble — fever-ague (takman), the chill, and the burning: that we charm away from you.
That which creeps along the thighs and also along the groins — balāsa (phlegmatic disease) from within the limbs we charm out and away.
Whether from desire or from aversion it is born and spreads from the heart — balāsa from the heart, from the limbs, we charm out and away.
Jaundice (harimāṇa) from your limbs, the nest of wasting-disease from within your inner self — all yakṣma from your limbs we charm out and away.
Let the balāsa become raw discharge; let the ailment become urine. The poison of all wasting-diseases I have now spoken out away from you.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Let the hollow drain outward — the kahā-bearer from your belly. The poison of all wasting-diseases I have now spoken out away from you.
From your belly, round about from your kloman (right lung), above from your navel, from your heart — the nest of wasting-disease from within your inner self we charm out and away.
Those [diseases] that break through the crown of the head, that flow back against the summit — may they, no longer harming, free of affliction, run outward through the opening.
Those that creep toward the heart and stretch along the vertebrae — [may they, no longer harming, free of affliction, run outward through the opening].
Those that flow up along the flanks and pierce along the ribs — [may they, no longer harming, free of affliction, run outward through the opening].
Those that flow up crosswise, the flowing ones from the flanks — [may they, no longer harming, free of affliction, run outward through the opening].
Those that creep along the rectum and also constrict the intestines — [may they, no longer harming, free of affliction, run outward through the opening].
Those that creep along the marrow and also break apart the joints — may they, no longer harming, free of affliction, run outward through the opening.
Those wasting-diseases that intoxicate the limbs, the festering ones — the poison of all wasting-diseases I have now spoken out away from you.
Of visalpaka, of vidradha (abscess), of vātīkāra (wind-disease), of vālaja — the poison of all wasting-diseases I have now spoken out away from you.
From your feet, from your ankles, from your shins, from your knees, from your thighs, from your hips, round about from your buttocks — from the spine, the flowing discharges, from the nape, from the neck, from the shoulders, from the head: I have caused the disease to perish.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The skull-plates of your head and of the heart — those who know them: the rising sun, Āditya, as he ascends, has caused the limb-disease to perish.
With ghee, with an oblation of clarified fat, I propitiate Kāma, the bull who slays rivals. Do thou, praised with great might, cast down my rivals low.
Whatever is not dear to my mind, not pleasing to my eye, whatever does not gladden my heart — that ill-dream I release upon my rival. Having duly praised Kāma, may I break free and rise.
O Kāma, release upon him the ill-dream, O Kāma the misdeed, childlessness, the indigence not of our making — O fierce lord, release it upon him who has treated us with hostility.
She who is called thy daughter, O Kāma, the cow, whom the seers name Speech, the far-shining — with her encircle my rivals; may life-breath, offspring, cattle, and vitality pass around them and encompass me.
By the power of Kāma, by the might of Indra, by the sovereignty of King Varuṇa, by Viṣṇu's strength, by Savitṛ's creative impulse, by Agni's priestly office — drive forth the rivals, as a helmsman a boat through the waters.
May Kāma, my fierce overlord, the prize-winner, make for me a world without rivals. May all the Viśvedevāḥ be my protectors; may all the gods come to this my invocation.
May those for whom Kāma is the foremost delight in this clarified fat and ghee here; may they make for me a world without rivals.
O Kāma, having mounted the same chariot as Indra and Agni, cast down my rivals low; and those who have fallen — their lowest dwellings, O Agni, burn through entirely.
Slay, O Kāma, those who are my rivals; cast them down into blind darkness. May they all be devoid of vital force and strength, so that not one of them shall remain alive.
Kāma has slain those who were my rivals and has made broad space for my flourishing. May the four cardinal quarters bow to me; may the six vast realms bring me ghee.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
That shelter of thine, O Kāma, triple-sheathed, the piercer, the spread-out armour of sacred power that is made impenetrable — with that encircle my rivals; may life-breath, offspring, cattle, and vitality pass around them and encompass me.
May they drift away downward, like a boat cut from its mooring. For those driven off by the arrow there is no returning.
Agni is the averter, Indra is the averter, Soma is the averter. O ye gods who drive away, drive that man — yonder son of yonder woman — from the world of the living to the world of the dead, the departed.
He wanders bereft of all heroes, driven off, hateful to friends, shunned by his own kin. And even lightnings strike down upon the earth — may the fierce god crush the rivals.
This great lightning, both the fallen and the unfallen, bears all thunderclaps. May Āditya, rising with his wealth of brilliance, drive off my rivals with power.
As the gods drove off the Asuras, as Indra pressed the Dasyus into the lowest darkness — so do thou, O Kāma, drive all those who are my rivals away from this world.
By that same means by which the gods always drove off the Asuras, by which Indra pressed the Dasyus into the lowest darkness — by that, O Kāma, drive those who are my rivals far away from this world.
Kāma was born first of all; before him there was nothing else. Neither the gods nor the Pitṛs nor mortals have attained unto him. Therefore thou art ever the greater, the mighty — to thee, O Kāma, homage alone I render.
Not even the wind has attained Kāma, nor fire, nor the sun, nor the moon. [...]
Not even the waters have attained Kāma; the appointed days and nights do not reach him. [...]
Not even the Puṇyajanas have attained Kāma, nor the Gandharvas and Apsarasas, nor the serpents. Therefore thou art ever the greater, the mighty — to thee, O Kāma, homage alone I render.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
As wide as heaven and earth in their expanse, as far as the waters have streamed, as far as fire reaches — so far thou art ever the greater, the mighty; to thee, O Kāma, homage alone I render.
As many as are the directions, the intermediate quarters reaching everywhere, as many as are the hopes that look upon the sky — so far thou art ever the greater, the mighty; to thee, O Kāma, homage alone I render.
As many as are the bees, the gnats, the kurūravaḥ, as many as are the vaghā creatures that creep upon trees — so far thou art ever the greater, the mighty; to thee, O Kāma, homage alone I render.
Those auspicious, gracious forms of thine, O Kāma, by which that which one chooses comes to be true — with those enter into us fully; drive the evil thoughts elsewhere away.
Those two limb-marks which your mother wiped off you at birth — the pativedanau auspices — let not the Evil-Named one covet them there, neither the aliṃśa nor the vatsapa.
The palāla, the anupalāla, the śarkuṇa, the koka, the malimruca, the palījaka, the āśleṣa, the vavrivāsasa, the ṛkṣagrīva, the pramīlina — we smite them away from her pudenda.
Let him not press close, let him not creep up against her thighs, let him not glide between them. I prepare for her this remedy, the baja-plant, banisher of the Evil-Named.
Both the Evil-Named and the Fair-Named desire a woman who is enclosed; we smite away the arāya — the Fair-Named desires what belongs to women.
He who is dark, hairy, a demon born of the tussock — and the taṇḍika as well — the arāyas from her hind parts and pudenda we drive away.
The arāya who sniffs after her and fondles her, the flesh-eater who licks her again and again, the dog-like śvakiṣkiṇa — Baja and Piṅga have utterly destroyed them.
He who steals upon you while you sleep, and he who seeks to harm you while you wake — as Sūrya in his circuit destroys shadows, so has he destroyed them all.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
He who falls upon you asleep, having taken the form of a brother or like a father — O Baja, you, strike down from here that impotent-shaped tirīṭina.
He who makes this woman miscarry or causes her calf to be born dead — O herb, destroy him with her kamala and her añjiva.
Those who dance around dwelling-places in the evening, braying like asses — the kusūlas, the kukṣilas, the kakubhas, the saramas, the sumas — O herb, scatter them in all directions with your fragrance and utterly destroy them.
Those kukundhas and kukūrabhas who wear pelts and unsightly garments, who dance about in the forest like eunuchs and raise a clamour — we drive them away from here.
Those whose toe-tips are behind and whose heels are in front and whose face is in front — the khalajās born of smoke-ash, the uruṇḍas, the maṭmaṭas, the kumbhamuṣkas, the ayāśavas — O Bṛhaspati, destroy them for her with your counter-awakening.
Those who cannot endure yonder Sūrya blazing in the sky — the arāyas who dwell in he-goats, the foul-smelling, red-mouthed makaka demons — we destroy them.
Those who creep away from Sūrya as a daughter-in-law avoids her father-in-law — let both Baja and Piṅga pierce them through the heart.
Those who carry themselves with excessive self-conceit, placing an undue portion upon themselves, and who prick women in the haunches — O Indra, destroy those rakṣases.
Those who walk ahead of the bride bearing horns in their hands, the grinning ones who stand at a distance, those who make a light upon a post — we drive them away from here.
Let them become rolling-eyed, clumsy, effeminate eunuchs — O remedy, strike down the man without a husband who seeks to uncover this woman who has a husband.
The arrogantly excited one, the matted-haired muni-like one, the gnashing one who fondles incessantly, the one who presses close with his udumbala, the tusk-snouted one, and the śāluḍa — pierce them with heel and foot as a cow kicks over the cooking pot.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
He who tampers with your womb or seeks to kill your child once born — let Piṅga of the fierce bow make him a heart-pierced one.
Those Gandharvas who lie down beside the lying-in women and kill the newly born — let Piṅga drive those claimants of women's portions away as the wind drives a cloud.
Hold fast what remains of the placenta; let not what was placed there fall away. Let the two fierce remedies, bearers of the girdle-knot, guard your womb.
You are the all-round protection of men and the expeller of Rakṣases. Scatter in all directions and utterly destroy all arāyas, the Evil-Named, the Yātudhānas.
From the pavīnasa, from the taṅgalva, from the śāyaka, and from the naked one — may Piṅga guard you for offspring and for your husband, keeping away the kimīdina demon.
Guard her from the two-mouthed one, from the four-eyed one, from the five-footed one, from the fingerless one — from those who creep forward from a cluster, and from the repeatedly encircling one.
Those keśavas who eat raw flesh and the flesh of men, who devour embryos — the arāyas from her hind parts and pudenda we drive away.
O Piṅga, guard the one being born; let them not turn the male into a female. Let not the egg-eating ones crush the embryo; drive the kimīdinas away from here.
Childlessness, the death of offspring, lamentation, evil, misfortune — making them as a garland stripped from a tree, hurl all that upon the enemy woman.
O Piṅga, smite the Yātudhānas, the foul-smelling, the red-mouthed ones. Driven forth by you, let the flesh-eaters go scattered in all directions, utterly slain.
In the Leavings are name and form; in the Leavings the worlds are established. In the Leavings are Indra and Agni; the whole universe is gathered within.
In the Leavings are Heaven and Earth; all that exists is gathered there. The waters and the ocean are in the Leavings; the moon and the wind are established therein.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Both the existent and the non-existent are in the Leavings — Death, vital prize, and Prajāpati. Whatever belongs to the world depends upon the Leavings; may the one who sees and the one who grants, and Śrī as well, be in me.
The firm, the strengthening, the steadfast, the other — Brahman, the ten all-creating ones: as a wheel surrounds the hub on every side, so the deities are fixed in the Leavings.
The Ṛc, the Sāman, the Yajus are the Leavings; the udgītha, the prastuta, that which stands firm. The hiṅkāra is in the Leavings, the musical note of the Sāman and its meḍi — may that be in me.
The Aindrāgna, the Pāvamāna, the Mahānāmnī verses, the Mahāvrata rite — the limbs of the sacrifice are in the Leavings, as an embryo within its mother.
The Rājasūya, the Vājapeya, the Agniṣṭoma and the soma-rite, the Arka and the Aśvamedha — in the Leavings, whose sacrificial grass is living and which is most exhilarating.
The Agnyādheya, and likewise the dīkṣā, the kāmaprā together with the metres — the lapsed sacrifices and the sattras are gathered in the Leavings.
The Agnihotra and faith, the vaṣaṭ-call, sacred vow, and austerity; the sacrificial gift and charitable work — all are gathered in the Leavings.
The one-night soma rite, the three-night rite, the sadyaḥkrī, the prakrī, the ukthya — woven and embedded in the Leavings are the minute particles of the sacrifice, by sacred knowledge.
The four-night rite, the five-night rite, the six-night rite, and both together; the ṣoḍaśī and the seven-night rite — from the Leavings were all born, all the sacrifices established in immortality.
The pratihāra, the nidhana, the Viśvajit and the Abhijit — the sāhna and the atirātra are in the Leavings, and the twelve-day rite as well — may that be in me.
Gracious speech, submission, security, the sweetness of food, nourishment, immortality, and vigor — all desires that incline toward us are in the Leavings; may desires be satisfied through desire.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The nine earths and the oceans are established in the Leavings of the sky. The sun shines forth from the Leavings; day and night too — may that be in me.
The upahavya, the viṣūvant, and whatsoever sacrifices are placed in the hidden realm — the Leavings sustains the sustainer of all; it is the father who begets.
The Leavings is the father of the begetter, the grandson of life itself, the grandfather. He is proclaimed lord of the universe, the bull upon the earth, beyond smiting.
Order, truth, austerity, consecration, exertion, dharma, and ritual action; the past and the future are in the Leavings — virility, Lakṣmī, strength within strength.
Prosperity, vital energy, resolve, lordly power, sovereignty, and the six broad realms — the year is established in the Leavings, as are the iḍā invocation, the praiṣā call, the ritual cups, and the oblation.
The four hotr-priests, the āprī hymns, the Cāturmāsya rites, the nivid litanies — sacrifices, priestly invocations, and animal offerings, those very iṣṭis, are in the Leavings.
The half-months and the months, the seasonal offerings together with the seasons — in the Leavings are the roaring waters, the thunder, sacred revelation, and the great earth.
Gravel, sand, and stones; herbs, plants, and grasses; clouds, lightning, and rain — they have taken refuge in the Leavings, dwelling therein.
Accomplishment, attainment, pervasion, completion, greatness, and growth; surpassing fulfilment — prosperity is placed in the Leavings, deeply embedded, well established.
Whatever breathes by breath, and whatever sees with the eye — from the Leavings were all born, the gods in heaven, those who dwell in the sky.
In-breath and out-breath, sight and hearing, the imperishable and whatever is perishable — [remainder of verse not preserved in this recension].

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The gods, the Pitṛs, human beings, and those who are Gandharvas and Apsarases — [remainder of verse not preserved in this recension].
The Ṛc-verses, the Sāmans, the metres, the Purāṇa together with the Yajus — [remainder of verse not preserved in this recension].
The Atharvan and Āṅgirasa sacred lore, and those who are serpents and holy folk — [remainder of verse not preserved in this recension].
Those who are joy and those who are delight, those who are rapture and exultation — from the Leavings were all born, the gods in heaven, those who dwell in the sky.
When Manyu brought forth the bride from the house of Saṃkalpa — who were the wedding-party, who were the suitors, and who became the chief suitor?
Tapas and Karman both dwelt within the great ocean — they were the wedding-party, they were the suitors, and Tapas was indeed the chief suitor.
Ten gods were born together, transcending the gods. Whoever truly knows their names would speak a great thing today.
Prāṇa and Apāna, sight and hearing, the imperishable and what perishes, Vyāna, Udāna, speech and mind — these carried purpose within them.
The seasons were yet unborn, and likewise Dhātṛ and Bṛhaspati, Indra, Agni, and the two Aśvins — whom did they then attend as eldest?
Tapas and Karman both dwelt within the great ocean; Tapas was born from Karman — him they attended as eldest.
Whence was Indra born, whence Soma, whence did Agni come into being? Whence did Tvaṣṭṛ come together, whence did Dhātṛ come together?
From Indra came Indra, from Soma came Soma, from Agni Agni was born; Tvaṣṭṛ was indeed born from Tvaṣṭṛ, Dhātṛ arose from Dhātṛ.
Those ten who were born, gods transcending the gods — having granted the world to their sons, in what world do they now abide?
That which was the primordial earth, which Addhātayas alone have known — what gods dwell upon it, and in what does it rest, with all therein?

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
From where did he bring the hair, from where the sinews, from where did he bring the bones? Who brought the limbs and joints and marrow, from where did he bring the flesh?
When he brought together hair, bone, sinew, flesh, and marrow — having fashioned a body with feet, into what world did he then enter?
Saṃsica — so are those gods named, who assembled him with their materials; having completely fashioned the mortal, the gods entered into the person.
The head and hands, and the arms, the tongue and neck and vertebrae, the back-ribs, the spine, and the flanks — what ṛṣi fitted all that together?
The thighs and feet, the knee-joints, the hips and hands, and the face — wrapping all that with skin, the great Saṃdhā joined it together.
That great body which took form, assembled together by Saṃdhā, by which this shines today — who brought color into it?
All the gods sought to learn it; yet the virtuous bride knew — she who is the wife, mistress of will: she it was who brought color into it.
When Tvaṣṭṛ had fashioned it, and the father who is beyond Tvaṣṭṛ — having made a home of the mortal, the gods entered into the person.
Sleep and languor, Nirṛti, and the deities named the Pāpmans — old age, baldness, and graying entered into the body.
Theft, evil deed, and iniquity; truth, sacrifice, and great glory; strength, lordship, and vital force — all entered into the body.
Prosperity and adversity, the gifts and the withheld gifts, all hungers and thirsts — all entered into the body.
The censurable and the praiseworthy, and that which strikes and that which withholds — faith, the sacred gift, and faithlessness entered the body.
Knowledge and ignorance, and whatever else is teachable — Brahman entered the body: the Ṛc, the Sāman, and the Yajus.
Bliss, joy, exhilaration, and the various forms of delight — laughter, festivity, and dances entered into the body.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Conversation and babble, and the various forms of excited speech and chatter — all entered the body: the unyoked, the preyoked, and the yoked.
Prāṇa and Apāna, sight and hearing, the imperishable and what perishes, Vyāna and Udāna, speech and mind — by means of the body, these move.
Blessings and commands, the shared commands and the distinct commands — all thoughts and intentions entered into the body.
Urgency and steadfastness, the prayer and the auspicious word — all entered the body: those that truly strive, the weapons, the diminishers.
The forces of blood and bone, the swift ones and the wretched — the hidden, the bright, the gross: the loathsome ones set them in order.
Making bone the sacrificial fuel, the eight waters set it in place; making semen the clarified butter, the gods entered into the person.
The waters, and the deities, and she who is Virāj together with Brahman — Brahman entered the body, and Prajāpati entered upon the body.
Sūrya apportioned the eye of the Puruṣa, Vāyu apportioned his breath; then the gods delivered his remaining self to Agni.
Therefore the knower holds this Puruṣa to be Brahman, for all the gods are gathered together upon the body within him.
When the Father apportioned the worlds as stations in the limbs for them, all the gods entered into the body limb by limb.
All the gods entered limb after limb of the body, for the Father granted them that unconquered world.
All the gods entered that unconquered world, the body laid down in manifold ways, which Prajāpati had brought forth.
O Agni, be born — Aditi, who seeks a patron, cooks this brahma-rice-oblation, desiring sons. May the seven sages, the makers of beings, churn you here together with offspring.
Make smoke, O vigorous friends, O guileless guardian, toward the sacred speech. This Agni, conqueror of armies, richly heroic, is he by whom the gods overpowered their enemies.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
O Agni, O Jātavedas, you were born for great heroic might, to cook the brahma-rice-oblation. The seven sages, the makers of beings, engendered you — bestow upon him riches replete with all heroes.
O Agni, kindled, you are kindled with fuel; you shall carry hither all the sacred gods. O Jātavedas, cooking the oblation for them, make him ascend to the heavenly world.
O Jātavedas, the share which has been set threefold before you — for the gods, for the Pitṛs, and for mortals — know your portions; I distribute that to you: that which belongs to the gods shall convey him across.
O Agni, you are mighty, the one who overpowers, the prevailing one; press down the rivals and enemies face downward. This measured portion, measured out, shall make your kindred bring tribute to you.
Thrive together with your kindred by means of milk; press him upward for great heroic might. Ascend erect upon the vault of the sky, upon the firmament — that which they call the heavenly world.
Let this great earth, the divine Pṛthivī, well-disposed in mind, receive the skin. May we attain the world of the well-doers on high.
Yoke these two pressing-stones joined together upon the skin; press out the soma-shoots well for the sacrificer. Smiting them down, strike down those who are hostile; lift up the offspring on high and raise it.
Take the pressing-stones, O hero of good deeds, with your hands; hither have the sacred gods come to your sacrifice. Three boons — whichever you choose — those prosperities I shall fulfil for you here.
Settle, you who are sacred, upon the press-board and the druvā ladle; scatter the husks away. May we surpass all those equal to us in prosperity, and may we bring our enemies underfoot.
This is your thought, this is your birthplace; may Aditi, mother of heroes, receive you. Purify and drive away those who are hostile to this one; bestow upon him riches replete with all heroes.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
O woman, go apart; come back quickly — the cow-pen of the waters has mounted over you for the purpose of bearing. Among these waters, let whichever is most sacred take hold; having distributed, let the more resolute one leap forward.
These women have come adorning themselves; arise, O woman, seize strength eagerly. The sacrifice has come to you as a good consort, fruitful with offspring for your husband — grasp the pot.
The share of strength that was deposited for you aforetime — bring hither these waters enjoined by the seers. May this sacrifice, knowing your need, knowing the path, knowing offspring, be fierce, rich in cattle, knowing heroes, for you.
O Agni, the sacred oblation-pot has mounted over you, the pure and most ardent; with fervor, scorch it. Let the seer-born and god-born ones assemble together, and let the most ardent heat this portion with the ritual seasons.
These pure, female, sacred waters — let these bright waters glide like an oblation-pot. Bestowing upon me offspring and many cattle, let him who cooked the rice-oblation go to the world of the well-doers.
These rice-grains, sacred, purified by brahman and cleansed with ghee, are the portions of Soma. Let it enter the waters; let the oblation-pot receive you; having cooked this, let him go to the world of the well-doers.
Turn back hither together with offspring; face him and unite him with the gods. Carry him jointly to the heavenly world — O divine Āditya, to the highest firmament.
Spread wide with great greatness, O thousand-ridged one, in the world of the well-doer. O grandfathers, O fathers, O progenitor of offspring — having cooked, I am your fifteenth.
The brahma-odana — thousand-backed, hundred-streamed, imperishable — is the celestial path to the gods. I assign these beings to you with offspring; harass him not — let him be gratified as the bearer of tribute; be gracious to me alone.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Rise up, O vedi; augment him with offspring; drive away the rakṣas; set him ever forward on the path. May we surpass in glory all who are our equals; may we make those who hate us fall beneath our feet.
This altar, fashioned by cosmic order, established by the mind, is set before the brahma-odana. O woman, place upon it the pure portioning-ladle; settle there the odana belonging to the gods.
This second ladle, born of Aditi's hand, which the seven seers — the makers of what has come into being — fashioned: may it, the ritual spoon that knows the limbs of the odana, gather him upon the altar.
May the divine beings take their seat beside you, O cooked oblation; gliding forth, O Agni, settle upon him once more; purified by Soma, abide in the belly. May those descended from the seers among the brāhmaṇas who partake of you suffer no harm.
O King Soma, bestow full recognition upon those noble brāhmaṇas, whoever they be, that sit in attendance upon you. The seers and their descendants born from fervent austerity — I invoke them again and again with good invocation into the brahma-odana.
These honey-sweet, ghee-dripping waters I separately settle in the hands of the brāhmaṇas. With whatever wish I sprinkle you, may Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, have granted that very thing to me.
This is my light, immortal and golden; cooked from the field, she is a wish-yielding cow for me. This wealth I deposit among the brāhmaṇas; I open the path among the ancestors that leads to heaven.
Scatter the husks into Agni Jātavedas; beyond them, be gracious to these kuṭaja worms. This share, we have heard, belongs to the lord of the house; and we know the portion that belongs to Nirṛti.
Be cooked, O toiling one; arise, O pressing one; cause him to ascend the heavenly realm, that by which he may attain the highest, whatever vitality he has.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
O adhvaryu, anoint this face of the brown one; knowing it, make way for the ghee; anoint all its limbs with ghee. I open the path among the ancestors that leads to heaven.
O brown one, scatter the demon of equal fury away from those brāhmaṇas, whoever sit in attendance upon you. Those who are first and foremost, filled with sacredness — may those descended from the seers who partake of you suffer no harm.
I place you, O odana, among those descended from the seers; here too there is a place for those not of diverse ṛṣi lineage. May Agni be my protector, and all the Maruts, and all the Viśve Devās guard what has been cooked.
Ever yielding the sacrifice, always well-nourished, a virile cow, a seat of riches — may we be seated near you for immortality through offspring, for long life, and for the abundance of wealth.
You are a bull, O heaven; go to the seers and their descendants. Settle in the world of those who have done good deeds — that is our compact.
Heap it together, follow along behind, O Agni; make ready the paths that lead to the gods. By means of these good deeds may we come to know him who stands at the sacrifice, on the vault of heaven, upon the seven rays.
By that light with which the gods ascended the sky — having cooked the brahma-odana, the world of the well-doer — that very light, the highest of lights, I cook you; grant us that light in the world of those who have done well.
Toward the eastern quarter I scatter you, hundred-streamed, free from hunger. Carry the one who has cooked you to the world of the well-doers, where the primordially born seers of old dwell.
Toward the southern quarter — [as above].
Toward the western quarter — [as above].
Toward the northern quarter — [as above].
Toward the fixed quarter — [as above].
Toward the upward quarter — [as above].

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
To heaven — [as above].
To the atmosphere — [as above].
To the earth — [as above].
To the cattle — [as above].
From all the divine beings I pour thee out, a hundredfold stream, unstinted. May it carry the cooker to the world of the well-doers, where the ancient seers, the first-born, abide.
As a male stand firm upon the hide of a male; let Jātavedas not scorch thy generative member. May thy virile power abide even among the Apsarases.
Great are Heaven and Earth; great is this mid-air. Great in greatness is the all-limbed odana — that one who cooks thee.
Seven suns surround him, and seven lotus-pools likewise; seven thousand Gandharvas — him who cooks thee, O all-limbed odana.
Dhātṛ was their udgātṛ; the gods were the hotṛ-priests, the officiants. Where they first assembled the all-limbed odana with truth.
The seven seers, the seers who are creators of beings, and those who are the Sādhyas — they verily first assembled the all-limbed odana with faith.
For him who cooks the all-limbed one and does not harm the Brāhmaṇa, King Yama guards a world full of light.
That all-limbed one, ghee-backed, of luminous measure, assembled by the gods — lay it down yonder as a treasure; may Brahman guard it for thee.
Of that odana the belly is the mid-air; heaven is its back; the directions are its flanks; the sun and moon are its two eyes; the seasons are its teeth; Pavamāna is its breath; the Aṅgirases are its form.
Lead this one hither, take hold of him; knowing fully, let him reach the world of the well-doers. Having crossed the darknesses and seeing manifoldly, may the unborn one step up to the third vault of heaven.
Wash clean the feet; whatever ill-conduct he has performed — with pure hooves let him step forward, knowing fully. Seeking the luminous world of the well-doers, stride out upon the third firmament.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Following along, O viśastar, sever this dark skin with a knife joint by joint — do not think too highly of thyself. Do not harm him by roughness; make him fit; set him down in the midst of the well-doers.
Set this earth upon the earth; pour water upon it; lay him down. O slaughterers, wrap him round with fire. Boiled, let him go to where the world of the well-doers lies.
Step up out of this, whether unheated or heated, from the cauldron to the third vault of heaven. Thou hast become fire upon fire; go luminous to where the world of the well-doers lies.
O five-part odana, stride out fivefold, about to be stepped upon — five lights. Go into the midst of the sacrificing well-doers; win for him the luminous world.
The unborn one is indeed fire, they say; the unborn one is indeed light. The unborn one should be given to the Brāhmaṇa without being vanquished, they say. The unborn one drives away the darknesses far; given in this world by one possessed of faith.
This is your third light, O Fathers — he gives the five-part unborn one to the Brāhmaṇa. The unborn one drives away the darknesses far; the five-part odana being given to the Brāhmaṇa.
The five-part odana being given to the Brāhmaṇa — may the unborn one step up to the third firmament. Striding through the world of the well-doer, it drives away darkness far with its light.
Stride, O unborn one, to where the world of the well-doers lies; like the śarabha beast, chased forth, it shall lead him beyond the difficult passages. The five-part odana being given to the Brāhmaṇa — thou art the one of all forms, the wish-milking cow.
Desiring the luminous world of the well-doers, he gives the goat of fivefold rice-dish to the brahmin. Spread yourself, win that world for him; be gracious to us, and become the accepted offering.
The goat bears the giver to the triple firmament, to the triple heaven, to the triple back of the sky, to the world of the well-doers. The five-rice-dish goat, being given to the brahmin, satisfies the giver with satiety.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
For the goat was born from the flame of Agni—the wise one, life-sustaining, born of the might of the wise. That which is offered, sacrificed, fulfilled, and consecrated with vaṣaṭ—may the gods arrange that in due season.
He should place an unwoven garment and gold as the sacrificial fee; thus he shall attain fully all the worlds, both those celestial and those earthly.
O goat, may these streams approach you from all sides—divine, belonging to Soma, their backs of ghee, dripping honey. Propping up the earth, accompany heaven; stand upon the vault of heaven, upon the seven-rayed one.
"From the back of the earth"—thus the four [verses are recited].
[Verse lost in transmission — text not preserved in this manuscript.]
[Verse lost in transmission — text not preserved in this manuscript.]
[Verse lost in transmission — text not preserved in this manuscript.]
Lift this five-rice dish with five fingers from the ladle, this fivefold rice offering. Stride out toward the eastern quarter, the southern, the western, the northern, the fixed, and the upward direction.
Place the goat's head in the eastern quarter; place the right flank in the southern quarter. Place its hindquarters in the western quarter; place the left flank in the northern quarter.
Place the goat's spine in the upward direction; place the chest in the fixed direction. Place its middle in the midst of the atmosphere; stand firm in the quarters with its four feet.
Cover the cooked goat with the cooked skin; it is assembled of all limbs, of universal form. Rise up, proceed to the highest vault of heaven; stand firm in the quarters with its four feet.
May all the quarters, unanimous and confluent, together with the intermediate regions, accept the radiance. May they protect this offering of yours, for you; unto them I offer with oblation and with ghee.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
What was deposited for the brahmin, and what was deposited among the people, whatever drops of the goat's rice-dish—may all that, O Agni, be known in the world of the well-doer; may the paths lead to our coming together.
The five-rice-dish goat strode forth extensively. This earth became its lap, the atmosphere its belly, the sky its back, and the directions its flanks.
Diti and Aditi are its two horns; Truth and Order are its two eyes; the universal form is its body; Faith is its breath; Virāj is its head.
This sacrifice is indeed boundless—namely, the five-rice-dish goat. He wins a boundless world, he obtains a boundless world, who gives the five-rice-dish goat to one who knows thus.
One should not break its bones, nor should one draw out the marrow. Having gathered all of them together, one should insert this and this [piece by piece back into the whole].
This and this is its form; by that one causes it to come together. It yields to him svadhā, vigor, inexhaustibility, and greatness—to one who gives the five-rice-dish goat to one who knows thus.
May Savitṛ make the share for Indra; may the lord of sacrifice, the generous patron, prosper this sacrifice. Pursue those who hate us; may all the heroes of the sacrificer be unharmed.
Five are the worlds, five are the seasons. He prospers in all five seasons who gives the five-rice-dish goat to one who knows thus.
This sacrifice is indeed the scorching fire—namely, the five-rice-dish goat. It burns away the hostile rival; by his own self he becomes one whose hostile rival has been driven off [from him].
Whoever knows the season as "the approaching one"—he takes away the approaching prosperity of the hostile rival; by his own self he becomes one [who has prevailed].
[He who knows the season called] "the converging one" — he takes away even the converging [prosperity of his rival — remainder not preserved in this manuscript].

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
[He who knows the season called] "the becoming one" — he takes away even the becoming [prosperity of his rival — remainder not preserved in this manuscript].
[He who knows the season called] "the overpowering one" — he takes away even the overpowering [prosperity of his rival — remainder not preserved in this manuscript].
[He who knows the season called] "the rising one" — he takes away even the rising [prosperity of his rival — remainder not preserved in this manuscript].
[He who knows the season called] "the summit" — he takes away even the summit [prosperity of his rival — remainder not preserved in this manuscript].
Whoever knows the season as "the all"—he takes away all the prosperity of the hostile rival; by his own self he becomes one whose hostile rival has been driven off from him—he who gives the five-rice-dish goat to one who knows thus.
As many as are the hairs of it that the brahmin strews upon the altar—so many are the inexhaustible streams that flow for him, as from the ocean.
May it yield milk; may there be ghee for these; having become spirituous liquor, may it attend upon the drinkers of surā. Yielding streams of mead for the drinkers of mead, may the goat stand rejoicing upon the vault of heaven.
By the Skambha are these two propped and held apart — heaven and earth stand firm. In the Skambha all this is established: whatever stirs, whatever breathes and blinks.
Single-wheeled it revolves, single-rimmed, with a thousand syllables — forward it moves and backward. With half of itself it has encompassed all this universe; as for the other half, what is that emblem?
A five-coursed team draws its van; the flanks, yoked, haul in sequence. Its yet-untraveled course cannot be seen, nor its traveled one — what is far is nearer, what is near is more remote.
Know this, O Savitṛ: six paired ones and one that is born singly. In him do they seek communion — he who among them is born as one.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
A cup whose opening faces sideways and whose base is upward — in it is laid the glory of all forms. Here together sat the seven seers who became the guardians of this great one.
Three creatures passed across the crossing; others poured inward around the sun. The great one stood as measurer of the atmosphere; into the tawny mares the golden one entered.
Twelve fellies, one wheel, three hubs — who has perceived this? In it are fixed three hundred and sixty pegs and sixty more — immovable they stand.
Infinite and spread across many places — the infinite and the finite meet face to face. The guardian of the vault of heaven moves knowing both: he who is wise knows what has come to be and what shall yet come to be.
Manifest yet concealed in the cave — ancient is the name, great is the station. In that is all this established: whatever stirs, whatever breathes and blinks.
Bearing water upward, as if a water-vessel fit to be carried — all behold it with the eye; not all know it with the mind.
From the deficient the full arises; from the full the deficient is drawn forth. The seer, the brahman, knows from whence it is poured around.
Prajāpati moves within the womb, unseen; in manifold ways he is born. With half of himself he engendered the whole world of beings — as for the other half, what did that bring forth?
What stirs and moves and what stands still — the breathless breathing, the blinking yet at rest — that of all forms has sustained the earth; coming together, it becomes one alone.
She who is yoked in front and likewise behind, she who is yoked on all sides and in every direction — she by whom the sacrifice is stretched forth toward the east: of her I ask you — which of these strands is she?
Whence the sun rises and where it sets — that alone I hold to be the highest; from that nothing whatsoever goes beyond.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
By truth it blazes upward; by brahman it looks downward; by breath it breathes laterally — upon this the highest is established.
He who would know those two fire-sticks from which wealth is churned forth — that knowing one would esteem the highest; he would know the great brahman.
Footless at first it came into being; at first it brought the sun forth. Having become four-footed and worthy of enjoyment, it took all nourishment.
It became worthy of enjoyment and thereafter consumed abundant food — he who worships the eternal god possessed of exaltation.
They call him eternal, yet today he shines again as new. Day and night are born in turn, each taking the form of the other.
A hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a billion — the incalculable treasure lodged within this: they smite it only while they look on it. Therefore the god shines; it is he.
No more than the tip of an awl has it been seen — and yet it is not seen at all. More embracing than all that is this deity; she is my beloved.
This auspicious one, unaging and immortal, dwells in the house of the mortal. He for whom she was made lies with her; he who fashioned her has reached that goal.
You are woman, you are man; you are the maiden and the boy. You, grown old, totter with a staff; you, once born, become the one whose face is everywhere.
And this one is the eldest, and likewise the youngest; this one is the brother and also the father. The one god who has entered the mind — first-born is he, yet even now he is within the womb.
Without stirring he sets all this in motion; all beings are borne around within him who bears all. That male, engendering from the male by cosmic law — standing firm, let him reach all ends.
Set in the midst of heaven, the speckled stone — and these two striding ones cleave the atmosphere asunder. He surveys all with his powers, between the eastern and the western light.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Those who speak on all sides of the knower of the Veda — whether of recent times or of ancient — all of them are speaking of Āditya alone, of Agni the second, and the triple-woven haṃsa.
A single ṛc they kindle with twelve fires. In it the waters are established, in it the cattle, in it the plants take refuge.
Seven fair-winged ones blow upon the arrow, this wind gathered in the anuṣṭubh. Let the mind purify that stretched-out thread, stretched and spread upon the surface of the water.
Seven seers are set within the body; seven guard it always without fail. Seven waters went to the world of one who sleeps — there the two gods who do not sleep, who arose from wakefulness, sat together at the sattra.
O Bhava and Śarva, show us grace; come not against us — you, Lords of Beings, Lords of Cattle, homage to you both. What has been aimed, let it turn back; release it not upon us; harm not our two-footed ones nor our four-footed ones.
Do not make our bodies a portion for the howling jackal, for the vultures, nor for those dark carrion-birds that are unfeathered. O Paśupati, the flies, the birds — let them be thine for the feast; let them not find us as their prey.
To thy cry, to thy breath, and to thy festering wounds, O Bhava — homage we render to thee, O Rudra, O thousand-eyed Immortal.
From the east we make homage to thee, from the north, from below as well; from the surrounding quarters, from across the sky — to thee, O Antarikṣa, homage.
To thy face, O Paśupati; to thy eyes, O Bhava; to thy skin, to thy form, to thine aspect, to thy western-turned presence — homage to thee.
To thy limbs, to thy belly, to thy tongue and to thy mouth, to thy teeth, to thy scent — homage to thee.
With Rudra of the blue crest-plume, the thousand-eyed, the vigorous, the slayer of wayfarers — with that one let us not come into collision.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
May Bhava encompass us on all sides; as fire encompasses water, so may Bhava encompass us. Let him not take aim at us — homage be to him.
Four times homage, eight times homage to Bhava; ten times, O Paśupati, homage to thee. Thine are these five categories of cattle apportioned: kine, horses, men, and then goats and sheep.
Thine are the four cardinal directions; thine is the sky; thine, O Fierce One, is this vast mid-air. Thine is all this that possesses breath, all that stirs upon the earth.
Wide is this treasury that bears wealth — thine it is — within which all these beings are contained. He, O Paśupati — show us grace, homage to thee. Let the howling jackals and the menacing dogs go far away; let the ill-voiced, dishevelled ones depart afar.
Thou bearest the tawny golden bow, O Crested One, slayer of thousands, smiter of hundreds. Rudra's arrow courses forth — the divine missile; to that one homage, in whichever direction it travels.
He who comes against thee, O Fierce One, who lies in wait desiring to injure thee — thou dost dispatch thine arrow after him from behind, as one tracking the footprints of the wounded.
Bhava and Rudra, yoked together and in accord, both fierce, move forth for the exercise of might. Between them are the earth, the mid-air, the sun, the sky — to those two we render homage with all that belongs to Bhava.
Homage to thee as thou comest; homage to thee as thou departest. Homage to thee, O Rudra, as thou standest still; and homage to thee as thou art seated.
Homage at evening, homage at dawn, homage by night, homage by day — to Bhava and to Śarva, to both of them together I have rendered homage.
I behold in front the thousand-eyed Rudra, shooting his shafts in many ways, the all-knowing. May I not cease from praising him who makes himself known through speech.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Him of dark bay horses, the black, the very dark, who crushes down, terrible, driving his dread chariot, the long-haired one — we meet him from the front; homage be to him.
Cast not down upon us the mortal divine missile; be not wrathful against us, O Paśupati — homage to thee. Elsewhere than toward us shake thy heavenly branch.
Harm us not; speak favorably over us; wrap us in thy protection; be not angry. Let us not come to collision with thee.
Covet not our horses, our kine, our men; covet not our goats and sheep, O Fierce One. Turn away elsewhere; slay the offspring of the revilers.
Whose weapon is the fever, the cough — his one missile — which goes roaring like the snorting of a stallion; he drives it out, from the front, successively — homage be to him.
He who stands firmly established in the mid-air, crushing down the non-sacrificers, the scorners of the gods — to him homage with ten Śakvarī verses.
To thee belong the forest animals, the wild beasts set in the woodland; to thee belong the birds and winged fowl. Thine, O Paśupati, is the wasting-disease hidden in the waters; to thee the heavenly waters flow for thy increase.
The Śiṃśumāras, the pythons, the Pulīkas, the crocodiles and fishes — upon all these thou dost shoot in the mist. Nothing is far from thee, nothing beyond thy reach, O Bhava; thou beholdest all the earth at once.
Thou strikest from the eastern ocean into the northern sea. Harm us not, O Rudra, with fever nor with poison; pour not down upon us the heavenly fire — let lightning strike elsewhere than upon us.
Bhava is lord of the sky; Bhava is lord of the earth; Bhava has filled the vast mid-air. Let no ill-omen whatsoever reach here to harm him.
O King Bhava, show grace to the sacrificer — for thou hast become the Lord of Cattle among cattle. He who has faith that the gods exist — show grace upon his four-footed and his two-footed ones.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Harm not our great one, nor our little one; harm not our waning one, nor our unwasted one. Injure not our father, nor our mother; O Rudra, wound not thine own body — harm us not.
To the dogs of Rudra that utter the sound ailabaka, whose voice is not well-spoken, to these wide-mouthed ones I have rendered homage.
Homage to you, the clamorous ones; homage to you, the long-haired ones. Homage to you, the restrained ones; homage to you, the ones full of reverence.
Homage to you at your coming-to-birth, and homage to you when born. To your tender parts, to your hooves, to your form, O inviolable cow — homage to you.
He who knows the seven near reaches, who knows the seven far reaches, he who knows the head of the sacrifice — he shall receive the cow as his due.
I know the seven near reaches, I know the seven far reaches; I know the head of the sacrifice, and the discerning Soma that dwells within her.
By her are heaven and earth sustained, by her these waters are guarded — the cow of a thousand streams, her we address with sacred formulas.
A hundred calves, a hundred milkers, a hundred guardians upon her back — the gods who breathe within her, they know the cow as the one undivided whole.
She whose footstep is the sacrifice, whose eye is the oblation, whose breath is the ancestral offering, the great and luminous one — the cow, Parjanya's wife, approaches the gods through sacred formulas.
Agni entered into you, Soma followed you, O cow. Parjanya is your udder, O auspicious one, the lightnings are your teats, O cow.
You milk the waters first, then the arable land, O cow; thirdly you milk sovereignty — food and milk you give, O cow.
When, being invoked by the Ādityas, you stood present, O guardian of truth, Indra made you drink Soma in a thousand vessels, O cow.
When, turning away from Indra, the bull called out to you — then the slayer of Vṛtra, enraged, brought you milk and cream, O cow.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
That milk which the lord of wealth, though enraged, brought to you, O cow — that very milk the vault of heaven today protects in three vessels.
In three vessels the divine cow brought that Soma — where Atharvan, consecrated, sat upon the golden sacrificial grass.
She came together with Soma and with all that moves on feet; the cow danced before the ocean, bearing the Ṛc and Sāman hymns.
She came together with the Sun and with all that has sight; the cow strode beyond the ocean together with the Gandharvas and the Kalis.
She came together with the Wind and with all winged creatures; the auspicious cow surveyed beyond the ocean, bearing the celestial lights.
Then the auspicious things came together — the cow as guide, and also the ancestral oblation — where Atharvan, consecrated, sat upon the golden sacrificial grass.
When you stood there, covered with gold, O guardian of truth, the ocean, having become a horse, leaped upon you, O cow.
The cow is the mother of the royal caste, the cow is your mother, O ancestral libation. From the cow was born the weapon, and from that arose thought.
The upward drop moved aloft, from the hump of brahman — from that you were born, O cow; from that the Hotṛ priest was born.
Let the sacred songs be born from your mouth; your strength comes from the Uṣṇih metres. From your girth the sacrifice was born, from your teats the rays of light, O cow.
From your shoulder-joints and your haunches, O cow, the path was born; from your entrails the food was produced, from your belly the plants sprang up.
When you entered into Varuṇa's belly, O cow, then the sacred formulation called you out — for he it was who found your eye.
All trembled at her birth, at the one being born from the womb — for she has given birth; they call her the cow, fashioned by sacred formulas, and she is a kinswoman to all.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The one who alone is the master of her joins together in battle; the swift-moving sacrifices came into being, the cow became the eye of the swift-moving ones.
The cow took hold of the Sun, the cow sustained the sacrifice; into the cow there entered the odana rice-cooked oblation along with sacred formulas.
The cow alone they call immortality; the cow they worship as death. All this became the cow — gods, humans, Asuras, the ancestors, and the seers.
He who knows thus shall receive the cow as his due — for in this way the sacrifice, complete on all feet, yields milk to the giver without withholding.
Three tongues of Varuṇa flash within the mouth; among them the one that shines in the middle — she is the cow, hard to receive.
The seed of the cow became fourfold: one quarter is the waters, one quarter immortality, one quarter the sacrifice, one quarter the animals. He who knows thus shall receive the cow as his due.
The cow is heaven, the cow is earth, the cow is Viṣṇu and Prajāpati. The Sādhyas and the Vasus drank the milk drawn from the cow.
Having drunk the milk of the barren cow, the Sādhyas and the Vasus — those who dwell upon the seat of Bradhna revere the milk of this one.
Some milk Soma from her, others attend upon her for clarified butter. Those who have given the barren cow to one who knows thus — they have gone to the triple heaven, to the sky.
By giving the barren cow to Brāhmaṇas one attains all the worlds; for truth is placed within her, as also brahman and austerity.
The gods live by the barren cow, and likewise human beings. All this that the sun surveys has come to be through the barren cow.
The joints [of the sacrificial animal] are whose kindling-materials; the Ṛc verses are whose recitation.
The metres are whose hairs; the spreading-layer indeed is the oblation; the Yajus is declared to be whose heart.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
When the host beholds his guests, he is beholding the divine sacrificial ground.
When he greets them, he enters consecration; when he asks for water and leads forward the waters — those very waters that are led forward at sacrifices, those are they.
When they bring the refreshing offering, that is indeed the beast sacred to Agni and Soma that is bound.
When they bring the excavated [vessel], those two are the rice-cakes; when they arrange the guest-halls, they are thereby arranging the sacrificial hall and the oblation-sheds.
When they spread the underlayer, that is the sacred grass indeed.
When they bring the mats and cushions, those are the enclosing sticks; when they bring the upper coverlet, by that one obtains the heavenly world.
When they bring the anointing substance, that is the clarified butter indeed; when they invoke [the guests] for eating, they are thereby invoking for the prepared oblation; when rice-grains and barley-grains are strewn, those stalks are what are strewn.
The mortar, the pestle, the pressing-stones, the winnowing fan, the strainer, the husks, the Soma-residue; the sacrificial ladle, the wooden spoon, the stirring-rod, the mixing-vessel, the waters, the pressing-board, the trough-jar, the water-pot —
This very black antelope skin, the vessels consecrated to Vāyu — the host makes of these the sacrificer or the Brāhmaṇa, when he looks upon the things that are to be carried [for the guests], saying: 'May this be more, may this [be enough].'
When he says 'Bring up more,' by that he increases progeny and cattle; by that he makes breath the greater. When he inquires [after the guests' desires], by that he obtains desire itself — for one who is asked out of regard does request what he desires.
When he sprinkles water, by that he obtains the waters themselves; when he presents [gifts], he establishes the oblations.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
When they are seated, the guest pours the oblation into himself — with the act of the ladle, with the vaṣaṭ-call, with the sacrificial spoon [that is] the hand, into the breath [that is] the sacrificial post.
Therefore one should not eat while harbouring hatred, nor should one eat the food of one who harbours hatred; nor the food of one who is under suspicion, nor of one who is being questioned with suspicion.
He whose food others eat is one whose sin has been consumed — he is wholly freed of evil.
He whose food others do not eat is one whose sin has not been consumed — he is wholly burdened with evil.
Those who present the offering follow in the stride of Prajāpati's own great stride.
The sacrifice spread forth by him who presents the offering is indeed the sacrifice belonging to Prajāpati.
He who presents the offering is at all times one for whom the soma has been pressed, the pressing-stones are yoked, the strainer is moist, the rite of the sacrifice has been performed, and the adhvara has been spread.
He who is for the guests is the āhavanīya fire; he who is the preparer of food is the dakṣiṇāgni; he who abides in the household is the gārhapatya.
He who eats before the guest eats up both the iṣṭa — the fruit of sacrificial rites — and the pūrta — the fruit of works of public merit.
He likewise eats away his progeny and his cattle — [he who eats before the guest].
He who eats before the guest eats away the vigour and the milk-wealth of the households.
He who is a learned Vedic scholar — he indeed is the true atithi, the guest.
Therefore one should not eat first; one should eat only after he has eaten — that is the vow, the sacred rule.
For the unbroken continuity of the sacrifice, for the protection of the sacrifice, for the sacrifice's identification with the self.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
When one presents the offering with milk poured over it, one thereby obtains as much merit as is obtained by sacrificing with a fully performed Agniṣṭoma — so much does one secure through this.
When one presents the offering with clarified butter poured over it, one thereby obtains as much as is obtained by a fully performed sāhna sacrifice — [so much does one secure through this].
When one presents the offering with honey poured over it, one thereby obtains as much as is obtained by a fully performed atirātra sacrifice — [so much does one secure through this].
When one presents the offering with meat poured over it, one thereby obtains as much merit as is obtained by sacrificing with a fully performed dvādaśāhna — so much does one secure through this.
When one presents the offering with water poured over it, it is for the procreation of progeny; he lives long, he attains the full span of life, and he does not die before old age — he who knows thus.
For him, Vāta and Uṣas intone the hiṅkāra; Savitṛ extols him with prosperity as the prastāva; Bṛhaspati chants the udgītha with vigour; Tvaṣṭṛ performs the pratihāra with nourishment; the Viśve Devāḥ perform the nidhana. The nidhana becomes one of prosperity, of progeny, and of cattle — for him who knows thus.
For him, the rising sun intones the hiṅkāra; the forenoon performs the prastāva; the midday chants the udgītha; the afternoon performs the pratihāra; the setting sun performs the nidhana — [and the nidhana becomes one of prosperity, of progeny, and of cattle, for him who knows thus].
For him, the forming cloud intones the hiṅkāra; the lightning flashing forth performs the prastāva; the thundering chants the udgītha; the raining performs the pratihāra; the clearing performs the nidhana — [and the nidhana becomes one of prosperity, of progeny, and of cattle, for him who knows thus].

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
He looks towards the guests — that is the hiṅkāra; he addresses them with welcome — that is the prastāva; he requests water — that is the udgītha; he brings the offering forward — that is the pratihāra; he performs the nidhana with the remnant. The nidhana becomes one of prosperity, of progeny, and of cattle — for him who knows thus.
These indeed — both the beloved and the unloved — are the officiating priests who lead one to the heavenly world, namely the guests (atithis).
