When he summons the doorkeeper and causes him to be called, and when he responds and causes the response to be heard in return.
When the servers enter the lodging-places, they are in truth the cup-bearing adhvaryus for those guests — not a single one of them is without the function of an hotṛ.
What one brings forth in the morning — that is verily the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana).
What one brings forth at midday — that is verily the midday pressing (mādhyaṃdina savana).
What one brings forth in the evening — that is verily the third pressing (tṛtīya savana).
When the lord of the guests, having served the guests all round, asks leave of his seat — he thereby approaches the avabhṛtha (the concluding ablution of the sacrifice).
What he distributes in common — thereby he distributes the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); and what he follows through to completion — thereby he indeed performs the udavasāna (final rite of dismissal).
He, being invoked, feasts upon the earth; invoked, he feasts upon whatever all-form (viśvarūpa) exists in the earth. He blazes within the earth, he shines forth upon the earth. He becomes the heavenly world — he who knows thus.
He, being invoked, feasts upon the atmosphere; invoked, he feasts upon whatever all-form exists in the atmosphere. He blazes within the atmosphere, he shines forth upon the atmosphere. [He becomes the heavenly world — he who knows thus.]

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
He, being invoked, feasts upon the sky; invoked, he feasts upon whatever all-form exists in the sky. He blazes within the sky, he shines forth upon the sky. [He becomes the heavenly world — he who knows thus.]
He, being invoked, feasts among the gods; invoked, he feasts upon whatever all-form exists among the gods. He blazes among the gods, he shines forth among the gods. [He becomes the heavenly world — he who knows thus.]
He, being invoked, feasts among the worlds; invoked, he feasts upon whatever all-form exists in the worlds. He blazes among the worlds, he shines forth among the worlds. He becomes the heavenly world — he who knows thus.
When, seated facing east, one scatters the grain — thereby one cuts off a portion for the sacrifice and for the gods.
When, seated facing south, one scatters the grain — thereby one cuts off a portion for Yama and for the ancestors (pitṛs).
When, seated facing west, one scatters the grain — thereby one cuts off a portion for Varuṇa, the one who dwells in the waters (apsuṣad).
When, seated facing north, one scatters the grain — thereby one cuts off a portion for Soma the king and for the Seven Seers (saptarṣis).
When, seated with the lap formed, one scatters the grain — thereby one cuts off a portion for Vāyu and for the atmosphere (antarikṣa).
When, standing upright, one scatters the grain — thereby one cuts off a portion for the sky (dyu) and for Āditya.
Whomsoever one desires to make inferior in self, in progeny, in livestock, in household, and in wealth — for him one should perform this oblation, and having performed it thus, one should follow it with this same oblation. Thereupon he indeed becomes inferior in self, in livestock, in household, and in wealth. This one should do: that is the expiation-rite.
Whomsoever one desires to make neither wealthier nor better in self, in progeny, in livestock, in household, and in wealth — for him one should perform this oblation, and having performed it thus, one should follow it with this same oblation. Thereupon he indeed becomes neither wealthier nor better in self, in progeny, in livestock, in household, and in wealth. This one should do: that is the expiation-rite.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Whomsoever one desires to make wealthier and better in self, in progeny, in livestock, in household, and in wealth — for him one should perform this oblation, and having performed it thus, one should follow it with this same oblation. Thereupon he indeed becomes wealthier and better in self, in progeny, in livestock, in household, and in wealth. This one should do: that is the expiation-rite.
When, as the grain is being husked, a rice-grain leaps out — the best kinsman of the same flesh becomes subject to death.
When the cooking-pot is not properly mounted, one performs a rite belonging to the Fathers.
When it drips and overflows — the milk of the household and of the livestock drips away.
When one pours it off prematurely — the milk of the household and of the livestock is poured away.
When the stirring-stick crumbles — the householder dies.
When the ladle crumbles — the mistress of the house dies.
When the pot cracks open — total loss ensues: both the giver and the receiver suffer defeat.
When one stirs it upward toward the east — it is cut off for the sacrifice and for the gods.
When one stirs it upward toward the south — it is cut off for Yama and for the Fathers.
When one stirs it upward toward the west — it is cut off for Varuṇa, the one who dwells in the waters.
When one stirs it upward toward the north — it is cut off for Soma the king and for the Seven Seers.
When one lifts it out with a circular motion — fear comes to him from every direction.
When one strews the barhis eastward, it is cut off for the sacrifice and for the gods.
When one strews the barhis southward, it is cut off for Yama and for the Pitṛs.
When one strews the barhis westward, one does what has never been done before.
When one strews the barhis northward, it is cut off for King Soma and for the Seven Sages.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
When one fashions the handle of the vessel in front, hemorrhoids arise in the mouth of the recipient.
When one fashions the handle of the vessel on the south side, it is cut off for Yama and for the Pitṛs.
When one fashions the handle of the vessel behind, a westward-flying arrow strikes the recipient.
When one fashions the handle of the vessel on the north side, it is cut off for King Soma and for the Seven Sages.
When it is bright, it attains the dear abode of the Ādityas. He who would eat of the bright one should eat it saying: 'I eat thee with the dear abode of the Ādityas.' Thereupon he eats it with another abode; and it is cut off for the Ādityas.
When it is husked, it is the dear (abode) of the Viśve Devās. He who would eat of the husked one should (eat it saying): 'I eat thee with the dear abode of all the gods'; (he eats it thus). It is cut off for the Viśve Devās.
When it is unhusked, it is the dear (abode) of the Maruts. He who would eat of the unhusked one should (eat it saying): 'I eat thee with the dear (abode) of the Maruts'; (he eats it thus). It is cut off for the Maruts.
When it is shrunken, it is (the dear abode) of Agni alone. He who would eat of the shrunken one should (eat it saying): 'I eat thee with the dear (abode) of Agni'; (he eats it thus). It is cut off for Agni.
When it is unshrunken, it is (the dear abode) of Mitra and Varuṇa. He who would eat of the unshrunken one should (eat it saying): 'I eat thee with the dear (abode) of Mitra and Varuṇa'; (he eats it thus). It is cut off for Mitra and Varuṇa.
When it is dry, it is (the dear abode) of Indra alone. He who would eat of the dry one should (eat it saying): 'I eat thee (with the dear abode) of Indra'; (he eats it thus). It is cut off for Indra.
When it is moist, it is (the dear abode) of the Pitṛs alone. He who would eat of the moist one should (eat it saying): 'I eat thee (with the dear abode) of the Pitṛs'; (he eats it thus). It is cut off for the Pitṛs.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
When it is small, it is (the dear abode) of the Waters alone. He who would eat of the small one should (eat it saying): 'I eat thee with the dear (abode) of the waters'; (he eats it thus). It is cut off for the Waters.
When it is loose, it is (the dear abode) of the Directions alone. He who would eat of the loose one should (eat it saying): 'I eat thee (with the dear abode) of the Directions'; (he eats it thus). It is cut off for the Directions.
When it is a gulantī grain, it is (the dear abode) of Prajāpati alone. He who would eat of the gulantī grain should (eat it saying): 'I eat thee (with the dear abode) of Prajāpati'; (he eats it thus). It is cut off for Prajāpati.
When it is withered, it attains the dear abode of the Uppermost Sky. He who would eat of the withered one should eat it saying: 'I eat thee with the dear abode of the Uppermost Sky.' Thereupon he eats it with another abode; and it is cut off for the Uppermost Sky.
If, having poured milk over it, one eats first, the recipient becomes a kilāsa (one afflicted with a leprous skin disease).
If, having poured ghee over it, one eats first, a serpent slays the recipient.
If, having poured honey over it, one eats first, Mahādeva slays the recipient.
If, having added meat to it, one eats first, Īśāna slays the recipient.
If, having poured water over it, one eats first — that is prosperous. He lives long, reaches his full lifespan, and does not die before old age — he who knows thus.
If, while about to eat, one wipes the food from in front — the life-breath of the recipient goes forward; rising up from there it departs; his head aches. He does not live beyond twelve. And so an onlooker catches this person as he eats.
If, while about to eat, one wipes the food from the south — the recipient's [life-breath goes] to the right [southward — remainder as above, ellipsis in source].

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
If, while about to eat, one wipes the food from the north — the life-breath of the recipient goes northward; rising up from there it departs; his head aches. He does not live beyond twelve. And so an onlooker catches this person as he eats.
If, while about to eat, one wipes it from behind forward — one thereby touches it with shelter and with armor. Both shelter and armor come to be his. He conquers the rice-dish; he becomes one whose world is the rice-dish — he who knows thus.
Ye are Indra's vital force; ye are Indra's might; ye are Indra's strength; ye are Indra's heroic power; ye are Indra's brilliance; ye are Indra's virility. For victorious yoking I yoke you with the yokings of Indra. For victorious yoking, may all forms attend upon me. Yoked to me, ye Waters, stand here.
[As 16.127.1, with:] I yoke you with the yokings of kṣatra for victorious yoking [remainder as 16.127.1, ellipsis in source].
[As 16.127.1, with:] I yoke you with the yokings of brahman for victorious yoking [remainder as 16.127.1, ellipsis in source].
[As 16.127.1, with:] I yoke you with the yokings of food (anna) for victorious yoking [remainder as 16.127.1, ellipsis in source].
Ye are Indra's vital force; ye are Indra's might; ye are Indra's strength; ye are Indra's heroic power; ye are Indra's brilliance; ye are Indra's virility. For victorious yoking I yoke you with the yokings of the Waters. For victorious yoking, may all forms attend upon me. Yoked to me, ye Waters, stand here.
You are the share of Agni. O divine Waters, place in us the bright essence of the waters, the vital lustre. By the ordinance of Prajāpati I settle you here for this world.
You are the share of Indra. O divine Waters, place in us the bright essence of the waters, the vital lustre. By the ordinance of Prajāpati I settle you here for this world.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
You are the share of Soma. O divine Waters, place in us the bright essence of the waters, the vital lustre. By the ordinance of Prajāpati I settle you here for this world.
You are the share of Varuṇa. O divine Waters, place in us the bright essence of the waters, the vital lustre. By the ordinance of Prajāpati I settle you here for this world.
You are the share of Yama. O divine Waters, place in us the bright essence of the waters, the vital lustre. By the ordinance of Prajāpati I settle you here for this world.
You are the share of the Pitṛs. O divine Waters, place in us the bright essence of the waters, the vital lustre. By the ordinance of Prajāpati I settle you here for this world.
You are the share of Bṛhaspati. O divine Waters, place in us the bright essence of the waters, the vital lustre. By the ordinance of Prajāpati I settle you here for this world.
You are the share of Prajāpati. O divine Waters, place in us the bright essence of the waters, the vital lustre. By the ordinance of Prajāpati I settle you here for this world.
You are the share of the god Savitṛ. O divine Waters, place in us the bright essence of the waters, the vital lustre. By the ordinance of Prajāpati I settle you here for this world.
That which among you, O Waters, is the share of the waters — the sacrificial, deity-worshipping one dwelling within the waters — I release this beyond him; let it not strike me. With it I drive beyond him who hates us, whom we hate. May I smite him, may I overwhelm him, by this sacred formulation, by this rite, by this mental intent.
That which among you, O Waters, is the wave of the waters — the sacrificial, deity-worshipping one dwelling within the waters — I release this beyond him; let it not strike me. With it I drive beyond him who hates us, whom we hate. May I smite him, may I overwhelm him, by this sacred formulation, by this rite, by this mental intent.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
That which among you, O Waters, is the current of the waters — the sacrificial, deity-worshipping one dwelling within the waters — I release this beyond him; let it not strike me. With it I drive beyond him who hates us, whom we hate. May I smite him, may I overwhelm him, by this sacred formulation, by this rite, by this mental intent.
That which among you, O Waters, is the drop of the waters — the sacrificial, deity-worshipping one dwelling within the waters — I release this beyond him; let it not strike me. With it I drive beyond him who hates us, whom we hate. May I smite him, may I overwhelm him, by this sacred formulation, by this rite, by this mental intent.
That which among you, O Waters, is the embryo of the waters — the sacrificial, deity-worshipping one dwelling within the waters — I release this beyond him; let it not strike me. With it I drive beyond him who hates us, whom we hate. May I smite him, may I overwhelm him, by this sacred formulation, by this rite, by this mental intent.
That which among you, O Waters, is the calf of the waters — the sacrificial, deity-worshipping one dwelling within the waters — I release this beyond him; let it not strike me. With it I drive beyond him who hates us, whom we hate. May I smite him, may I overwhelm him, by this sacred formulation, by this rite, by this mental intent.
That which among you, O Waters, is the bull of the waters — the sacrificial, deity-worshipping one dwelling within the waters — I release this beyond him; let it not strike me. With it I drive beyond him who hates us, whom we hate. May I smite him, may I overwhelm him, by this sacred formulation, by this rite, by this mental intent.
That which among you, O Waters, is the speckled heavenly stone of the waters — the sacrificial, deity-worshipping one dwelling within the waters — I release this beyond him; let it not strike me. With it I drive beyond him who hates us, whom we hate. May I smite him, may I overwhelm him, by this sacred formulation, by this rite, by this mental intent.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
That which among you, O Waters, is Hiraṇyagarbha of the waters — the sacrificial, deity-worshipping one dwelling within the waters — I release this beyond him; let it not strike me. With it I drive beyond him who hates us, whom we hate. May I smite him, may I overwhelm him, by this sacred formulation, by this rite, by this mental intent.
Those which among you, O Waters, are the fires of the waters — the sacrificial, deity-worshipping ones dwelling within the waters — I release these beyond him; let them not strike me. With them I drive beyond him who hates us, whom we hate. May I smite him, may I overwhelm him with blazing force, by this sacred formulation, by this rite, by this mental intent.
Whatever untruth we have uttered since the past year up to the present — from that sin, from that transgression, may the Waters guard me on every side.
O stainless Waters, carry the stain away from us; of fair countenance, carry far from us sin, transgression, evil omen, and pollution.
I release you back to the ocean — return to your own source. Whole and unharmed for all our years, let nothing whatsoever afflict us.
You are the stride of Viṣṇu, slayer of rivals, whetted by the Earth, radiant with the fire of Agni. Along the Earth do I stride wide; from the Earth we expel him who hates us and whom we hate. The rivals born before — I press those very ones down; I stride beyond them — driven away and expelled is the rival.
You are the stride of Viṣṇu, slayer of rivals, whetted by the atmosphere, radiant with the wind of Vāyu. Along the atmosphere do I stride wide; from the atmosphere we expel him who hates us and whom we hate. The rivals born together — [I press those very ones down; I stride beyond them — driven away and expelled is the rival].
You are the stride of Viṣṇu, slayer of rivals, whetted by the sky, radiant with the light of Sūrya. Along the sky do I stride wide; from the sky we expel him who hates us and whom we hate. The rivals born after — [I press those very ones down; I stride beyond them — driven away and expelled is the rival].

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
[You are the stride of Viṣṇu,] slayer of rivals, whetted by the directions, radiant with the power of the wind. Along the directions do I stride wide; from the directions him — [we expel who hates us and whom we hate; I press the rivals down, I stride beyond them — driven away and expelled is the rival].
[You are the stride of Viṣṇu,] slayer of rivals, whetted by the horizons, radiant with the power of the mind. Along the horizons do I stride wide; from the horizons him — [we expel who hates us and whom we hate; I press the rivals down, I stride beyond them — driven away and expelled is the rival].
[You are the stride of Viṣṇu,] slayer of rivals, whetted by the waters, radiant with the power of Varuṇa. Along the waters do I stride wide; from the waters him — [we expel who hates us and whom we hate; I press the rivals down, I stride beyond them — driven away and expelled is the rival].
[You are the stride of Viṣṇu,] slayer of rivals, whetted by the Ṛc hymns, radiant with the power of the Sāman. Along the Ṛc hymns do I stride wide; from the Ṛc hymns him — [we expel who hates us and whom we hate; I press the rivals down, I stride beyond them — driven away and expelled is the rival].
[You are the stride of Viṣṇu,] slayer of rivals, whetted by the sacrifice, radiant with the power of brahman. Along the sacrifice do I stride wide; from the sacrifice him — [we expel who hates us and whom we hate; I press the rivals down, I stride beyond them — driven away and expelled is the rival].
[You are the stride of Viṣṇu,] slayer of rivals, whetted by the plants, radiant with the power of Soma. Along the plants do I stride wide; from the plants him — [we expel who hates us and whom we hate; I press the rivals down, I stride beyond them — driven away and expelled is the rival].
[You are the stride of Viṣṇu,] slayer of rivals, whetted by tillage, radiant with the power of the Puruṣa. Along the tillage do I stride wide; from the tillage him — [we expel who hates us and whom we hate; I press the rivals down, I stride beyond them — driven away and expelled is the rival].

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
You are the stride of Viṣṇu, slayer of rivals, whetted by the breath, radiant with the power of food. Along the breath do I stride wide; from the breath we utterly expel him who hates us and whom we hate.
I have reached the sun, I have reached the light; I have stood over all hostile armies and foes-without-gift. He who hates us and whom we hate — his breath and life-span I here wind off; I send this man to the lowest darkness.
I turn back following Sūrya's circuit; I turn back following the southern course. I circle back toward the luminous directions; I circle back toward the Seven Ṛṣis; I circle back toward brahman; I circle back toward the Brāhmaṇas. May they bestow wealth upon me; may they bestow upon me the brilliance of brahman.
O Lord of the Earth, whatever food of yours dwells distributed along the Earth — of that, O Lord of the Earth, O Prajāpati, do generously grant us a share. Him whom we hunt down, let us lay low with the slaying blow.
Into the open jaws of Parameṣṭhin we have thrust him with brahman's force. Death has fully overtaken him through the fangs of Vaiśvānara.
Let this oblation, the divine kindling-stick of surpassing strength, devour him. You are the bond of King Varuṇa — bind yonder one, the son of that woman, that scion of that lineage, in food and in breath.
Knowingly I hurl against him the four-pointed thunderbolt of the waters to cleave his skull. Let it shatter all his joints — may all the gods take cognisance of this for me.
O Agni, when we look upon you through your heat and fervent energy, may we be dear to the Renowned One — long-lived and of keen wisdom.
Verily, Virāj was born first here. When she was born, all things were afraid, thinking: 'This one alone will become all this; not we.'
She then stepped forth; she descended into the Dakṣiṇāgni. He who knows this becomes fit for sacrifice, a dweller in the abode.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
[She then stepped forth;] she descended into the Gārhapatya [fire]. [He who knows this] becomes a householder devoted to the household rites, a master of the house — [he who knows this].
[She then stepped forth;] she descended into the Āhavanīya [fire]. The gods come to his invocation of the gods; he becomes dear to the gods — [he who knows this].
[She then stepped forth;] she descended into the assembly hall. [Men] come to his assembly; he becomes a respected member of the assembly — [he who knows this].
[She then stepped forth;] she descended into the council. [Men] come to his council; he becomes a member of authority in the council — [he who knows this].
[She then stepped forth;] she descended into the deliberation. [Men] come to his deliberation; he becomes one worthy of being consulted — he who knows this.
[She then stepped forth;] she stood in the atmosphere striding fourfold. The gods and men said of her: 'This one knows that by which we both could live — let us call upon her.' They called upon her: 'Come, O Vigor; come, O Self-sufficiency; come, O Truth; come, O Bounty.' Of her, Agni was the calf, the Gāyatrī was the vessel over her, the cloud was the udder.
Of her, the Bṛhat and the Rathantara were the two teats, and the Yajñāyajñiya and the Vāmadevya were the two. The Rathantara — the gods milked the plants from it; the Bṛhat — they milked wide space; the Vāmadevya — the waters; the Yajñāyajñiya — the sacrifice.
These indeed are the wish-yielding teats of Virāj. He milks wish after wish from Virāj — he who knows this.
She went forth; she came to the forest-trees, the forest-trees smote her, and she became whole in a year. Therefore in a year even a felled tree of the forest grows again. They strike down the unloved rival of him who knows this.
She came to the Pitṛs, the Pitṛs smote her, and she became whole in a month. Therefore in a month they make offerings to the Pitṛs; one who does so becomes possessor of svadhā among the Pitṛs and knows well the path of the Pitṛyāṇa—he who knows this.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
She came to the gods, the gods smote her, and she became whole in a half-month. Therefore in a half-month they offer to the gods; one offers the Agnihotra and knows well the path of the Devayāna—he who knows this.
She came to human beings, human beings smote her, and she became whole that very day. Therefore on both days humans bring offerings; they bring them reverently into the house—he who knows this.
She went forth; she came to the Asuras. The Asuras called out to her: 'O Māyā, come!' Her calf was Virocana son of Prahrāda, and her pail was of iron. Dvimūrdhan the Ārtvijaḥ milked her; he milked forth Māyā. On that Māyā the Asuras subsist. He becomes one on whom others subsist—he who knows this.
She came to the Pitṛs. The Pitṛs called out to her: 'O Svadhā, come!' Her calf was Yama Vaivasvata, and her pail was of silver. Antaka son of Mṛtyu milked her; he milked forth Svadhā. On that Svadhā the Pitṛs subsist—he who knows this.
She came to human beings. Human beings called out to her: 'O Irāvatī, come!' Her calf was Manu Vaivasvata, and her pail was the earth. Pṛthu son of Vena milked her; he milked forth both ploughing and grain. On that ploughing and grain human beings subsist—he who knows this.
She came to the gods. The gods called out to her: 'O Ūrjā, come!' Her calf was Indra, and her pail was of wood. Savitṛ milked her; he milked forth Ūrjā. On that Ūrjā the gods subsist—he who knows this.
She came to the Seven Sages. The Seven Sages called out to her: 'O Brahmaṇvatī, come!' Her calf was Soma, and her pail was the metres. Bṛhaspati of the lineage of Āṅgiras milked her; he milked forth both brahman and tapas. On that brahman and tapas the Seven Sages subsist—he who knows this.
She came to the Gandharvas and Apsarasas. The Gandharvas and Apsarasas called out to her: 'O Puṇyagandhā, come!' Her calf was Citraratha son of Sūryavarcas, and her pail was a lotus leaf. Vasurucis son of Sūryavarcas milked her; he milked forth the holy fragrance. On that holy fragrance the Gandharvas and Apsarasas subsist—he who knows this.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
She came to the Puṇyajanas. The Puṇyajanas called out to her: 'O Tirodhā, come!' Her calf was Kubera Vaiśravaṇa, and her pail was of unbaked clay. Rajatanābhi the Kāberaka milked her; he milked forth invisibility. On that invisibility the Puṇyajanas subsist—he who knows this.
She went forth; she came to the Serpents. The Serpents called out to her: 'O Viṣavatī, come!' Her calf was Takṣaka of Vaiśāla, and her pail was a gourd vessel. Dhṛtarāṣṭra son of Airāvata milked her; he milked forth venom. On that venom the Serpents subsist. He becomes one on whom others subsist—he who knows this.
Therefore upon whomsoever one sprinkles with a gourd vessel, saying in the mind 'I strike you back,' let him strike that one back. What one strikes back is venom he strikes back; yet when one does not strike it back, the venom flows on after him. He slays the venom, the unloved rival of him—he who knows this.
Bind shut the mouths of those who scheme evil; hurl this thunderbolt upon the rivals. The first Śataudanā, given by Indra, slays rivals and clears the way for the sacrificer.
Let the altar-ground be your hide, let the sacrificial grass be your body-hair. This halter has seized you; let this pressing-stone dance upon you.
Let your tail-hairs be the sprinkling-waters; let your tongue lick the altar-grass, O inviolable one. Pure, having become fit for sacrifice, go to heaven, O Śataudanā.
He who cooks the Śataudanā with love fulfils his purpose; for his officiating priests, well pleased, all go each to his proper place.
O goddess, your slaughterers and those persons who are your cooks—all these will protect you; do not be afraid of them, O Śataudanā.
He ascends to heaven, to yonder triple heaven of the sky, making it resplendent with gold—he who gives the Śataudanā.
He attains fully those worlds in which the gods dwell, making an apūpa cake its navel—he who gives the Śataudanā.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The Vasus will guard you from the south, the Maruts from the north; the Ādityas will guard you from the west. Run beyond the Agniṣṭoma with the Atirātra.
The Gandharvas, the Apsarasas, O goddess, the Rudras, the Āṅgirasas will guard you. All these will protect you. Run beyond the Agniṣṭoma with the Atirātra.
The atmosphere, the sky, the earth, the Ādityas, the Maruts, the directions—all the worlds he attains—he who gives the Śataudanā.
She the auspicious one, sprinkling ghee, shall go as a goddess to the gods. O inviolable cow, do not injure the one who cooks thee; ascend to heaven, O thou of a hundred offerings.
Those Fathers who dwell in heaven, and those who abide in the atmosphere, and those here upon the earth — for them do thou yield at all times milk, and ghee, and honey.
Whatever is thy head, thy two horns, thy two ears, and thy two eyes — from these let the ones who milk thee yield to the giver curdled milk, ghee, and honey.
Whatever is thy mouth, thy tongue, thy teeth, and thy two jaws — [yield to the giver curdled milk, ghee, and honey].
Whatever is thy lung, thy heart, thy entrails together with the throat — [yield to the giver curdled milk, ghee, and honey].
Whatever is thy liver, thy kidneys, thy intestines, and thy lower bowels — [yield to the giver curdled milk, ghee, and honey].
Whatever is thy spleen, thy lower belly, thy two flanks, and thy abdomen — [yield to the giver curdled milk, ghee, and honey].
Whatever is thy marrow, thy bones, thy flesh, and thy blood — [yield to the giver curdled milk, ghee, and honey].
Whatever are thy two forelegs, thy two shoulders, thy two forearms, and thy hump — [yield to the giver curdled milk, ghee, and honey].
Whatever are thy shoulder-blades, thy neck, thy ribs, and thy side-bones — [yield to the giver curdled milk, ghee, and honey].

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Whatever are thy two thighs, thy two knee-joints, thy two haunches, and thy hindquarters — [yield to the giver curdled milk, ghee, and honey].
Whatever is thy tail, thy tail-hairs, thy udder, and thy teats — [yield to the giver curdled milk, ghee, and honey].
Whatever are thy shanks, thy pasterns, thy fetlock-joints, and thy hooves — [yield to the giver curdled milk, ghee, and honey].
Whatever is thy skin, O thou of a hundred offerings, whatever are thy hairs, O inviolable one — from these let those who milk thee yield to the giver curdled milk, ghee, and honey.
This teat of thine yields curdled milk, this one ghee, this one honey. May this teat of thine, O goddess, O thou of a hundred offerings, milk forth all desires.
May thy two flanks become the two sacrificial rice-cakes sprinkled over with ghee. Making those thy wings, O goddess, carry the giver to heaven.
Whatever grains and husks are in the mortar, in the pestle, in the hide, or in the winnowing fan — whatever Mātariśvan the wind has churned, may Agni the purifier make that a well-offered oblation.
The divine waters, sweet-flowing and dripping with ghee, I place severally into the hands of the Brāhmaṇas. With whatever desire I now sprinkle you, may that be granted to us; may we become lords of riches.
Prajāpati and Parameṣṭhin are the two horns; Indra is the head; Agni is the brow; Yama is the nape of the neck; King Soma is the brain. Truth is the right eye; Ṛta is the left ear; Prāṇa and Apāna are the two nostrils; Heaven is the upper jaw; Earth is the lower jaw.
Agni is the mouth; lightning is the tongue; the Maruts are the teeth; Pavamāna is the breath. The All is the throat of Vāyu; the heavenly world is Kṛṣṇadra; Vidharaṇī and Vikeśī are [its parts].
The Revatī stars are the neck; the Kṛttikā stars are the shoulders; the Gharma is the back-carrier; the hawk is the chest; the atmosphere is the Pājasya. Mitra and Varuṇa are the two shoulder-joints; Tvaṣṭṛ and Aryaman are the two forearms.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Mahādeva is the two forelegs; Bṛhaspati is the hump; the Bṛhatī metres are the spine-bones. The wives of the gods are the back-ridges; the Upasad rites are the ribs.
Indrāṇī is the hindquarters; Vāta is the tail; Pavamāna is the tail-hairs. Brahman and Kṣatra are the two haunches; Strength is the two thighs; Dhātṛ and Savitṛ are the two knee-joints.
The Gandharvas and the Apsarases are the shanks; Aditi is the pasterns; the hooves are [hers]. The mind is the heart; the liver is wisdom; jaundice is the bile; the sacred vow is the entrails.
Hunger is the flank; Irā is the lower belly; mountains are the spleen; divine beings are the lower bowels; humans are the intestines; the other beings are the contents of the stomach; Rakṣases are the blood. Anger is the two kidneys; fury is the two testicles; progeny is the phallus.
The ocean is the bladder; the river is the urinary canal; thunder is the udder; the lords of rain are the teats. All-pervading space is the hide; plants are the body-hairs; the lunar asterisms are the form.
The cloud is the fat; marrow is the final resting-place. He who knows thus becomes the foundation of prosperity, of offspring, and of cattle.
Indra stands to the east; Yama stands to the south; Dhātṛ stands to the west; Savitṛ stands to the north. King Soma, having reached the grasses, is Ānanda turned away. Being seen, he is in Mitra; being yoked, he is Vaiśvadeva; when yoked, Prajāpati; when unyoked, the All. This is verily the form of the cow. Cattle possessed of fair form attend upon him who knows thus.
Created by exertion and austerity, she rests sheltered in Brahman; enveloped by truth, clothed in splendour, encompassed by fame, girt round with svādhā, borne along by faith, guarded by consecration, established in sacrifice — the world is her final abode.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The metres are her form, the Aṅgirases her fervour, Brahman her path — this Brāhmaṇa is her sovereign lord. From that kṣatriya who seizes her — the cow of Brahman — and thereby despoils the Brāhmaṇa, sweet speech departs, heroic power departs, and auspicious prosperity departs.
This is she — the dreadful brahmin's cow, filled with the poison of sin, the sorcery-spell wound round a reed-bundle; in her dwell all cruelties and all deaths; in her dwell all terrors and all slayings of men.
She, the brahmin's cow, when she is taken from one who has wronged a brahmin, flies straight into the snare of Death; for she is wrath carrying a hundredfold slaughter — she is indeed the ruin of the brahmin-wronger.
Therefore the cow of the brahmins is not to be assailed by one who knows; she has Vaiśvānara as her breath upward, she is Mahādeva watching over her, she is the thunderbolt running, the missile tearing up with her hooves.
With a razor-edged wheel as she surveys, Death as she lows — the brahmin's cow, as she bellows, thunders down upon the brahmin-wronger.
The fierce god is she who swishes her tail — total loss as she shakes her ears — royal consumption as she urinates — wrath as she is milked — headache as the milk is drawn; when she rises up she is mutual strife — when her mouth is stopped she is the arrow-shot.
As she is struck she is affliction — as she is dragged away she is utter decline — as she swoops down she is the poison of evil — as she falls she is darkness fallen; following after, the brahmin's cow enslaves the breath-forces of the brahmin-wronger.
As she is cut up she is enmity — as she is apportioned from grandchildren onward she is the god-hurled weapon — as she is carried off, bewilderment is set in place and Nirṛti is established; as evil is heaped upon her, cruelty is placed upon her — sterility is implanted.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
As she is encircled she is the sacrificial heat — Vaiśvānara is wrapped all around her — as she is sent forth she is poison — as she is dispatched she is the fever-sickness; as she is turned about she is the uprooter of roots — destruction is turned all around.
As she is cooked she is evil-ripening — when fully cooked she is utter overthrow; as she is tended and stirred, she is the venomous serpent drawn forth, unconsciousness by her very smell.
As she is brought near she is non-being — when brought near she is complete destruction; as she is minced, she is Śarva in his wrath — when minced to pieces she is demon-slaughter minced.
As she is eaten she is affliction — when eaten she is utter dismemberment; eaten, the brahmacārin cuts the brahmin-wronger off from this world and from yonder world.
The kṛtyā strikes her blow; the meni is her curse; the valaga is the noose; she wanders without a horse, hemmed in on all sides. Having become the flesh-devouring fire, the brahman-cow, upon entering, devours the one who has wronged a brahman.
She cuts and severs the roots of all his limbs; she causes his father's kinsmen to perish, and his mother's kinsmen as well. The brahman-cow, when not returned by the kṣatriya, burns away all his relatives by marriage and all his kin.
She renders him homeless, without cattle, without progeny; he becomes unable to pass beyond and wastes away — the kṣatriya who thus takes the cow of a knowing brahman.
Soon indeed at the striking of him do vultures perform the ailava rite. The dishevelled ones dance around his burning place, beating their breasts with their hands, performing the evil ailava.
Wolves howl in his homesteads. Soon they ask of him: what was there once — where now is it, O father?
Cut, cut through, cut to pieces; burn down, burn utterly away. O Āṅgirasī, make subservient the brahman-wronger who seizes.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
For you are called the Vaiśvadevī, the kṛtyā enveloped in kūlbajā plants, burning and consuming utterly — the thunderbolt of the brahman.
Having become Death with a razor's edge, she pursues him. She takes away the radiance of those who conquer, along with the fruit of oblations and charitable gifts and their blessings.
Having taken what is won, you hand it over to the victorious in that other world. O Aghniyā, follow the path; be the curse of the brahman-wronger.
Become the meni, become the arrow; become the deadly poison of evil. O Aghniyā, smite off the head of the brahman-wronger who has committed transgression.
Let fire burn the silver set in motion by you, the evil deed of the god-scorner and the ungrateful one. Hack, hack through; cut, cut apart; slash, slash to pieces; tear, tear asunder; scorch, scorch completely; burn, burn utterly. O goddess Aghniyā, burn the brahman-wronger from the root throughout.
Whatever ill-fortune is clinging to your head, lodged in your hair, placed upon your forehead — let this Apāmārga, the universal healer, wipe that away.
Whatever ill-fortune is seated in your eyebrows, placed in your ears and eyes — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune is in your face and nostrils, in your speech and lips — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune is placed in your teeth, in your tongue, in your chin — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune is deposited in your mind and intention, in your vital breath — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune is spread through your jaws, in your throat and lungs — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune is in your shoulders and neck, in your vertebrae and spine — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune is in your forearms, in your shoulders and armpits — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Whatever ill-fortune is in your upper arms, along your elbows and wrists — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune is in your hands, along your palms and fingers — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune lodged in your back, placed in your haunches and buttocks — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune in your chest, placed in your flanks and breasts — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune in your heart, along the navel and the belly — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune in your spleen, or in the liver and the kidneys — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune in your bowels and intestines, placed in the belly — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune in your bladder, deposited in the vaniṣṭhau and the plāśau — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune in your pudendum, or in the seminal vesicles and testicles — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune in your hips, placed in the avacālūśa joints — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune in your posterior, placed in your thighs and knees — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune in your calves, placed in the shin-bones and heels — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune in your ankles, along the feet and toes — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune in your joints, in your flesh, bones, and marrow — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune, in whatever limb it has settled, or that is lodged in the hairs — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune in your dice-play, in the game of chance and gambling — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever ill-fortune in your cattle, placed in the field and in [loss through] thunderbolt — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
That ill-luck of yours born of fetus-slaying, and likewise your sonlessness — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever of yours has been fated by sitting with the Fathers, and likewise your [ill] destiny unfulfilled — [let Apāmārga wipe that away].
Whatever evil fortune is yours, and likewise your lack of livestock — let this Apāmārga, the all-healer, wipe all that away.
Whatever guilt toward the gods has accrued to those throat-deep, to those tormented by the serpent — let these waters carry that defilement away; let the hundred-streamed purifier purify me.
Bathe off all defilement and impurity; having deposited sin in dark garments, forsake adversity, Nirṛti, and the snares of death — come forward to the light of Sūrya, to Agni.
Rising up from the great ocean, being released from distress and from sin — may mind return to us, may life-force return to us; let not the Paṇis and Yātudhānas deceive me.
We wash off the defilement, the ill-spoken word from ourselves. Let brilliance be placed in me, let radiance be placed in me; let prāṇa and apāna not forsake me — may I attain full life-span.
Brahman, blazing, has risen up into the atmosphere and heaven; Brahman has shaken off death with amṛta; Brahman, overseer, is the direct witness of good deeds — may Brahman drive away from us impurity and darkness.
Westward-stretching, spread out, extended — we see them; that iron [net] of the Asuras, placed in the ocean, in the waters.
The tawny Suparṇa has climbed to heaven with his flame. O Jātavedas, those who seek to harm you as you fly up to heaven — strike them down with your blaze; fearless and mighty, mount heaven with your flame, O Sūrya.
The Asuras are iron-netted sorcerers, those who roam marked with iron fetters; I subject them to your consuming fire, O Jātavedas — go, O Vajra of a thousand edges, crushing my rivals.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The hot-drink offering, lord of the gods, proceeds, blazing with ṛta, beholding the immortal; golden-hued, divine Sūrya, the Gharma blazing with light traverses the ends of heaven with lightning.
The lightnings flash, flame-tongued, golden-hued, immortal, dwelling within the waters, within the ocean; the swift lightning of Rudra amid the thunder — may the weapon of that Vaiśvānara encircle and protect us.
Blazing with lightning, Agni goes to the heart, where the terrible tigers lurk in the waters; Rudra moves with the strides of Viṣṇu, thundering, driving back enemies and battling foes — may he make my quarters free of rivals.
Clothed in the waters, he comes together with the atmosphere and with heaven; the kindled, celestial, heat-bearing Agni — Vaiśvānara, O cool-formed one, bring calm; the eagle of the waters goes along the back of the sky.
Vaiśvānara traverses the ocean, bright, the Gharma blazing, shining with splendor; driving away enemies, burning my rivals, the wise Āditya has mounted the sky.
Vaiśvānara burns together the atmosphere and heaven; the divine fire, blazing, born of fervent heat. May they render service to him — they who press the soma; shining by sacred order (ṛta), he clothes himself in immortality as a garment.
The two awe-inspiring forms of him — the cold and the hot — gleam and do not rest. He goes about assuming many forms, robing himself in diverse shapes, concealing his bodies in secret, turning them away to remote places.
Upon the five-spoked wheel revolving, all the worlds mount together. Its axle, bearing the immense burden, grows hot; from of old it is never severed together with its hub.
Heated by the five, he burns in turn; they attend upon him of a thousand abodes. The seven bay mares draw thee, O Sūrya; Āditya, with Brahman, with the triple-twined mouth.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
He flashes apart, he flashes, and he flashes back — the immortal Gharma (heat-vessel) rising within the waters. The slayer of Vṛtra, the host of the bay ones, the bodies of Sūrya — unassailable.
The Gharma from behind and the Gharma from before — we set them against the iron-fanged foe who hates us. Vaiśvānara, robing himself in cold and in heat, let him smite all my rivals who bear enmity toward me.
He cooks the seasons by means of the seasons; the Gharma, the solitary hero of Brahman, purified, kindled with sacrificial fuel. The Brahmin sacrificer heats thee with sacred formula and with fiery splendour.
Brahman (the sacred power), born first, was taken together — that which is coming into being was not split apart and is not split. That which moves in the limbs speaks to the father; its veins are stretched out, spread wide — stretched indeed are they.
From the existent he bore away that which was unborn; he who begot it — he indeed is its sustainer. Prajāpati, coming to understanding with his creatures, holds the three lights — the immature one does not.
Prajāpati moves within the womb; being born, he is born manifold. The wise (vedhas) behold his footstep; upon him all the worlds are strung.
In whom gods, ancestors, and men are rested like spokes at the hub — thee, the flower of the waters, I ask: where is it deposited by māyā (creative power)?
Where the flower of the waters is placed, set exceedingly by māyā in a hidden place — he who would know that directly, he would know the great Brahman.
The jewel threaded on three (threads), set in place, the heaven-knower — upright, across-turned, may it enter, being aware. That virile one, generating from the man by sacred order, let him reach all the ends straightway.
May Āditya wholly burn through the entire night together with Jātavedas (fire). Mounting up to heaven above the fire, let him anoint me with life-span; may he unite me with vital lustre (varcas).

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The Gharma of a thousand (fires), kindled with sacrificial fuel — let it make the quarters of the sky free of rivals for me. Let Sūrya, Vaiśvānara, the tawny one, smite all my rivals.
The Gharma, made hot, let it utterly burn the rivals, those who hate me. Let Āditya, Sūrya rising, give over to (our keeping) the enemies who wage battle.
Vaiśvānara the bull, let him utterly burn the rivals, those who hate (me). The brilliant Āditya rising, Sūrya — let him crush and smite my adversaries.
The brilliant, fair-winged, tawny Brahman — the unfailing, shining light stretched out through heaven. The tawny fair-winged one, swift, ever ready to smite — let him strike down rivals with his great weapon.
The tawny fair-winged one, bringer of fair days, maker of fearlessness, of golden hue, hard to overcome, swift — Sūrya, Āditya, let him smite all my rivals with his rays.
Let him straightway encompass the great goal — the brilliant one rising, distributing day and night. Let Sūrya, Vaiśvānara burning, go against all my rivals.
"Rising today, O great Mitra" — thus (goes) the one (verse, cited by incipit).
You bear fiery splendour and austerities before your face; bliss, prosperity, and the standing-ground of greatness. Moving all around, you go toward glory from every side — unfailing, true is the fame raised aloft that is yours.
The fiery brahmacārin (student of sacred knowledge) moves through both worlds, the earth and heaven; in him the gods become of one mind. He upheld this earth and yonder heaven — let him by austerity sustain the teacher.
The teacher, initiating the brahmacārin, makes him an embryo within. Three nights he carries him in his belly; the gods come together to behold him when born. The ancestors, men, divine beings, and gandharvas — all of them follow after this brahmacārin.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
He nourishes by austerity all the gods — the thirty-three, the three hundred, the six thousand. This earth is (his) fuel-stick, heaven the second — and the atmosphere he fills with sacrificial fuel. The brahmacārin, fuel-laden, girded with the sacred cord, nourishes the worlds by toil and by austerity.
Born first of Brahman, the brahmacārin, robing himself in the Gharma (heat), stood supreme over austerity. From him was born the brahmaṇa, the eldest Brahman — and all the gods together with immortality.
The brahmacārin, kindled with sacrificial fuel, wearing a black antelope skin, consecrated (dīkṣita), long-bearded — he goes straightway from the eastern to the western ocean, grasping the worlds, roaming about repeatedly.
The brahmacārin generating Brahman, the waters, the world, Prajāpati, Parameṣṭhin, and Virāj — having become an embryo in the womb of immortality, having become Indra, he crushed the asuras.
The brahmacārin, first of all, bore alms from this earth and from heaven. They who make Brahman and tend the (sacred fire) with fuel — upon those two all the worlds are strung.
The teacher fashioned the two firmaments — the two vast, deep (spaces) — the earth and the heaven. The brahmacārin guards both of them with austerity; upon those two the gods rejoice together in exhilaration.
One (treasure) is this side, another is beyond — two hidden hoards set in the hidden place of the brahmaṇa. The brahmacārin guards both of them with austerity; the one who knows makes that Brahman entire and sole.
One fire is on this side, below the back of heaven; another is here, above the earth — the two meet in the midspace between the two worlds. Upon them the firm rays are arrayed; the brahmacārī ascends to them by means of his austerity.
Ruddy and dark-necked, great-membered, roaring — he bore his seed along upon the earth. The brahmacārī pours seed upon her ridge; by that the four quarters live upon the earth.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Parjanya, Mṛtyu, Varuṇa, Soma, the herbs, and the milk — these were the mighty ones, the vigorous beings; by them they brought forth this heavenly light.
In Agni, in Sūrya, in the moon, in Mātariśvan, in the waters — the brahmacārī places the fuel-offering. Their flames move separately in the cloud; their clarified butter is Man, their horse is the rain.
He renders the clarified butter pure at home; having become the ācārya, whatever Varuṇa desired from Prajāpati — that the brahmacārī delivered; Mitra from his own self bestowed it.
The ācārya is the brahmacārī; the brahmacārī is Prajāpati. Prajāpati reigns supreme; Virāj became Indra, the sovereign.
By brahmacarya and austerity the king protects his realm. By brahmacarya the ācārya seeks out the brahmacārī.
By brahmacarya a maiden wins a young husband. The draft-ox, by brahmacarya, and the horse strive to obtain their fodder.
By brahmacarya and austerity the gods drove away Death. Indra indeed by brahmacarya brought forth the immortal heavenly light.
The herbs, what has been and what shall be, day and night, the forest trees, the year together with its seasons — these were born as brahmacārīs.
The cattle of the earth and of the sky, those of the forest and those of the village, and those without wings and those winged — these too were born as brahmacārīs.
All beings of Prajāpati, each separately, bear the vital breaths within themselves. Brahman, sustained in the brahmacārī, protects all of them.
The brahmacārī bears the blazing brahman; in him all the gods have assembled together. He, the snātaka — tawny and ruddy-brown — shines brilliantly upon the earth.
This, pressed out by the gods, unascended, moves resplendently. In him are all cattle, in him the sacrifices, in him food together with the divine powers.
Generating prāṇa and apāna, then vyāna, generating sight and hearing, O brahman, and intelligence — set in us the highest speech and glory.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Food, seed, blood, and the womb — shaping these, the brahmacārī stood performing austerity upon the back of the waters, glowing with heat in the ocean.
Truth, the vast, cosmic order fierce, consecration, austerity, sacred knowledge, and sacrifice — these uphold the Earth. She, the mistress of what has been and what shall be, may Earth make a wide world for us, unobstructed, in the midst of humankind.
She who bears the upland slopes, the plains, and the level stretches, the many-powered herbs — may Earth spread wide for us, may she prosper us.
She in whom the ocean, the river, and the waters dwell; she in whom the gods discovered the untruth; she who sustains in manifold ways the living breath that stirs — may that Earth bestow upon us cattle, horses, and food.
She upon whom the ancestors of old moved about; she upon whom the gods turned back the asuras; she in whom all this living, stirring universe dwells — may that Earth grant us the first draft of life.
She in whom the four directions of Earth exist; she in whom food and cultivated peoples arose — the station of cattle, horses, and birds — may Earth grant us fortune and vital radiance.
The all-sustaining, wealth-holding, steady foundation, golden-breasted resting place of the world — bearing Vaiśvānara, the universal fire, Earth, whose bull is Indra, may she bestow wealth upon us.
She on whom the gathering waters flow in their rounds, pouring day and night without ceasing — may that Earth, abundant-streamed, milk nourishment for us, and also sprinkle us with vital radiance.
She whom the gods guard, ever-wakeful, at all times, the Earth, the wide one, without negligence — may she milk sweet, dear nourishment for us, and also sprinkle us with vital radiance.
She who was the primordial waters above the ocean; whom the wise have traced through their visionary powers; she whose heart, in the highest sky, is wrapped in truth, the immortal essence of Earth — may that Earth place brilliance and strength in my realm for me.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
She whom the two Aśvins measured out, upon whom Viṣṇu strode; she whom Indra, lord of power, made enemy-free for himself — may that Earth release milk for us as a mother for her son.
Your hills, your mountains, your snow-bearing ranges, your forests, O Earth — may it be gentle for us. I stand upon the tawny, black, reddish, all-formed, firm Earth, protected by Indra — unconquered, unslain, unwounded, I take my stand upon the Earth.
What is your center, O Earth, what is your navel, and those bodily energies that have arisen from you — set us there, purify us.
Earth is the mother, I am the son of Earth; Parjanya is the father — may he fill us with nourishment.
She on whose surface they set up the altar, on whom the all-skilled ones spread out the sacrifice; she on whose surface the wooden stakes are measured out, and the bright oblations ascend before — may that growing Earth increase us.
Whoever hates us, O Earth, whoever attacks us, whoever with his mind intends to slay us — deliver that one to us, O Earth, as you have done in former times.
Born from you, mortals move about on you; you sustain the two-footed and the four-footed. In you, O Earth, are these five races of humans, for whom the rising sun stretches out the immortal light with its rays to mortal beings.
May all those offspring be milked for us completely; O Earth, place the sweetness of speech in me.
The mother of all, of herbs, the firm Earth, the wide one, held firm by cosmic law — may we ever walk in her, benign and gentle, all our days.
Great is your assembly place; you have become great; great is the speed, your trembling, your quaking. Great Indra guards you with his might — O Earth, make us glorious in sight, as though shining with gold.
Fire is in the Earth, fire is in the herbs; the waters carry fire, fire is in the stones. Fire is within human beings; fires are in cattle and horses.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Fire blazes from the sky; from divine Fire comes the broad atmosphere. Mortals kindle Fire, the carrier of oblations, the lover of clarified butter.
Earth, the abode of fire, dark-kneed — may she not make me shrunken, wasted, or without brilliance. On the Earth they pour out the sacrifice, the duly prepared oblation, for the gods. On the Earth mortals live, sustained by food according to their nature. May that Earth grant us breath and long life; may Earth not make us bitten by old age.
That fragrance of yours, O Earth, which has arisen, which the herbs carry, which the waters carry, which the gandharvas and apsarases have shared, which befits a cow and a horse — with that make us fragrant; let no one hate us.
That fragrance of yours which entered the lotus, which was gathered at the wedding of Sūryā — the immortals, O Earth, took the fragrance first. With that make us fragrant; let no one hate us.
That lustre and splendor of yours, O Earth, which is in men and in women, which is in brides and in bridegrooms, which is in cattle and horses, in wild beasts, and in elephants — that vital radiance which is in a maiden, O Earth — with that unite us; let no one hate us.
Rock, Earth, stone, sand — the Earth that has been gathered together and held firm; she on whose surface the forest trees stand firm forever — to that golden-breasted, steadily held Earth we address our words.
Rising, sitting, standing, walking about — may we not stumble upon the Earth with our right and left feet.
I address the wide Earth, the patient Earth, the ground swelling with sacred power, bearing vigor, nourishment, and a share of food — upon you, O Earth, upon clarified butter, I take my seat.
May pure waters flow over my body; whoever my foe is in what is not dear to me, him I lay low. With the purifying strainer I purify the Earth.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Bearing treasures in many hidden places — gems, gold — may Earth bestow wealth on us. The goddess, wealth-giving, graciously bestowing, of good mind, may she grant us riches.
O Earth, may your eastern directions, your northern ones, those below you and those behind — may they all be pleasant for me as I travel; may I not fall in the world wherein I take my dwelling.
Push me not from behind, push me not from the front — O Earth, grant me well-being and breadth; drive away slaughter; let those who lie in ambush not find me.
As far as I look upon you, O Earth, with the shining sun, so long may my sight not be extinguished — year after year, ever higher.
Whatever I dig from you, O Earth, as a medicinal herb — may that grow back again; may I not pierce your vital parts, O one whom many search; may I not wound your heart.
When lying down I turn upon my right or my left side, O Earth; when we stretch out on our backs, lying facing you with our spines — do not harm us then, O Earth, you who bestow healing on all things.
Summer is yours, O Earth, and the rains, autumn, early winter, the cold season, and spring — your seasons are ordained year by year; may Earth with day and night yield nourishment to us.
She who drives away the serpent and searches out all things, in whom the fires dwell within the waters — she who drives off the Dasyus who scoff at the gods, Earth who chose Indra as Vṛtra did not choose him, bearing him up for the mighty, the virile bull — may he point us toward the wealth from the Earth that we desire.
May Bhaga set things in motion; may Indra go as the leader of the herd; she upon whom stand the sacrificial hall and the offering-shed, upon whom the post is fixed, upon whom the brahmins chant with Ṛgvedic hymns, those who know the Yajurveda with Sāman, upon whom the ritual priests are yoked to press soma for Indra to drink — may that Earth, well-disposed, place us graciously on the southern side at the sacrifice.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
She upon whom the ancient world-making seers sang forth the cows, the seven wise ones together through sacrifice, ascetic rite, and the extended soma session — may she bestow on us cattle of every kind; may Savitṛ grant me long life.
She upon whom are food, rice, and barley, upon whom these five peoples dwell — to Earth, whose lord is Parjanya, let there be homage; let rain increase.
She upon whom mortals, the people of the village settlements, sing and dance; upon whom the battle-cry is raised, upon whom the war-drum sounds — may that Earth drive away our rivals; may she bring low the one who hates us.
She upon whom the divine-built cities stand, upon whose field they display their power — may Prajāpati make this Earth, who bears all creatures in her womb, delightful for us in every direction.
Earth bearing in many ways a people of diverse speech and diverse customs, each as if at home — like a steady cow that does not kick, may she yield us a thousand streams of wealth.
Whatever serpent, scorpion, sharp-fanged, frost-roused, buzzing worm lies in a crevice — the worm that stirs in the swampy ground in the rainy season, O Earth — may that crawler not creep upon us; and whatever is auspicious in it, with that be gracious to us.
Your roads that lead people in many directions, the track of the chariot, and the paths along which the mind travels — upon which both the good and the wicked walk — may we conquer on that path, free from foes, free from thieves.
Bearing the sluggish (or the soft?), heavy-bearing, enduring the dissolution of both good and evil — Earth, in accord with the boar, opens herself wide for the wild boar.
Your forest-dwelling animals, the beasts set loose in the woods, lions and tigers that roam man-eating — O Earth, drive away from here the hyena, the wolf, the evil omen, the she-bear, and the demon.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Gandharvas and Apsarases, those who wander about, the kimīdins — Piśācas, all the Rakṣasas — O Earth, drive all of them away from us.
She to whom winged two-footed creatures fly — swans, eagles, birds, and fowl; upon whom the wind, Mātariśvan, moves, raising dust-clouds and shaking the trees; the flame that blows along the forward and the inward current of the wind — she upon whom the black and the red are gathered together, upon whom day and night are ordained, spread out over the Earth.
Earth, enveloped and re-enveloped by the rain — may she sustain us with blessing in each beloved dwelling-place and resting-place.
Sky and Earth — this expanse — and the midspace have given me room; Fire, the Sun, the Waters, and all the gods together have bestowed wisdom upon me.
I am the prevailing one, named the Higher, here on Earth; I am the overpowerer, the all-conqueror, ever victorious in every direction.
O goddess, when you first spread out there in front, sent forth by the gods, you pervaded greatness — well-being entered into you at that very moment; you arranged the four directions.
In the villages, in the wildernesses, in the assembly halls that are upon the Earth — among them, O goddess Earth, may I rise up with honey-sweet speech.
What I speak, may I speak it sweetly; what I see, may the soma-pressers purify me; I am lustrous, I am impelled — those whom I strike down are the agitators.
Like a horse she has milked the dust — she scattered that people who oppressed the Earth when she was born; the gracious one, guardian of the world, embracing the forest trees and the herbs.
Peaceful, fragrant, pleasant, her udder filled with sweet drink, milk-laden — may Earth speak over us; may the Earth speak together with her milk.
O Mother Earth, set me down well-established in blessing; you who are in accord with Heaven — set me in splendor, in prosperity.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
She whom Viśvakarmā sought out with an oblation, in whom the fires dwell within the waters — the vessel of enjoyment was laid hidden in a secret place; it became manifest with its riches, possessed of motherly powers.
You are the scattering-ground of peoples, Aditi, yielding all desires, of all forms; whatever is deficient in you, Prajāpati, in accord with his creatures, fills that up for you.
In which limb does his austerity abide? In which limb is his cosmic order established? Where do his vow and his faith stand? In which limb is his truth firmly founded?
Where is the sacred power, where do the waters stand? In which limb are the directions established? Along which limb do day and night, in mutual accord, move together as one?
In which limb does his earth stand? In which limb does the atmosphere stand? In which limb is heaven set in place? In which limb stands what is beyond the sky?
From which limb does his fire blaze? From which limb does Mātariśvan blow? From which limb does the moon measure out, measuring the great limb of the Pillar?
Striving to reach where does fire blaze upward? Striving to reach where does Mātariśvan blow? Where do the encompassing forces approach in their striving? Tell us that Pillar — which one precisely is it?
Striving to reach where do the two young women of different forms, day and night, run in mutual accord? Where do the waters approach in their striving? — [that Pillar, tell us which one precisely it is].
Where do the fortnights go? Where do the months go, in accord together with the year? Where the seasons go, where the seasonal moments go — [that Pillar, tell us which one precisely it is].
He upon whose branches Prajāpati upheld all the worlds — tell us that Pillar, which one precisely is it?
What is the highest, what is the lowest, and what is the middle, all-formed — which Prajāpati created — how far did the Pillar enter there? What did not enter it, where did that come to be?

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
How far did the Pillar enter into what has come to be? How much of what is yet to be lies latent within it? The one limb that it made thousandfold — how far did the Pillar enter there?
Where the worlds and the treasuries are, where people know the sacred power to be, where non-being and being are within — tell us that Pillar, which one precisely is it?
Where austerity, having gone forth beyond, holds up the higher cosmic order; where vow and faith, sacred power and the waters are gathered together — [that Pillar, tell us which one precisely it is].
In which earth, atmosphere, and heaven are set aloft; where fire, the moon, the sun, and wind stand fixed in place — [that Pillar, tell us which one precisely it is].
He in whose limb all thirty-three gods are gathered together — [that Pillar, tell us which one precisely it is].
Where the seers who brought things into being, the Ṛc verses, the Sāman, the Yajus, and the great earth — the solitary seer in whom they are all fixed — [that Pillar, tell us which one precisely it is].
Whose four directions stand as arteries stretched to their reach; in whom sacrifice has gone forth beyond — [that Pillar, tell us which one precisely it is].
Where immortality and death and the Person are gathered together; whose arteries are the ocean — tell us that Pillar, which one precisely is it?
Those who know the sacred power in the Person, they truly know the Pillar. He who knows Parameṣṭhin, and he who knows Prajāpati — those who know the eldest Brahman, they truly know the Pillar.
Whose head is Vaiśvānara, whose eyes the Aṅgirases became; whose limbs are the demonic forces — tell us that Pillar, which one precisely is it?
Whose mouth they call the sacred word, and whose tongue the honey-whip; whose udder they call the Virāj — [that Pillar, tell us which one precisely it is].

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
From whom they carved the Ṛc verses, from whom they scraped out the Yajus; whose body-hairs are the metres — tell us that Pillar, which one precisely is it?
People know the branch of non-being as if it were the highest support; yet those of lesser insight who worship his branch consider it to be being.
Where the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus are gathered together — tell us that Pillar, which one precisely is it?
Whose treasure the thirty-three gods always guard — who today knows that treasure which the gods protect?
Where the gods who know the sacred power worship the eldest Brahman — he who truly knows that Brahman, the knowers of Brahman know him.
Those gods named the Bṛhant ones were born from non-being; that one limb of the Pillar, further-knowing people call non-being.
Where the Pillar, bringing forth, set the ancient tradition in motion — that one limb of the Pillar those who follow the ancient way truly know.
Where the thirty-three gods took their portions as limbs and body-parts — those very thirty-three gods certain knowers of the sacred power truly know.
People know the Golden Embryo as the supreme, as the unexcellable risen one; the Pillar poured out that golden light in the beginning, within the world.
In the Pillar are the worlds; in the Pillar is austerity; upon the Pillar is cosmic order established. We know you, the Pillar, directly — in Indra all is gathered together.
In Indra are the worlds, in Indra is heat, in Indra is cosmic order established. We know you as Indra directly — in the Skambha all is gathered together.
I call out name by name, before the sun, before the dawn. That which first came into being — together with it, sovereignty departed; beyond that there is no being whatsoever.
He whose measure is the earth, whose belly is the atmosphere — who made heaven his head — to that greatest Brahman, homage.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
He whose eye is the sun and whose moon is ever renewed — who made fire his mouth — to that greatest Brahman, homage.
He whose in-breath and out-breath is the wind, whose eyes became the Aṅgirases — who made the directions his cognizing faculty — to that greatest Brahman, homage.
He who was born from toil and austerity and pervaded all the worlds — who made Soma his alone — to that greatest Brahman, homage.
The Skambha upheld the earth and yonder heaven; the Skambha upheld the vast atmosphere. The Skambha upheld the six broad directions; the Skambha entered into this entire world of beings.
Why does the wind never cease? Why does the mind not rest? Why do the waters, ever seeking truth, keep moving on forever?
A great Yakṣa in the midst of the world, suffused with austerity upon the surface of the waters — upon it all the gods whatsoever take their refuge, like branches around the trunk of a tree.
He to whom with both hands and both feet, with voice, with hearing, with sight — to whom the gods ever offer tribute, the bounded to the boundless — tell me of that Skambha: who indeed is he?
From him darkness has been struck away; he has turned back from evil. All three lights that exist in Prajāpati — all are in him.
He who knows the golden reed standing in the waters — that one is truly the hidden Prajāpati.
No one surpasses Prajāpati, no one surpasses Parameṣṭhin. And yet there too our attention was turned, where the eldest passed beyond the beyond.
That truly exists beyond the earth; that truly exists beyond the sky. The worlds are strung upon it, and upon it these creatures are woven.
You who lick inside the pot, O ill-looking seeker of misplaced things — O Uruṇḍa, O Abhicaṅkrama, O Vakmaka, O Bastavāsini — we know all your names together, O she-demons. As many as are born among you, so many shall perish from here, O Sadānvāḥ.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Karṇa, Dṛṣadrathāmahā, Urukī, Keśinī, Kraku, Khaḍurī, Ambarīṣyā — we destroy these Sadānvāḥ she-demons.
Paṇḍugirā, Phāladatī, she who swallows without proper incantation — all of you we declare harmful; perish from here, O Sadānvāḥ.
Those she-demons who devour one who is lying down, who seek by night the sick man, and who lick from the mouth and hand of a sleeping person — accustomed to gnawing with their teeth — those we drive away from here.
The Sadānvāḥ she-demons who come flying and scattering, smelling of goat — I will pierce them with the Bhaṇvā sword, as a bull with sharp horns.
O Sadānvāḥ, O progeny of Sādānvī — both women and men together. With strength, powerfully, with might, I crush and smite the Rakṣasas.
The four-fanged ones, the jar-testicled ones, the long-haired ones, the blood-faced ones, those smelling of bottle-gourd, the rats — ill-named ones, we destroy you.
Born in the thicket, upon the tender one who weeps and wails from you — all of you ill-named ones together with your offspring, we destroy, O Sadānvāḥ.
Those whose offspring cry out within the clefts, and who blaze in the forest, who lie down upon the trees — [the remainder of the verse is lost in the manuscript].
Those who roam when storm-clouds rise, along with rain and lightning, who quickly seek out dwellings — all of you ill-named ones together with your offspring, we destroy, O Sadānvāḥ.
Those [demon-women] who arise from grain, from a field that has been sown, from what has been threshed — the fierce ones that attack what has been done, let those sadānvāḥ perish from here.
Those [women-demons] who take human form, who always have an evil stench, ever rough, with scattered feet — drive them away with the thunderbolt, expel them, O lord of Śacī!
Rise up! Run away! There is no shelter for you here. Indra will shatter together all your embryos and eggs at once.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Indra, strike down the thick-shelled one; crush the ill-fated kuha; the greed-demon, the one reeking of dung-smoke — we destroy these sadānvāḥ.
Why do they brew the naked-caller and the goat-snatcher who slays? The sharp-prodding viṭiṭiṅga-demons — we destroy those sadānvāḥ.
You bhaṇva-sadānvā demons subdue whose brew? Make the broth bitter! And when you are sated with the liquor — then you urinate out the surā.
After drinking of her [brew], one vomits and then lies down with a splitting head-pain. Those that corrupt the shared meal — we destroy those sadānvāḥ.
Let the foul-smelling dung-smoke demons go quickly to the trees! And let the evil-hearted arāyī-goblins stroke the house [to their ruin].
Among those [demons]: the solitary lurker, the bent-horned one, the forest-screamer, the sole laugher, the chattering one — all your names together, O bhaṇvā-demons, we know them. As many as have been born among you, let that many perish from here, O sadānvāḥ.
I drive forward the herb endowed with power, this victorious [plant] that overcomes poison, the herb that slays the sadānvāḥ — we speak it forth for victory.
O ill-seen one, terrible-eyed, naked bhaṇvā, sadānvā — the rushing, blazing, pure fire [is here] — what do you want here, arāyī? Do not come near my smoke! I press you down, O sadānvā.
The solitary heron-like one, the solitary digger — what do they seek, lurking by the fire? The ill-named arāyī-demons that wander at night seeking women in childbed — we drive those away from here.
The boaster, the fire-croucher, the dancing one full of restless curiosity, the granary-haunter, the chariot-breaker, the three-humped ones born from the threshing floor — we drive those away from here.
Those disheveled, maddened, broad-chested, terrible-eyed ones — some sit as if stretching out the heads of others, O sadānvā-demons. O Bṛhaspati, hurl their embryos far away!

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
Those whose odor of many forms circles a person on the path — let Agni Jātavedas overpower and drive away those sadānvāḥ from here.
Those who wish to devour a person being cremated, [who prey upon] the vacant [body] on the fire — you are called bhaṇvā niṣkuṣṭā ('the winnowed one'); we drive those sadānvāḥ away from here with the tip of the fist.
Those accustomed to the fire-pit who eat dry ash, like mares and she-asses — we destroy those sadānvāḥ.
Those sadānvāḥ who devour fetuses one by one at every morśa, who are accustomed to the body of a woman like red cows [attached to their spot] — we drive those away from here.
Those sadānvāḥ who arise from the ancestral realm, born of Indra, coming to us — we send those back again, as if returning a load that was brought.
Eaters of the raw, eaters of the cruel, eaters of what smells of no fire — eat that corpse carried off to the beyond, O sadānvāḥ! A bare corpse is your proper fare; what indeed do you seek in houses?
Those sadānvāḥ who are girls, who are old women, who are young women — let all go as kurūṭinī-demons, as the cowless outcast clan; let the arāyī-goblin creep away in awe from here.
Let Rudra loose against them his fury that slays wayfarers; let the archer smite them with lightning and the faultless thunderbolt. O Śakra, do not spare them; O Indra, shatter the bhaṇvā-demons!
Those gluttonous ones who devour boys — some — and old men — let Indra the Vṛtra-slayer destroy them, the god who repels all demons from all sides.
Those who are slave-women of the asuras and those made [to harm] humans as well — let both kinds go far away, beyond the distance of ninety [river-crossings] by boat.
Those whose din when gathered sounds like the growling of wolves — those that offer pracaṅkaśā ['the harsh snatcher'] as a gift-in-return — we destroy those sadānvāḥ.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
The yakṣa-spirits that are stirred up at evening from wherever they station themselves to roam the night — let Agni, overpowering them all, repel those demons from all sides.
Those ṛkṣīkā-demons, the egg-laying kalīlā-ones, the pulīkā-beings born in the waters — one guardian alone knows their origin. Those sadānvāḥ who have been born — we drive them away from here.
The heavy-shadowed one, the one borne upward, the child-devourer, the echo-maker, the over-milker, the wanderer, the cotton-tufted one — all these granddaughters of Caṇḍa among the sadānvāḥ we destroy.
The loudly speaking one, the name-caller, the thundering one, the claw-footed one, the protruding-toothed one, the noseless one — we destroy these sadānvāḥ.
The incessant babbler, the unintelligible mutterer, the disheveled one, the blabbering one, the roaming one, the arāyī, the one that makes the voice tremble — we destroy these sadānvāḥ.
He should simply say "I give," and then accompany her; the cow given to the Brahmins who ask for her — that act yields offspring and progeny.
He pays with his offspring and wastes away his cattle — he who refuses to give the cow of the gods to those sages who ask for her.
By the deformed cow his bones crumble; by the lame cow he is ground down at the joint; by the mutilated cow his houses burn; by the one-eyed cow his property is lost.
From the standing-place of the red-spotted one, the dog finds the cow-owner — such is the covenant of the vaśā cow; for she is truly called the hard-to-deceive.
He who clips her ears is cut off among the gods; he thinks he is merely making a mark, but he diminishes his own fortune.
From the place where her hooves stand, he obtains the disease called viklindu; the limbs of one who sniffs her from the front crumble.
When a crow truly defiled the hair of the vaśā cow while she was in her owner's keeping, from that act the colts die and the wolf, the killer, takes the calves.

title: Atharvaveda (Paippalāda)
text:
If someone cuts her tail-hairs for his own enjoyment, from that act the young boys die and disease strikes through the limbs.
If a slave woman gathers her dung for use as fuel, from that a misbegotten child is born; therefore one should keep away from this transgression.
At birth the vaśā cow is born together with the gods and Brahmins; therefore she must be given to the Brahmins — that, they say, is the protection of one's own welfare.
The vaśā cow, made by the gods, belongs to those who come to her as petitioners; what they called "robbing the Brahmins" is what he does who dishonors her.
